shown (issue 14), as\n// in diff tools and Compiler Explorer:\n//\n// - every group of matched lines has a background colour of a cycling\n//   palette, the same in both editors, and a bar of that colour beside its\n//   line numbers;\n// - the group under the cursor (in either editor) is coloured stronger;\n// - a strip between the editors joins the lines of each group on the left\n//   to its lines on the right.\n//\n// The colours are CSS classes (styles.css: map-line, map-c0 … map-c5,\n// map-active). Nothing here needs Monaco: editor-sync.js gives the\n// decorations to the editors and the paths to the strip.\n\n// Monaco decorations for one side (0 the source, 1 the target) of a link\n// (line-map.js); `active` is the group under the cursor, if any.\nexport function mappingDecorations(link, side, active, lineCount = Infinity) {\n  const decorations = [];\n  for (const group of link.groups) {\n    const colour = `map-c${group.colour}`;\n    const strong = group === active ? ' map-active' : '';\n    for (const line of group.lines[side]) {\n      if (line >= lineCount) {\n        continue;\n      }\n      decorations.push({\n        range: {\n          startLineNumber: line + 1,\n          startColumn: 1,\n          endLineNumber: line + 1,\n          endColumn: 1,\n        },\n        options: {\n          isWholeLine: true,\n          className: `map-line ${colour}${strong}`,\n          linesDecorationsClassName: `map-gutter ${colour}${strong}`,\n        },\n      });\n    }\n  }\n  return decorations;\n}\n\n// The lines of a group on one side that are next to each other.\nfunction runs(lines) {\n  const all = [];\n  for (const line of lines) {\n    const last = all.at(-1);\n    if (last && line === last[1] + 1) {\n      last[1] = line;\n    } else {\n      all.push([line, line]);\n    }\n  }\n  return all;\n}\n\n// The shapes of the strip between the editors, `width` wide. `span(side,\n// first, last)` gives where lines first … last of a side are in the strip,\n// as { top, bottom } clipped to the editor, or undefined when they cannot\n// be seen. A group of lines on both sides is one band per run of lines.\nexport function connectorPaths(link, span, width, active) {\n  const middle = width / 2;\n  const paths = [];\n  for (const group of link.groups) {\n    const [left, right] = group.lines.map(runs);\n    const count = Math.max(left.length, right.length);\n    for (let at = 0; at < count; at += 1) {\n      const from = left[Math.min(at, left.length - 1)];\n      const to = right[Math.min(at, right.length - 1)];\n      const a = span(0, ...from);\n      const b = span(1, ...to);\n      if (!a || !b) {\n        continue;\n      }\n      paths.push({\n        colour: group.colour,\n        active: group === active,\n        d: [\n          `M0 ${a.top}`,\n          `C${middle} ${a.top} ${middle} ${b.top} ${width} ${b.top}`,\n          `L${width} ${b.bottom}`,\n          `C${middle} ${b.bottom} ${middle} ${a.bottom} 0 ${a.bottom}`,\n          'Z',\n        ].join(' '),\n      });\n    }\n  }\n  return paths;\n}\n# 15: CST by default, linked Monaco editors, comment translation, nested grammars, machine dialects and language versions\n\n## Summary\n\nFixes #14\n\nThis PR addresses issue 14 and the requirements of earlier issues and pull requests that had not been delivered. Every change is made in both JavaScript and Rust, and the two command lines print byte-identical output. The full case study is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-14/`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/tree/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14):\n\n- `README.md`: timeline, the issue's requirements R1–R24, root causes and alternatives;\n- `previous-requirements.md`: every earlier requirement with its status;\n- `prior-art.md` and `architecture.md`;\n- `requirements.lino`: CI fails while any requirement is neither done nor reported as blocked with a reason.\n\n### Issue 14 requirements\n\n- **A concrete syntax tree (CST) by default.** Whitespace and blank lines now survive a translation. The layout pass (`js/src/translation/layout.js`, `rust/src/layout.rs`) aligns the tokens of the output with those of the source and returns a `lineMap`. `--layout target` restores the emitter's own formatting.\n  - `main`: `console.log( \"Hello World!\");` → `console.log(\"Hello World!\");`\n  - this branch: `console.log( \"Hello World!\");` → `console.log( \"Hello World!\");`\n- **Monaco by default, with linked editors.**\n  - Folding regions now work for every language.\n  - Folding, selection, the cursor and scrolling are shared by both editors. Scrolling is mapped block by block, so blocks of different sizes stay aligned.\n  - Lines that map to each other get matching colours, as in Compiler Explorer.\n- **Comment and identifier language selectors on both sides.** The option checkboxes are now below the editors.\n- **Comments are translated.** A shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`) is used both to detect a comment's language and to translate it.\n  - `// Привет мир` → `// Hello world`.\n  - «Привет» is now detected as Russian.\n  - «Как хорошо покакать?» translates to \"How good to poop?\" (free prose translation).\n- **Deeper grammars.**\n  - Prose reads as `Prose > Sentence > Word`, with concepts and parts of speech.\n  - Comments and strings are read with their own grammars (code in prose, prose in code). Long texts are stored once and referred to by id. Use `--shallow` for the plain tree.\n- **A more general meta language.** `print` is a call to the library function `print-line`.\n- **Assembly and intermediate languages.** NASM, GNU as, ARM64, LLVM IR, WebAssembly text, CIL and JVM bytecode are written and read back.\n- **Language versions.** `javascript@es5`, `php@5`, `csharp@5`, `python@2`, `python@3.5`, `lua@5.1`, `java@1.4`, `swift@1` and `scala@2.9` are available. `registerLanguageVersion` adds a version of your own.\n- **More tasks and corpora.**\n  - 22 Rosetta Code tasks go through all 33 programming languages and the 7 machine targets.\n  - 33 of the 34 programs of the Hello World Collection are read.\n  - `check-equivalence` checks that a translation does what its source does.\n- **Debugging and research.**\n  - `--trace` prints the tree after every stage, and the web app logs translations and editor-sync events with `?debug`.\n  - formal-ai was tried on six tasks; its failures are reported as link-assistant/formal-ai#1641 and link-assistant/formal-ai#1642.\n\n### Screenshots\n\nLine mapping in the linked Monaco editors:\n\n![mapping](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-mapping.png?raw=true)\n\nComment and identifier language selectors on both sides:\n\n![selectors](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-selectors.png?raw=true)\n\n![style](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-style.png?raw=true)\n\n### Tests\n\n- JavaScript: `npm test` passes 1823 tests, with 1 skipped (shellcheck is not on the PATH locally).\n  - Tests touched by this PR include `layout`, `comments`, `prose`, `nesting`, `language-versions`, `machine-dialects`, `hello-world-dialects`, `identifiers` and `ranking`. The web app has unit tests and end-to-end tests.\n  - `npm run lint` and `node scripts/check-requirements.mjs` pass.\n- Rust: every JavaScript test above has a twin under `rust/tests/` (for example `layout.rs`, `prose.rs`, `nesting.rs`, `language_versions.rs` and `hello_world_dialects.rs`).\n  - `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo fmt` pass.\n  - The full `cargo test` runs in CI.\n\n### Still open or blocked\n\nThese items are tracked in `docs/case-studies/issue-14/previous-requirements.md` (\"Concise list: everything still open\"). The full case study is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-14/`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/tree/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14):\n\n- `README.md`: timeline, the issue's requirements R1–R24, root causes and alternatives;\n- `previous-requirements.md`: every earlier requirement with its status;\n- `prior-art.md` and `architecture.md`;\n- `requirements.lino`: CI fails while any requirement is neither done nor reported as blocked with a reason.\n\n### Issue 14 requirements\n\n- **A concrete syntax tree (CST) by default.** Whitespace and blank lines now survive a translation. The layout pass (`js/src/translation/layout.js`, `rust/src/layout.rs`) aligns the tokens of the output with those of the source and returns a `lineMap`. `--layout target` restores the emitter's own formatting.\n  - `main`: `console.log( \"Hello World!\");` → `console.log(\"Hello World!\");`\n  - this branch: `console.log( \"Hello World!\");` → `console.log( \"Hello World!\");`\n- **Monaco by default, with linked editors.**\n  - Folding regions now work for every language.\n  - Folding, selection, the cursor and scrolling are shared by both editors. Scrolling is mapped block by block, so blocks of different sizes stay aligned.\n  - Lines that map to each other get matching colours, as in Compiler Explorer.\n- **Comment and identifier language selectors on both sides.** The option checkboxes are now below the editors.\n- **Comments are translated.** A shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`) is used both to detect a comment's language and to translate it.\n  - `// Привет мир` → `// Hello world`.\n  - «Привет» is now detected as Russian.\n  - «Как хорошо покакать?» translates to \"How good to poop?\" (free prose translation).\n- **Deeper grammars.**\n  - Prose reads as `Prose > Sentence > Word`, with concepts and parts of speech.\n  - Comments and strings are read with their own grammars (code in prose, prose in code). Long texts are stored once and referred to by id. Use `--shallow` for the plain tree.\n- **A more general meta language.** `print` is a call to the library function `print-line`.\n- **Assembly and intermediate languages.** NASM, GNU as, ARM64, LLVM IR, WebAssembly text, CIL and JVM bytecode are written and read back.\n- **Language versions.** `javascript@es5`, `php@5`, `csharp@5`, `python@2`, `python@3.5`, `lua@5.1`, `java@1.4`, `swift@1` and `scala@2.9` are available. `registerLanguageVersion` adds a version of your own.\n- **More tasks and corpora.**\n  - 22 Rosetta Code tasks go through all 33 programming languages and the 7 machine targets.\n  - 33 of the 34 programs of the Hello World Collection are read.\n  - `check-equivalence` checks that a translation does what its source does.\n- **Debugging and research.**\n  - `--trace` prints the tree after every stage, and the web app logs translations and editor-sync events with `?debug`.\n  - formal-ai was tried on six tasks; its failures are reported as link-assistant/formal-ai#1641 and link-assistant/formal-ai#1642.\n\n### Screenshots\n\nLine mapping in the linked Monaco editors:\n\n![mapping](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-mapping.png?raw=true)\n\nComment and identifier language selectors on both sides:\n\n![selectors](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-selectors.png?raw=true)\n\n![style](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-style.png?raw=true)\n\n### Tests\n\n- JavaScript: `npm test` passes 1823 tests, with 1 skipped (shellcheck is not on the PATH locally).\n  - Tests touched by this PR include `layout`, `comments`, `prose`, `nesting`, `language-versions`, `machine-dialects`, `hello-world-dialects`, `identifiers` and `ranking`. All-or-nothing\n// translation throws the whole text away for that one part. Partial\n// translation keeps everything it can read and marks the rest.\n//\n// The text is cut into parts along its own layout, so the method needs no\n// grammar of its own and works for every language:\n//\n// 1. Scrolling is mapped block by block, so blocks of different sizes stay aligned.\n  - Lines that map to each other get matching colours, as in Compiler Explorer.\n- **Comment and identifier language selectors on both sides.** The option checkboxes are now below the editors.\n- **Comments are translated.** A shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`) is used both to detect a comment's language and to translate it.\n  - `// Привет мир` → `// Hello world`.\n  - «Привет» is now detected as Russian.\n  - «Как хорошо покакать?» translates to \"How good to poop?\" (free prose translation).\n- **Deeper grammars.**\n  - Prose reads as `Prose > Sentence > Word`, with concepts and parts of speech.\n  - Comments and strings are read with their own grammars (code in prose, prose in code). Use `--shallow` for the plain tree.\n- **A more general meta language.** `print` is a call to the library function `print-line`.\n- **Assembly and intermediate languages.** NASM, GNU as, ARM64, LLVM IR, WebAssembly text, CIL and JVM bytecode are written and read back.\n- **Language versions.** `javascript@es5`, `php@5`, `csharp@5`, `python@2`, `python@3.5`, `lua@5.1`, `java@1.4`, `swift@1` and `scala@2.9` are available. `registerLanguageVersion` adds a version of your own.\n- **More tasks and corpora.**\n  - 22 Rosetta Code tasks go through all 33 programming languages and the 7 machine targets.\n  - 33 of the 34 programs of the Hello World Collection are read.\n  - `check-equivalence` checks that a translation does what its source does.\n- **Debugging and research.**\n  - `--trace` prints the tree after every stage, and the web app logs translations and editor-sync events with `?debug`.\n  - formal-ai was tried on six tasks; its failures are reported as link-assistant/formal-ai#1641 and link-assistant/formal-ai#1642.\n\n### Screenshots\n\nLine mapping in the linked Monaco editors:\n\n![mapping](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-mapping.png?raw=true)\n\nComment and identifier language selectors on both sides:\n\n![selectors](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-selectors.png?raw=true)\n\n![style](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-style.png?raw=true)\n\n### Tests\n\n- JavaScript: `npm test` passes 1823 tests, with 1 skipped (shellcheck is not on the PATH locally).\n  - Tests touched by this PR include `layout`, `comments`, `prose`, `nesting`, `language-versions`, `machine-dialects`, `hello-world-dialects`, `identifiers` and `ranking`. Every node\n// is one line: its kind, its main value as a plain word and its other plain\n// fields as (name value) links. On PR 15 the same workflow passes (run 45757026472).\n\n# Prior art for issue 14\n\nResearch date: 2026-11-25. This file surveys existing projects relevant to the\nrequirements of issue 14 (lossless concrete syntax trees, nested grammars, a\ndeeper natural-language grammar and dictionary, a synchronized two-editor web\nUI, more assembly dialects and intermediate languages) and ends each section\nwith a concrete recommendation for this repository.\n\nFacts below were read from the linked pages or repositories on the research\ndate. Where a fact could not be confirmed it is marked **(unverified)**.\n\nRepository context used for the recommendations: the translator is a pipeline\n`lexer/table-driven parser -> understanding rules -> meta program -> type\ninference -> meaning/context rules -> emitter` (see `README.md`); sources live\nin `js/src/{translation,natural,meta,formal}`; machine targets are NASM, CIL\n(ILAsm) and JVM (Jasmin); CI already installs `nasm` and `jasmin-sable` with\n`apt` and downloads ILAsm from NuGet (`.github/workflows/release.yml`); the web\napp is `examples/universal-app` and already depends on `monaco-editor ^0.58.0`.\n\nContents:\n\n1. [Concrete syntax trees and whitespace preservation](#1-concrete-syntax-trees-and-whitespace-preservation)\n2. [Grammar nesting and language injection](#2-grammar-nesting-and-language-injection)\n3. [Natural-language architecture, grammar and dictionary](#3-natural-language-architecture-grammar-and-dictionary)\n4. [Side-by-side mapping UI and Monaco synchronization](#4-side-by-side-mapping-ui-and-monaco-synchronization)\n5. [Assembly dialects and intermediate languages](#5-assembly-dialects-and-intermediate-languages)\n6. [Related link-foundation and link-assistant projects](#6-related-link-foundation-and-link-assistant-projects)\n7. [Consolidated recommendations](#7-consolidated-recommendations)\n\n---\n\n## 1. Concrete syntax trees and whitespace preservation\n\nThe recurring design question is **where whitespace and comments live**. There\nare four answers in the wild, and they determine how reprinting works.\n\n| Approach                                         | Used by                       | Idea                                                                  |\n| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Trivia attached to tokens (leading and trailing) | Roslyn, swift-syntax          | Whitespace, comments and directives belong to the neighbouring token  |\n| Trivia as ordinary tree elements                 | rust-analyzer/rowan, IntelliJ | Whitespace and comment tokens are siblings of real tokens in the tree |\n| Trivia on a hidden channel or in \"extras\"        | ANTLR, Tree-sitter            | The parser skips them, but they stay in the token stream or tree      |\n| Trivia as typed fields of each node              | LibCST                        | Every node owns the exact spacing around it                           |\n| Original text kept next to the AST               | recast                        | Reuse the original source for every node that did not change          |\n\n### 1.1 Roslyn (C# and VB compiler)\n\n- What it is: Microsoft's compiler platform. Syntax trees are immutable,\n  \"full fidelity\" (every token, whitespace, comment and preprocessor directive)\n  and can reproduce the exact text they were parsed from, even for\n  malformed input. Source:\n  [Work with syntax](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/work-with-syntax).\n- Architecture: nodes, tokens and trivia. Trivia are not children of nodes;\n  each is attached to one token as `LeadingTrivia` or `TrailingTrivia`. The\n  attachment rule is simple and worth copying verbatim: \"a token owns any\n  trivia after it on the same line up to the next token. Any trivia after\n  that line is associated with the following token\", the first token owns the\n  initial trivia and the end-of-file token owns the final trivia. Each node has\n  `Span` (without trivia) and `FullSpan` (with trivia). Errors are kept in the\n  tree as zero-width _missing_ tokens and `SkippedTokensTrivia`.\n- Internals: a **green tree** (immutable, persistent, stores widths, no parent)\n  and a **red tree** (a façade built on demand with parent links and absolute\n  positions). Source:\n  [Eric Lippert, Persistence, façades and Roslyn's red-green trees](https://ericlippert.com/2012/06/08/persistence-facades-and-roslyns-red-green-trees/).\n  (Short summary form: [Red-green trees](https://ericlippert.com/2012/06/08/red-green-trees/).)\n- Recommendation: adopt the **Roslyn trivia rule** as the single, documented\n  attachment rule for all 32 languages (trailing trivia up to and including the\n  end of line, everything else leading on the next token). It is language\n  independent, so one `trivia` model serves every grammar table. Expose both a\n  \"span\" and a \"full span\" per tree node; the UI mapping in section 4 needs\n  them.\n\n### 1.2 rust-analyzer and rowan\n\n- What it is: `rowan` is \"a library for lossless syntax trees, inspired in part\n  by Swift's libsyntax\"\n  ([rust-analyzer/rowan](https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rowan)). The\n  rust-analyzer syntax guide is\n  [docs/book/src/contributing/syntax.md](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/master/docs/book/src/contributing/syntax.md).\n- Architecture: the parser never sees whitespace; a `TreeSink` layer inserts\n  whitespace and comment tokens into the tree afterwards, and comments are\n  attached to nodes heuristically. Every token stores its full text, so\n  concatenating all token texts reproduces the file. Green tree = untyped,\n  interned, text only at leaves; red tree = cursor with parents and offsets.\n  Parse errors are stored beside the tree and wrapped in `ERROR` nodes, so the\n  tree stays lossless for invalid input. A **typed AST layer** of thin\n  checked-cast wrappers (all accessors optional so incomplete code is\n  representable) sits on top of the untyped tree.\n- Recommendation: keep an **untyped, lossless CST as the single source of\n  truth** and generate typed views over it. This matches the issue's request\n  \"CST by default\": the meta program should be derived from the CST, with an\n  AST view that points back into it (node id plus text span). The parser should\n  not need to know about whitespace; a sink step inserts trivia, which keeps\n  the existing table-driven parsers unchanged.\n\n### 1.3 Swift: libSyntax and swift-syntax\n\n- What it is: swift-syntax provides a \"source-accurate tree representation of\n  Swift source code\" and underpins Swift macros\n  ([swiftlang/swift-syntax](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-syntax)). The\n  README does not describe trivia; the leading/trailing-trivia model is the\n  same as Roslyn's. **(unverified on the fetched page; see the Swift\n  documentation on `Trivia` at\n  [swiftpackageindex.com](https://swiftpackageindex.com/swiftlang/swift-syntax/documentation/swiftsyntax).)**\n- Relevant idea: the tree is **round-trippable and also the macro/rewrite\n  substrate**: tools edit by building new nodes, then print. rowan cites\n  libsyntax as inspiration.\n- Recommendation: model rewriting as \"build a new tree, then print\"; do not\n  patch strings. Provide factory helpers (`makeCall(name, args)`) that\n  produce nodes with _default trivia_ (single space after comma, newline after\n  statement) so generated code
[2026-11-26T21:27:51.905Z] [STDOUT]  is readable even when no source trivia exists.\n\n### 1.4 Tree-sitter\n\n- What it is: an incremental parser generator that produces concrete syntax\n  trees and re-parses only the edited region\n  ([tree-sitter.github.io](https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/)).\n- `extras`: \"an array of tokens that may appear anywhere in the language\" -\n  by default whitespace; comments are added here. Extras appear in the tree as\n  ordinary nodes (`comment`), so the tree is lossless over _tokens_; whitespace\n  itself is recovered from byte offsets between nodes\n  ([grammar DSL](https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/creating-parsers/2-the-grammar-dsl.html)).\n  Other useful DSL fields: `inline`, `supertypes`, `word`.\n- Recommendation: use the Tree-sitter trick for storage: **every node has\n  `startByte`/`endByte` into the original text; whitespace is the gap between\n  siblings.** That gives a lossless tree without a whitespace node for every\n  space, and makes `print(parse(x)) === x` a cheap invariant. Also consider\n  Tree-sitter grammars as a **grammar source** for languages that the repo's own\n  tables do not yet cover; many exist and the node-types JSON is machine\n  readable. **(Evaluate licensing per grammar.)**\n\n### 1.5 ANTLR\n\n- What it is: a parser generator. Whitespace and comments can be sent to a\n  channel with `WS : [ \\t\\r\\n\\f]+ -> channel(HIDDEN) ;` instead of `-> skip`\n  (which discards the text)\n  ([lexer rules](https://github.com/antlr/antlr4/blob/master/doc/lexer-rules.md)).\n  Hidden tokens stay in the `CommonTokenStream`, so they can be queried\n  (`getHiddenTokensToLeft/Right`).\n- `TokenStreamRewriter` queues `insertBefore`/`insertAfter`/`replace`/`delete`\n  edits against the token stream without mutating it and applies them lazily on\n  `getText()`; several independent \"programs\" may share one buffer\n  ([API](https://www.antlr.org/api/Java/org/antlr/v4/runtime/TokenStreamRewriter.html)).\n  Because the unchanged tokens (including hidden ones) are emitted verbatim,\n  formatting survives.\n- Lexer modes (`pushMode`/`popMode`) are ANTLR's built-in way to nest\n  sub-languages such as string interpolation.\n- Recommendation: the **lazy edit-list printer** is a good model for\n  same-language edits (rename, replace) and for the UI's \"edit translation and\n  map back\" scenario; implement it over the CST as a list of (span, new text)\n  edits applied at print time.\n\n### 1.6 Lark\n\n- What it is: a Python parsing toolkit with Earley (default, dynamic lexer)\n  and LALR engines. Relevant options:\n  `keep_all_tokens` (default `False`, drops punctuation tokens from the tree),\n  `propagate_positions` (adds line, column, `start_pos`, `end_pos` to node\n  `meta`), `maybe_placeholders`\n  ([parser classes](https://lark-parser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/classes.html)).\n  `%ignore` drops matched terminals\n  ([grammar reference](https://lark-parser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/grammar.html));\n  to keep comments you must capture them with `lexer_callbacks` **(unverified\n  on these pages; documented in the Lark FAQ)**. `lark.reconstruct.Reconstructor`\n  rebuilds text from a tree and is documented as experimental; it does not\n  restore ignored whitespace or comments **(unverified)**.\n- Recommendation: Lark is a cautionary example. A parser that **discards**\n  ignorable tokens must be paired with a side channel of positions, otherwise\n  the printer can never be lossless. Do not derive the output printer from the\n  grammar by reversal; keep an explicit emitter per language and feed it\n  trivia.\n\n### 1.7 LibCST (Python)\n\n- What it is: a lossless Python CST whose node types follow Python semantics\n  rather than the grammar, so semantic edits stay easy\n  ([Why LibCST?](https://libcst.readthedocs.io/en/latest/why_libcst.html)).\n- Whitespace: instead of `prefix` strings it parses whitespace into explicit\n  nodes owned by the node they belong to: `leading_lines` (blank lines and\n  comments above a statement), `trailing_whitespace` (spaces, comment and\n  newline at line end), `whitespace_before_args`, `whitespace_after_arg`; the\n  `Module` stores `default_indent`, `default_newline` and `has_trailing_newline`.\n  Removing an argument therefore removes its own comma and spacing.\n- Recommendation: copy two ideas. (a) Store document-level formatting\n  defaults (indent unit, newline style, final newline) on the root so\n  translated output can be re-indented to the **target** language's convention\n  while keeping the source's _structure_ of blank lines. (b) Give comments and\n  blank lines to the **statement** that follows them (`leading_lines`), so\n  deleting or moving a statement moves its comment with it.\n\n### 1.8 recast (JavaScript)\n\n- What it is: parse JavaScript, modify the AST, print it back \"while keeping\n  the original formatting of untouched code\". `parse` keeps a shadow copy with\n  `.original` references; `print` finds changed nodes and **reuses the original\n  source text for everything else**, falling back to a pretty printer for\n  nodes it cannot reprint; `print(parse(src)).code === src` is guaranteed\n  ([benjamn/recast](https://github.com/benjamn/recast)).\n- Recommendation: for _same-language_ round trips (the property test the issue\n  implies) implement recast's reuse strategy: each translated node remembers\n  its source node; when the translator emits an unchanged node into the same\n  language, copy the original text. For _cross-language_ output there is no\n  original text to reuse, so carry only trivia (comments, blank lines,\n  relative indentation) and pretty-print the rest.\n\n### 1.9 How cross-language translation changes the problem\n\nAll the tools above reprint in the **same** language. Translation to another\nlanguage needs three extra decisions, which are the real design work:\n\n1. **Comment re-delimiting.** `// x` -> `# x` -> `-- x` -> `(* x *)`. Store the\n   comment _text_ and a `style` (line, block, doc) and let the target emitter\n   choose delimiters. The repo already has `js/src/natural/comments.js` and\n   `js/src/translation/comment-language.js`, which translate comment text.\n2. **Blank-line and grouping fidelity.** Keep the _count_ of blank lines\n   between statements (capped), not the exact whitespace.\n3. **Indentation re-basing.** Store indentation as a depth number plus the\n   document's indent unit, not as raw spaces; Python/Nim-style significant\n   indentation then translates cleanly to brace languages.\n\nTest oracle: `print(parse(x)) === x` byte for byte for every example in\n# Grammar Structure\n\nA grammar is essentially a grammar declaration followed by a list of rules, but has the general form:\n\n```\n/** Optional javadoc style comment */\ngrammar Name; ①\noptions {...}\nimport ... ;\n \t\ntokens {...}\nchannels {...} // lexer only\n@actionName {...}\n \t \nrule1 // parser and lexer rules, possibly intermingled\n...\nruleN\n```\n\nThe file name containing grammar `X` must be called `X.g4`. You can specify options, imports, token specifications, and actions in any order. There can be at most one each of options, imports, and token specifications. All of those elements are optional except for the header ① and at least one rule. Rules take the basic form:\n\n```\nruleName : alternative1 | ... | alternativeN ;\n```\n\nParser rule names must start with a lowercase letter and lexer rules must start with a capital letter.\n\nGrammars defined without a prefix on the `grammar` header are combined grammars that can contain both lexical and parser rules. To make a parser grammar that only allows parser rules, use the following header.\n\n```\nparser grammar Name;\n...\n```\n\nAnd, naturally, a pure lexer grammar looks like this:\n\n```\nlexer grammar Name;\n...\n```\n\nOnly lexer grammars can contain `mode` specifications.\n\nOnly lexer grammars can contain custom channels specifications\n\n```\nchannels {\n  WHITESPACE_CHANNEL,\n  COMMENTS_CHANNEL\n}\n```\n\nThose channels can then be used like enums within lexer rules:\n\n```\nWS : [ \\r\\t\\n]+ -> channel(WHITESPACE_CHANNEL) ;\n```\n\nSections 15.5, [Lexer Rules](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference) and Section 15.3, [Parser Rules](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference) contain details on rule syntax. Section 15.8, Options describes grammar options and Section 15.4, Actions and Attributes has information on grammar-level actions.\n\n## Grammar Imports\n\nGrammar `imports` let you break up a grammar into logical and reusable chunks, as we saw in [Importing Grammars](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference). ANTLR treats imported grammars very much like object-oriented programming languages treat superclasses. A grammar inherits all of the rules, tokens specifications, and named actions from the imported grammar. Rules in the “main grammar” override rules from imported grammars to implement inheritance.\n\nThink of `import` as more like a smart include statement (which does not include rules that are already defined). The result of all imports is a single combined grammar; the ANTLR code generator sees a complete grammar and has no idea there were imported grammars.\n\nTo process a main grammar, the ANTLR tool loads all of the imported grammars into subordinate grammar objects. It then merges the rules, token types, and named actions from the imported grammars into the main grammar. In the diagram below, the grammar on the right illustrates the effect of grammar `MyELang` importing grammar `ELang`.\n\n<img src=images/combined.png width=400>\n\n`MyELang` inherits rules `stat`, `WS`, and `ID`, but overrides rule `expr` and adds `INT`. Here’s a sample build and test run that shows `MyELang` can recognize integer expressions whereas the original `ELang` can’t. The third, erroneous input statement triggers an error message that also demonstrates the parser was looking for `MyELang`’s expr not `ELang`’s.\n\n```\n$ antlr4 MyELang.g4\n$ javac MyELang*.java\n$ grun MyELang stat\n=> \t34;\n=> \ta;\n=> \t;\n=> \tEOF\n<= \tline 3:0 extraneous input ';' expecting {INT, ID}\n```\n\nIf there are modes in the main grammar or any of the imported grammars then the import process will import those modes and merge their rules where they are not overridden. In the event any mode becomes empty as all its\nrules have been overridden by rules outside the mode this mode will be discarded.\n\nIf there were any `tokens` specifications, the main grammar would merge the token sets. If there were any `channel` specifications, the main grammar would merge the channel sets. Any named actions such as `@members` would be merged. In general, you should avoid named actions and actions within rules in imported grammars since that limits their reuse. ANTLR also ignores any options in imported grammars.\n\nImported grammars can also import other grammars. ANTLR pursues all imported grammars in a depth-first fashion. If two or more imported grammars define rule `r`, ANTLR chooses the first version of `r` it finds. In the following diagram, ANTLR examines grammars in the following order `Nested`, `G1`, `G3`, `G2`.\n\n<img src=images/nested.png width=350>\n\n`Nested` includes the `r` rule from `G3` because it sees that version before the `r` in `G2`.\n\nNot every kind of grammar can import every other kind of grammar:\n\n* Lexer grammars can import lexers, including lexers containing modes.\n* Parsers can import parsers.\n* Combined grammars can import parsers or lexers without modes.\n\nANTLR adds imported rules to the end of the rule list in a main lexer grammar. That means lexer rules in the main grammar get precedence over imported rules. For example, if a main grammar defines rule `IF : 'if' ;` and an imported grammar defines rule `ID : [a-z]+ ;` (which also recognizes `if`), the imported `ID` won’t hide the main grammar’s `IF` token definition.\n\n## Tokens Section\n\nThe purpose of the `tokens` section is to define token types needed by a grammar for which there is no associated lexical rule. The basic syntax is:\n\n```\ntokens { Token1, ..., TokenN }\n```\n\nMost of the time, the tokens section is used to define token types needed by actions in the grammar as shown in Section 10.3, [Recognizing Languages whose Keywords Aren’t Fixed](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference):\n\n```\n// explicitly define keyword token types to avoid implicit definition warnings\ntokens { BEGIN, END, IF, THEN, WHILE }\n \n@lexer::members { // keywords map used in lexer to assign token types\nMap<String,Integer> keywords = new HashMap<String,Integer>() {{\n\tput(\"begin\", KeywordsParser.BEGIN);\n\tput(\"end\", KeywordsParser.END);\n\t...\n}};\n}\n```\n\nThe `tokens` section really just defines a set of tokens to add to the overall set.\n\n```\n$ cat Tok.g4\ngrammar Tok;\ntokens { A, B, C }\na : X ;\n$ antlr4 Tok.g4\nwarning(125): Tok.g4:3:4: implicit definition of token X in parser\n$ cat Tok.tokens\nA=1\nB=2\nC=3\nX=4\n```\n\n## Actions at the Grammar Level\n\nCurrently there are only two defined named actions (for the Java target) used outside of grammar rules: `header` and `members`. The former injects code into the generated recognizer class file, before the recognizer class definition, and the latter injects code into the recognizer class definition, as fields and methods.\n\nFor combined grammars, ANTLR injects the actions into both the parser and the lexer. To restrict an action to the generated parser or lexer, use `@parser::name` or `@lexer::name`.\n\nHere’s an example where the grammar specifies a package for the generated code:\n\n```\ngrammar Count;\n \n@header {\npackage foo;\n}\n \n@members {\nint count = 0;\n}\n \ndata/natural/grammar.lino\ndata/translation/ranked-grammar-programs.lino\ndocs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/tree-sitter-grammar.html\ndocs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/link-grammar.txt\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Concrete syntax trees and whitespace preservation\n\nThe recurring design question is **where whitespace and comments live**. There\nare four answers in the wild, and they determine how reprinting works.\n\n| Approach                                         | Used by                       | Idea                                                                  |\n| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Trivia attached to tokens (leading and trailing) | Roslyn, swift-syntax          | Whitespace, comments and directives belong to the neighbouring token  |\n| Trivia as ordinary tree elements                 | rust-analyzer/rowan, IntelliJ | Whitespace and comment tokens are siblings of real tokens in the tree |\n| Trivia on a hidden channel or in \"extras\"        | ANTLR, Tree-sitter            | The parser skips them, but they stay in the token stream or tree      |\n| Trivia as typed fields of each node              | LibCST                        | Every node owns the exact spacing around it                           |\n| Original text kept next to the AST               | recast                        | Reuse the original source for every node that did not change          |\n\n### 1.1 Roslyn (C# and VB compiler)\n\n- What it is: Microsoft's compiler platform. Syntax trees are immutable,\n  \"full fidelity\" (every token, whitespace, comment and preprocessor directive)\n  and can reproduce the exact text they were parsed from, even for\n  malformed input. Source:\n  [Work with syntax](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/work-with-syntax).\n- Architecture: nodes, tokens and trivia. Trivia are not children of nodes;\n  each is attached to one token as `LeadingTrivia` or `TrailingTrivia`. The\n  attachment rule is simple and worth copying verbatim: \"a token owns any\n  trivia after it on the same line up to the next token. Any trivia after\n  that line is associated with the following token\", the first token owns the\n  initial trivia and the end-of-file token owns the final trivia. Each node has\n  `Span` (without trivia) and `FullSpan` (with trivia). Errors are kept in the\n  tree as zero-width _missing_ tokens and `SkippedTokensTrivia`.\n- Internals: a **green tree** (immutable, persistent, stores widths, no parent)\n  and a **red tree** (a façade built on demand with parent links and absolute\n  positions). Source:\n  [Eric Lippert, Persistence, façades and Roslyn's red-green trees](https://ericlippert.com/2012/06/08/persistence-facades-and-roslyns-red-green-trees/).\n  (Short summary form: [Red-green trees](https://ericlippert.com/2012/06/08/red-green-trees/).)\n- Recommendation: adopt the **Roslyn trivia rule** as the single, documented\n  attachment rule for all 32 languages (trailing trivia up to and including the\n  end of line, everything else leading on the next token). It is language\n  independent, so one `trivia` model serves every grammar table. Expose both a\n  \"span\" and a \"full span\" per tree node; the UI mapping in section 4 needs\n  them.\n\n### 1.2 rust-analyzer and rowan\n\n- What it is: `rowan` is \"a library for lossless syntax trees, inspired in part\n  by Swift's libsyntax\"\n  ([rust-analyzer/rowan](https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rowan)). The\n  rust-analyzer syntax guide is\n  [docs/book/src/contributing/syntax.md](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/master/docs/book/src/contributing/syntax.md).\n- Architecture: the parser never sees whitespace; a `TreeSink` layer inserts\n  whitespace and comment tokens into the tree afterwards, and comments are\n  attached to nodes heuristically. Every token stores its full text, so\n  concatenating all token texts reproduces the file. Green tree = untyped,\n  interned, text only at leaves; red tree = cursor with parents and offsets.\n  Parse errors are stored beside the tree and wrapped in `ERROR` nodes, so the\n  tree stays lossless for invalid input. Concrete syntax trees and whitespace preservation\n\nThe recurring design question is **where whitespace and comments live**. There\nare four answers in the wild, and they determine how reprinting works.\n\n| Approach                                         | Used by                       | Idea                                                                  |\n| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Trivia attached to tokens (leading and trailing) | Roslyn, swift-syntax          | Whitespace, comments and directives belong to the neighbouring token  |\n| Trivia as ordinary tree elements                 | rust-analyzer/rowan, IntelliJ | Whitespace and comment tokens are siblings of real tokens in the tree |\n| Trivia on a hidden channel or in \"extras\"        | ANTLR, Tree-sitter            | The parser skips them, but they stay in the token stream or tree      |\n| Trivia as typed fields of each node              | LibCST                        | Every node owns the exact spacing around it                           |\n| Original text kept next to the AST               | recast                        | Reuse the original source for every node that did not change          |\n\n### 1.1 Roslyn (C# and VB compiler)\n\n- What it is: Microsoft's compiler platform. Syntax trees are immutable,\n  \"full fidelity\" (every token, whitespace, comment and preprocessor directive)\n  and can reproduce the exact text they were parsed from, even for\n  malformed input. Source:\n  [Work with syntax](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/roslyn-sdk/work-with-syntax).\n- Architecture: nodes, tokens and trivia. Trivia are not children of nodes;\n  each is attached to one token as `LeadingTrivia` or `TrailingTrivia`. The\n  attachment rule is simple and worth copying verbatim: \"a token owns any\n  trivia after it on the same line up to the next token. Any trivia after\n  that line is associated with the following token\", the first token owns the\n  initial trivia and the end-of-file token owns the final trivia. Each node has\n  `Span` (without trivia) and `FullSpan` (with trivia). Errors are kept in the\n  tree as zero-width _missing_ tokens and `SkippedTokensTrivia`.\n- Internals: a **green tree** (immutable, persistent, stores widths, no parent)\n  and a **red tree** (a façade built on demand with parent links and absolute\n  positions). Source:\n  [Eric Lippert, Persistence, façades and Roslyn's red-green trees](https://ericlippert.com/2012/06/08/persistence-facades-and-roslyns-red-green-trees/).\n  (Short summary form: [Red-green trees](https://ericlippert.com/2012/06/08/red-green-trees/).)\n- Recommendation: adopt the **Roslyn trivia rule** as the single, documented\n  attachment rule for all 32 languages (trailing trivia up to and including the\n  end of line, everything else leading on the next token). It is language\n  independent, so one `trivia` model serves every grammar table. Expose both a\n  \"span\" and a \"full span\" per tree node; the UI mapping in section 4 needs\n  them.\n\n### 1.2 rust-analyzer and rowan\n\n- What it is: `rowan` is \"a library for lossless syntax trees, inspired in part\n  by Swift's libsyntax\"\n  ([rust-analyzer/rowan](https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rowan)). The\n  rust-analyzer syntax guide is\n  [docs/book/src/contributing/syntax.md](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/master/docs/book/src/contributing/syntax.md).\n- Architecture: the parser never sees whitespace; a `TreeSink` layer inserts\n  whitespace and comment tokens into the tree afterwards, and comments are\n  attached to nodes heuristically. Every token stores its full text, so\n  concatenating all token texts reproduces the file. Green tree = untyped,\n  interned, text only at leaves; red tree = cursor with parents and offsets.\n  Parse errors are stored beside the tree and wrapped in `ERROR` nodes, so the\n  tree stays lossless for invalid input. A **typed AST layer** of thin\n  checked-cast wrappers (all accessors optional so incomplete code is\n  representable) sits on top of the untyped tree.\n- Recommendation: keep an **untyped, lossless CST as the single source of\n  truth** and generate typed views over it. This matches the issue's request\n  \"CST by default\": the meta program should be derived from the CST, with an\n  AST view that points back into it (node id plus text span). The parser should\n  not need to know about whitespace; a sink step inserts trivia, which keeps\n  the existing table-driven parsers unchanged.\n\n### 1.3 Swift: libSyntax and swift-syntax\n\n- What it is: swift-syntax provides a \"source-accurate tree representation of\n  Swift source code\" and underpins Swift macros\n  ([swiftlang/swift-syntax](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-syntax)). The\n  README does not describe trivia; the leading/trailing-trivia model is the\ndocs/case-studies/issue-16/data/discussion-17.md:64:- [View complete solution draft log](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/konard/216442f7cda270d3057eefed99f77590/raw/d7cc8f4128227afd1db5d88c8196853afd4fe5d3/tmp-hive-mind-log-upload-77ILTr-sanitized.log.txt)\ndocs/case-studies/issue-16/data/discussion-17.md:113:- [View complete solution draft log](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/konard/127f887febd31a00f18b6f2ba65bc705/raw/db1d2748c885e88c252a986338e5d0c5b7cccc7d/tmp-hive-mind-log-upload-ynKCjr-sanitized.log.txt)\ndocs/case-studies/issue-16/data/discussion-17.md:164:- [View complete solution draft log](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/konard/c204622813d3e7e4a2b67e2701d15074/raw/92a4bc1b89028213d33ab393f2320a1062a85e36/tmp-hive-mind-log-upload-Nb6zsp-sanitized.log.txt)\ndocs/case-studies/issue-16/data/discussion-7.md:248:- [View complete solution draft log](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/konard/e9d784510ebebc6270f2f445ff87504e/raw/ec4d2eb3b5deae0476e3672744980e5b5b39bdde/tmp-hive-mind-log-upload-d8aH7v-sanitized.log.txt)\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

then write that\n// machine code as assembly (x86-64 NASM and GNU as, ARM64), CIL (ILAsm),\n// JVM bytecode (Jasmin), LLVM IR or WebAssembly text.\n//\n// The stack machine has these instructions:\n//\n//   push n          load slot        store slot       pop\n//   arithmetic op   (add subtract multiply divide remainder negate)\n//   label L         jump L           compare-jump relation L\n//   call name count return           return-nothing\n//   print-integer   print-text value print-newline\n//   comment text\n//   new-array       (length, fill → array)       dup\n//   element-index   (makes the integer on top an element index)\n//   load-element    (array, index → value)       store-element (array,\n//   array-length    (array → length)                 index, value → )\n//\n// Integers are 64-bit. Text exists only as literal parts of printed values,\n// so every program that prints text, integers and their interpolations and\n// computes with integer functions, loops and conditions can be lowered.\n// Arrays of integers live in local slots; an array literal is a new array\n// of zeros whose elements are stored one by one.\n\nconst relations = [\n  'equal',\n  'notEqual',\n  'less',\n  'lessOrEqual',\n  'greater',\n  'greaterOrEqual',\n];\n\nconst opposite = {\n  equal: 'notEqual',\n  notEqual: 'equal',\n  less: 'greaterOrEqual',\n  lessOrEqual: 'greater',\n  greater: 'lessOrEqual',\n  greaterOrEqual: 'less',\n};\n\nconst arithmetic = {\n  add: 'add',\n  subtract: 'subtract',\n  multiply: 'multiply',\n  divide: 'divide',\n  integerDivide: 'divide',\n  remainder: 'remainder',\n};\n\nconst compoundOperators = {\n  '+=': 'add',\n  '-=': 'subtract',\n  '*=': 'multiply',\n  '/=': 'divide',\n  '%=': 'remainder',\n};\n\n// How much each instruction changes the stack depth.\nconst stackEffect = {\n  push: 1,\n  load: 1,\n  store: -1,\n  pop: -1,\n  arithmetic: -1,\n  negate: 0,\n  'compare-jump': -2,\n  return: -1,\n  'print-integer': -1,\n  'new-array': -1,\n  dup: 1,\n  'load-element': -1,\n  'store-element': -3,\n};\n\nfunction unsupported(what) {\n  return new Error(`Machine targets cannot lower ${what}`);\n}\n\nclass FunctionLowering {\n  constructor(name, parameters, returns, functions) {\n    this.name = name;\n    this.returns = returns;\n    this.functions = functions;\n    this.slots = new Map(\n      parameters.map(({ name: item }, index) => [item, index])\n    );\n    this.parameterCount = parameters.length;\n    this.arrays = new Set();\n    this.code = [];\n    this.labels = 0;\n    this.depth = 0;\n    this.maxDepth = 0;\n  }\n\n  emit(operation, ...operands) {\n    this.code.push([operation, ...operands]);\n    const effect =\n      operation === 'call'\n        ? 1 - operands[1] - (this.functions.get(operands[0]).returns ? 0 : 1)\n        : (stackEffect[operation] ?? 0);\n    this.depth += effect;\n    this.maxDepth = Math.max(this.maxDepth, this.depth);\n  }\n\n  label() {\n    this.labels += 1;\n    return `L${this.labels}`;\n  }\n\n  slot(name) {\n    if (!this.slots.has(name)) {\n      this.slots.set(name, this.slots.size);\n    }\n    return this.slots.get(name);\n  }\n\n  known(name) {\n    if (!this.slots.has(name)) {\n      throw new Error(`\"${name}\" is used before it is declared`);\n    }\n    return this.slots.get(name);\n  }\n\n  block(node) {\n    for (const statement of node.statements) {\n      this.statement(statement);\n    }\n  }\n\n  statement(node) {\n    const lower = this[`lower${node.kind}`];\n    if (!lower) {\n      throw unsupported(`the ${node.kind} statement`);\n    }\n    lower.call(this, node);\n  }\n\n  lowerComment(node) {\n    for (const line of node.text.split('\\n')) {\n      this.emit('comment', line);\n    }\n  }\n\n  // Machine code has no layout to keep.\n  lowerBlank() {}\n\n  lowerDeclaration(node) {\n    const isArray =\n      node.type === 'array' ||\n      ['ArrayLiteral', 'NewArray'].includes(node.value?.kind);\n    this.value(node.value);\n    if (isArray) {\n      this.arrays.add(node.name);\n    }\n    this.emit('store', this.slot(node.name));\n  }\n\n  lowerIndexAssignment(node) {\n    this.emit('load', this.known(node.name));\n    this.value(node.index);\n    this.emit('element-index');\n    this.value(node.value);\n    this.emit('store-element');\n  }\n\n  // [a, b] is a new array of two zeros whose elements become a and b.\n  arrayLiteral(node) {\n    this.emit('push', node.elements.length);\n    this.emit('push', 0);\n    this.emit('new-array');\n    node.elements.forEach((element, index) => {\n      this.emit('dup');\n      this.emit('push', index);\n      this.emit('element-index');\n      this.value(element);\n      this.emit('store-element');\n    });\n  }\n\n  lowerAssignment(node) {\n    const slot = this.known(node.name);\n    if (node.operator === '=') {\n      this.value(node.value);\n    } else if (compoundOperators[node.operator]) {\n      this.emit('load', slot);\n      this.value(node.value);\n      this.emit('arithmetic', compoundOperators[node.operator]);\n    } else {\n      throw unsupported(`the ${node.operator} assignment`);\n    }\n    this.emit('store', slot);\n  }\n\n  lowerIf(node) {\n    const otherwise = this.label();\n    const done = this.label();\n    this.whenFalse(node.condition, otherwise);\n    this.block(node.then);\n    this.emit('jump', done);\n    this.emit('label', otherwise);\n    if (node.otherwise) {\n      this.statementOrBlock(node.otherwise);\n    }\n    this.emit('label', done);\n  }\n\n  statementOrBlock(node) {\n    if (node.kind === 'Block') {\n      this.block(node);\n    } else {\n      this.statement(node);\n    }\n  }\n\n  lowerWhile(node) {\n    const top = this.label();\n    const done = this.label();\n    this.emit('label', top);\n    this.whenFalse(node.condition, done);\n    this.block(node.body);\n    this.emit('jump', top);\n    this.emit('label', done);\n  }\n\n  lowerCountingLoop(node) {\n    const slot = this.slot(node.variable);\n    const top = this.label();\n    const done = this.label();\n    this.value(node.start);\n    this.emit('store', slot);\n    this.emit('label', top);\n    this.emit('load', slot);\n    this.value(node.end);\n    this.emit('compare-jump', 'greaterOrEqual', done);\n    this.block(node.body);\n    this.emit('load', slot);\n    this.emit('push', 1);\n    this.emit('arithmetic', 'add');\n    this.emit('store', slot);\n    this.emit('jump', top);\n    this.emit('label', done);\n  }\n\n  lowerReturn(node) {\n    if (node.value) {\n      this.value(node.value);\n      this.emit('return');\n    } else {\n      this.emit('return-nothing');\n    }\n  }\n\n  lowerPrint(node) {\n    const parts =\n      node.value.kind === 'Interpolation' ? node.value.parts : [node.value];\n    for (const part of parts) {\n      if (part.kind === 'Text') {\n        if (part.value) {\n          this.emit('print-text', part.value);\n        }\n      } 'untyped'} value`);\n      }\n    }\n    if (node.newline) {\n      this.emit('print-newline');\n    }\n  }\n\n  lowerEvaluate(node) {\n    this.value(node.expression);\n    if (node.expression.kind !== 'Call' || this.returnsValue(node.expression)) {\n      this.emit('pop');\n    }\n  }\n\n  returnsValue(call) {\n    return this.functions.get(call.callee)?.returns;\n  }\n\n  // Push the value of an integer or boolean expression.\n  value(node) {\n    switch (node.kind) {\n      case 'Number':\n        if (!Number.isInteger(node.value) || node.type === 'real') {\n          throw unsupported(`the number ${node.value}`);\n        }\n        this.emit('push', node.value);\n        return;\n      case 'Boolean':\n        this.emit('push', node.value ? 1 : 0);\n        return;\n      case 'Name':\n        this.emit('load', this.known(node.name));\n        return;\n      case 'Call':\n        this.call(node);\n        return;\n      case 'Unary':\n        return this.unary(node);\n      case 'Binary':\n        return this.binary(node);\n      case 'ArrayLiteral':\n        return this.arrayLiteral(node);\n      case 'NewArray':\n        this.value(node.length);\n        this.value(node.fill);\n        this.emit('new-array');\n        return;\n      case 'Index':\n        this.value(node.array);\n        this.value(node.index);\n        this.emit('element-index');\n        this.emit('load-element');\n        return;\n      case 'Length':\n        this.value(node.array);\n        this.emit('array-length');\n        return;\n      default:\n        throw unsupported(`a ${node.kind} value`);\n    }\n  }\n\n  call(node) {\n    const callee = this.functions.get(node.callee);\n    if (!callee) {\n      throw unsupported(`a call to the unknown function \"${node.callee}\"`);\n    }\n    for (const argument of node.arguments) {\n      this.value(argument);\n    }\n    this.emit('call', node.callee, node.arguments.length);\n  }\n\n  unary(node) {\n    if (node.operator === 'negate') {\n      this.value(node.operand);\n      this.emit('negate');\n    } else {\n      this.booleanValue(node);\n    }\n  }\n\n  binary(node) {\n    if (node.operator === 'realDivide') {\n      throw unsupported('true division, which gives a real');\n    }\n    if (arithmetic[node.operator]) {\n      this.value(node.left);\n      this.value(node.right);\n      this.emit('arithmetic', arithmetic[node.operator]);\n    } else {\n      this.booleanValue(node);\n    }\n  }\n\n  // A condition used as a value becomes 1 or 0.\n  booleanValue(node) {\n    const otherwise = this.label();\n    const done = this.label();\n    this.whenFalse(node, otherwise);\n    this.emit('push', 1);\n    this.emit('jump', done);\n    this.emit('label', otherwise);\n    this.depth -= 1;\n    this.emit('push', 0);\n    this.emit('label', done);\n  }\n\n  // Jump to the label when the condition is false; fall through otherwise.\n  whenFalse(node, target) {\n    this.branch(node, target, false);\n  }\n\n  branch(node, target, jumpWhen) {\n    if (node.kind === 'Binary' && relations.includes(node.operator)) {\n      this.value(node.left);\n      this.value(node.right);\n      this.emit(\n        'compare-jump',\n        jumpWhen ? node.operator : opposite[node.operator],\n        target\n      );\n    } else if (node.kind === 'Unary' && node.operator === 'not') {\n      this.branch(node.operand, target, !jumpWhen);\n    } else if (\n      node.kind === 'Binary' &&\n      ['and', 'or'].includes(node.operator)\n    ) {\n      // \"a and b\" is false when either part is false; \"a or b\" is true when\n      // either part is true. {\n  const parts = [];\n  for (const byte of new globalThis.TextEncoder().encode(text)) {\n    const printable = byte >= 0x20 && byte < 0x7f && byte !== 0x22;\n    const last = parts.at(-1);\n    if Summary\n\nFixes #16\nFixes #1\nFixes #6\nFixes #8\nFixes #12\nFixes #14\n\nThis draft addresses translation correctness and the unfinished requirements inherited from earlier issues. **The full acceptance criteria are not yet met; keep this PR unmerged while implementation continues.**\n\nImplemented and checked so far:\n\n- Explicit meta fields distinguish conditions, bodies, expression statements, operands and arguments in JavaScript and Rust.\n- Correcting the source language preserves the original source. The footer has Source code and Report issue links; the report includes source, result, detected language, options, rules and errors.\n- Translated comments preserve the following blank line. Multiline comment tokens contribute every covered line to the map.\n- Powers inside interpolation retain the entire expression, with right association and grouping. Unread interpolation tokens raise an error. Power support across every target remains unfinished.\n- JavaScript const array bindings with mutating calls become mutable Rust containers.\n- An isolated ambiguous name such as `c` parses as English and ranks first on a tie.\n- Russian boolean objects and comparison referents share grammatical-case rules; sequence and iteration vocabulary is available in all 30 natural languages.\n- Java method/parameter annotations, nested generic types, and continued fluent calls survive translation. The Spring example translates to Python and its small framework doubles verify the 201 response.\n- C++ typed throw/catch values retain their meaning in Python and JavaScript, including nested rethrows. The exact issue example compiles and exits with status 8 in all three runtimes.\n- Formal parsers retain lossless tokens, trivia and grammar production ranges by default, with UTF-8 byte offsets and exact reconstruction in JavaScript and Rust.\n- Source ownership follows semantic nodes through parsing, rewrites and emission. The complete Java Fibonacci interpolation maps to both the Bash call and echo, and both map back to the Java print without colouring the loop. All 30 controlled natural languages map statements in both directions.\n\nStill being implemented: semantic mapping across every language family, the reported gutter artifact, agreement throughout all natural languages and comments, full operator coverage, remaining exception targets, questions/introspection/SQL/LINQ, grammar import/update/merge/transformation support, concrete syntax for natural/machine/incomplete input, and every inherited coverage gap. Passing CI for the completed pieces does not establish completion of those criteria.\n\n## Reproduce and verify\n\n- Source corruption: paste the C++ try/catch example from issue 16, then correct the source selector to C++. Before this change the source becomes error comments; afterward it stays byte-for-byte intact and translates to executable Python.\n- `console.log(`${2 ** 10}`);` from JavaScript to Python must retain `2 ** 10`.\n- Translate `// Привет`, a blank line, and `console.log( \"Hello World!\");` to Python with English comments: the blank line and the space before the string remain.\n- Translate a const JavaScript array followed by `.push(3)` to Rust: its declaration uses `let mut`.\n\nAutomated checks include `js/tests/issue-16.test.js`, `annotations.test.js`, `exceptions.test.js`, `concrete-syntax.test.js`, `natural-wordings.test.js`, `issue-report.test.js`, `universal-app-editors.test.js`, the web end-to-end suite, and matching focused Rust targets. Run `node examples/translation/verify-exceptions.mjs` for native C++/Python/JavaScript exit-status verification and `python3 examples/translation/spring/verify.py` for the Spring example. ①\noptions {...}\nimport ... ;\n \t\ntokens {...}\nchannels {...} // lexer only\n@actionName {...}\n \t \nrule1 // parser and lexer rules, possibly intermingled\n...\nruleN\n```\n\nThe file name containing grammar `X` must be called `X.g4`. You can specify options, imports, token specifications, and actions in any order. There can be at most one each of options, imports, and token specifications. All of those elements are optional except for the header ① and at least one rule. Rules take the basic form:\n\n```\nruleName : alternative1 | ... | alternativeN ;\n```\n\nParser rule names must start with a lowercase letter and lexer rules must start with a capital letter.\n\nGrammars defined without a prefix on the `grammar` header are combined grammars that can contain both lexical and parser rules. To make a parser grammar that only allows parser rules, use the following header.\n\n```\nparser grammar Name;\n...\n```\n\nAnd, naturally, a pure lexer grammar looks like this:\n\n```\nlexer grammar Name;\n...\n```\n\nOnly lexer grammars can contain `mode` specifications.\n\nOnly lexer grammars can contain custom channels specifications\n\n```\nchannels {\n  WHITESPACE_CHANNEL,\n  COMMENTS_CHANNEL\n}\n```\n\nThose channels can then be used like enums within lexer rules:\n\n```\nWS : [ \\r\\t\\n]+ -> channel(WHITESPACE_CHANNEL) ;\n```\n\nSections 15.5, [Lexer Rules](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference) and Section 15.3, [Parser Rules](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference) contain details on rule syntax. Section 15.8, Options describes grammar options and Section 15.4, Actions and Attributes has information on grammar-level actions.\n\n## Grammar Imports\n\nGrammar `imports` let you break up a grammar into logical and reusable chunks, as we saw in [Importing Grammars](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference). ANTLR treats imported grammars very much like object-oriented programming languages treat superclasses. A grammar inherits all of the rules, tokens specifications, and named actions from the imported grammar. Rules in the “main grammar” override rules from imported grammars to implement inheritance.\n\nThink of `import` as more like a smart include statement (which does not include rules that are already defined). The result of all imports is a single combined grammar; the ANTLR code generator sees a complete grammar and has no idea there were imported grammars.\n\nTo process a main grammar, the ANTLR tool loads all of the imported grammars into subordinate grammar objects. It then merges the rules, token types, and named actions from the imported grammars into the main grammar. In the diagram below, the grammar on the right illustrates the effect of grammar `MyELang` importing grammar `ELang`.\n\n<img src=images/combined.png width=400>\n\n`MyELang` inherits rules `stat`, `WS`, and `ID`, but overrides rule `expr` and adds `INT`. Here’s a sample build and test run that shows `MyELang` can recognize integer expressions whereas the original `ELang` can’t. The third, erroneous input statement triggers an error message that also demonstrates the parser was looking for `MyELang`’s expr not `ELang`’s.\n\n```\n$ antlr4 MyELang.g4\n$ javac MyELang*.java\n$ grun MyELang stat\n=> \t34;\n=> \ta;\n=> \t;\n=> \tEOF\n<= \tline 3:0 extraneous input ';' expecting {INT, ID}\n```\n\nIf there are modes in the main grammar or any of the imported grammars then the import process will import those modes and merge their rules where they are not overridden. In the event any mode becomes empty as all its\nrules have been overridden by rules outside the mode this mode will be discarded.\n\nIf there were any `tokens` specifications, the main grammar would merge the token sets. If there were any `channel` specifications, the main grammar would merge the channel sets. Any named actions such as `@members` would be merged. In general, you should avoid named actions and actions within rules in imported grammars since that limits their reuse. ANTLR also ignores any options in imported grammars.\n\nImported grammars can also import other grammars. ANTLR pursues all imported grammars in a depth-first fashion. If two or more imported grammars define rule `r`, ANTLR chooses the first version of `r` it finds. In the following diagram, ANTLR examines grammars in the following order `Nested`, `G1`, `G3`, `G2`.\n\n<img src=images/nested.png width=350>\n\n`Nested` includes the `r` rule from `G3` because it sees that version before the `r` in `G2`.\n\nNot every kind of grammar can import every other kind of grammar:\n\n* Lexer grammars can import lexers, including lexers containing modes.\n* Parsers can import parsers.\n* Combined grammars can import parsers or lexers without modes.\n\nANTLR adds imported rules to the end of the rule list in a main lexer grammar. That means lexer rules in the main grammar get precedence over imported rules. For example, if a main grammar defines rule `IF : 'if' ;` and an imported grammar defines rule `ID : [a-z]+ ;` (which also recognizes `if`), the imported `ID` won’t hide the main grammar’s `IF` token definition.\n\n## Tokens Section\n\nThe purpose of the `tokens` section is to define token types needed by a grammar for which there is no associated lexical rule. The basic syntax is:\n\n```\ntokens { Token1, ..., TokenN }\n```\n\nMost of the time, the tokens section is used to define token types needed by actions in the grammar as shown in Section 10.3, [Recognizing Languages whose Keywords Aren’t Fixed](http://pragprog.com/book/tpantlr2/the-definitive-antlr-4-reference):\n\n```\n// explicitly define keyword token types to avoid implicit definition warnings\ntokens { BEGIN, END, IF, THEN, WHILE }\n \n@lexer::members { // keywords map used in lexer to assign token types\nMap<String,Integer> keywords = new HashMap<String,Integer>() {{\n\tput(\"begin\", KeywordsParser.BEGIN);\n\tput(\"end\", KeywordsParser.END);\n\t...\n}};\n}\n```\n\nThe `tokens` section really just defines a set of tokens to add to the overall set.\n\n```\n$ cat Tok.g4\ngrammar Tok;\ntokens { A, B, C }\na : X ;\n$ antlr4 Tok.g4\nwarning(125): Tok.g4:3:4: implicit definition of token X in parser\n$ cat Tok.tokens\nA=1\nB=2\nC=3\nX=4\n```\n\n## Actions at the Grammar Level\n\nCurrently there are only two defined named actions (for the Java target) used outside of grammar rules: `header` and `members`. The former injects code into the generated recognizer class file, before the recognizer class definition, and the latter injects code into the recognizer class definition, as fields and methods.\n\nFor combined grammars, ANTLR injects the actions into both the parser and the lexer. To restrict an action to the generated parser or lexer, use `@parser::name` or `@lexer::name`.\n\nHere’s an example where the grammar specifies a package for the generated code:\n\n```\ngrammar Count;\n \n@header {\npackage foo;\n}\n \n@members {\nint count = 0;\n}\n \nlist\n@after {System.out.println(count+\" ints\");}\n: INT {count++;} (',' INT {count++;} )*\n;\n \nINT : [0-9]+ ;\nWS : [ \\r\\t\\n]+ -> skip ;\n```\n\nThe grammar itself then should be in directory `foo` so that ANTLR generates code in that same `foo` directory (at least when not using the `-o` ANTLR tool option):\n\n```\n$ cd foo\n$ antlr4 Count.g4 # generates code in the current directory (foo)\n$ ls\nCount.g4\t\tCountLexer.java\tCountParser.java\nCount.tokens\tCountLexer.tokens\nCountBaseListener.java CountListener.java\n$ javac *.java\n$ cd ..\n$ grun foo.Count list\n=> \t9, 10, 11\n=> \tEOF\n<= \t3 ints\n```\n\nThe Java compiler expects classes in package `foo` to be in directory `foo`.\n# Grammar Reference\n\n## Definitions\n\nA **grammar** is a list of rules and terminals, that together define a language.\n\nTerminals define the alphabet of the language, while rules define its structure.\n\nIn Lark, a terminal may be a string, a regular expression, or a concatenation of these and other terminals.\n\nEach rule is a list of terminals and rules, whose location and nesting define the structure of the resulting parse-tree.\n\nA **parsing algorithm** is an algorithm that takes a grammar definition and a sequence of symbols (members of the alphabet), and matches the entirety of the sequence by searching for a structure that is allowed by the grammar.\n\n### General Syntax and notes\n\nGrammars in Lark are based on [EBNF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Backus–Naur_form) syntax, with several enhancements.\n\nEBNF is basically a short-hand for common BNF patterns.\n\nOptionals are expanded:\n\n```ruby\n  a b? c    ->    (a c | a b c)\n```\n\nRepetition is extracted into a recursion:\n\n```ruby\n  a: b*    ->    a: _b_tag\n                 _b_tag: (_b_tag b)?\n```\n\nAnd so on.\n\nLark grammars are composed of a list of definitions and directives, each on its own line. A definition is either a named rule, or a named terminal, with the following syntax, respectively:\n\n```html\n  rule: <EBNF-EXPRESSION>\n      | etc.\n\n  TERM: <EBNF-EXPRESSION>   // Rules aren't allowed\n```\n\n\n**Comments** start with\neither `//` (C++ style) or `#` (Python style, since version 1.1.6)\nand last to the end of the line.\n\nLark begins the parse with the rule 'start', unless specified otherwise in the options.\n\nNames of rules are always in lowercase, while names of terminals are always in uppercase. This distinction has practical effects, for the shape of the generated parse-tree, and the automatic construction of the lexer (aka tokenizer, or scanner).\n\n\n## Terminals\n\nTerminals are used to match text into symbols. They can be defined as a combination of literals and other terminals.\n\n**Syntax:**\n\n```html\n<NAME> [. <priority>] : <literals-and-or-terminals>\n```\n\nTerminal names must be uppercase.\n\nLiterals can be one of:\n\n* `\"string\"`\n* `/regular expression+/`\n* `\"case-insensitive string\"i`\n* `/re with flags/imulx`\n* Literal range: `\"a\"..\"z\"`, `\"1\"..\"9\"`, etc.\n\nTerminals also support grammar operators, such as `|`, `+`, `*` and `?`.\n\nTerminals are a linear construct, and therefore may not contain themselves (recursion isn't allowed).\n\n### Templates\n\nTemplates are expanded when preprocessing the grammar.\n\nDefinition syntax:\n\n```javascript\n  my_template{param1, param2, ...}: <EBNF EXPRESSION>\n```\n\nUse syntax:\n\n```javascript\nsome_rule: my_template{arg1, arg2, ...}\n```\n\nExample:\n```javascript\n_separated{x, sep}: x (sep x)*  // Define a sequence of 'x sep x sep x ...'\n\nnum_list: \"[\" _separated{NUMBER, \",\"} \"]\"   // Will match \"[1, 2, 3]\" etc.\n```\n\n### Priority\n\nTerminals can be assigned a priority to influence lexing. Terminal priorities\nare signed integers with a default value of 0.\n\nWhen using a lexer, the highest priority terminals are always matched first.\n\nWhen using Earley's dynamic lexing, terminal priorities are used to prefer\ncertain lexings and resolve ambiguity.\n\n### Regexp Flags\n\nYou can use flags on regexps and strings. For example:\n\n```perl\nSELECT: \"select\"i     //# Will ignore case, and match SELECT or Select, etc.\nMULTILINE_TEXT: /.+/s\nSIGNED_INTEGER: /\n    [+-]?  # the sign\n    (0|[1-9][0-9]*)  # the digits\n /x\n```\n\nSupported flags are one of: `imslux`. See Python's regex documentation for more details on each one.\n\nRegexps/strings of different flags can only be concatenated in Python 3.6+\n\n#### Notes for when using a lexer:\n\nWhen using a lexer (basic or contextual), it is the grammar-author's responsibility to make sure the literals don't collide, or that if they do, they are matched in the desired order. Literals are matched according to the following precedence:\n\n1. Highest priority first (priority is specified as: TERM.number: ...)\n2. Length of match (for regexps, the longest theoretical match is used)\n3. Length of literal / pattern definition\n4. Name\n\n**Examples:**\n```perl\nIF: \"if\"\nINTEGER : /[0-9]+/\nINTEGER2 : (\"0\"..\"9\")+          //# Same as INTEGER\nDECIMAL.2: INTEGER? \".\" INTEGER  //# Will be matched before INTEGER\nWHITESPACE: (\" \" | /\\t/ )+\nSQL_SELECT: \"select\"i\n```\n\n### Regular expressions & Ambiguity\n\nEach terminal is eventually compiled to a regular expression. All the operators and references inside it are mapped to their respective expressions.\n\nFor example, in the following grammar, `A1` and `A2`, are equivalent:\n```perl\nA1: \"a\" | \"b\"\nA2: /a|b/\n```\n\nThis means that inside terminals, Lark cannot detect or resolve ambiguity, even when using Earley.\n\nFor example, for this grammar:\n```perl\nstart           : (A | B)+\nA               : \"a\" | \"ab\"\nB               : \"b\"\n```\nWe get only one possible derivation, instead of two:\n\n```bash\n>>> p = Lark(g, ambiguity=\"explicit\")\n>>> p.parse(\"ab\")\nTree('start', [Token('A', 'ab')])\n```\n\nThis is happening because Python's regex engine always returns the best matching option. There is no way to access the alternatives.\n\nIf you find yourself in this situation, the recommended solution is to either use the \"dynamic_complete\" lexer, or use rules instead.\n\nExample using rules:\n\n```python\n>>> p = Lark(\"\"\"start: (a | b)+\n...             !a: \"a\" | \"ab\"\n...             !b: \"b\"\n...             \"\"\", ambiguity=\"explicit\")\n>>> print(p.parse(\"ab\").pretty())\n_ambig\n  start\n    a   ab\n  start\n    a   a\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}
