[2026-11-26T23:33:19.469Z] [STDOUT] {"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_1513","type":"command_execution","command":"/bin/bash -lc \"wc -l docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/*.readable.txt && sed -n '1,240p' docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/tree-sitter-grammar.readable.txt && sed -n '1,200p' docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/tree-sitter-incremental.readable.txt && sed -n '190,340p' docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/lark.txt\"","aggregated_output":" 26809 docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/gf.readable.txt\n  1194 docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/spacy.readable.txt\n   112 docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/stanza.readable.txt\n   129 docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/tree-sitter-grammar.readable.txt\n   130 docs/case-studies/issue-16/data/prior-art/tree-sitter-incremental.readable.txt\n 28374 total\nThe Grammar DSL - Tree-sitter\nKeyboard shortcuts\nPress ← or → to navigate between chapters\nPress S or / to search in the book\nPress ? to show this help\nPress Esc to hide this help\nAuto\nLight\nRust\nCoal\nNavy\nAyu\nTree-sitter\nThe Grammar DSL\nThe following is a complete list of built-in functions you can use in your grammar.js to define rules. Use-cases for some\nof these functions will be explained in more detail in later sections.\nSymbols (the $ object) — Every grammar rule is written as a JavaScript function that takes a parameter conventionally\ncalled $. The syntax $.identifier is how you refer to another grammar symbol within a rule. Names starting with $.MISSING\nor $.UNEXPECTED should be avoided as they have special meaning for the tree-sitter test command.\nString and Regex literals — The terminal symbols in a grammar are described using JavaScript strings and regular\nexpressions. Of course during parsing, Tree-sitter does not actually use JavaScript’s regex engine to evaluate these regexes;\nit generates its own regex-matching logic based on the Rust regex syntax as part of each parser. Regex literals are just\nused as a convenient way of writing regular expressions in your grammar. You can use Rust regular expressions in your grammar\nDSL through the RustRegex class. Simply pass your regex pattern as a string:\nnew RustRegex('(?i)[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*') // matches a simple identifier\nUnlike JavaScript’s builtin RegExp class, which takes a pattern and flags as separate arguments, RustRegex only\naccepts a single pattern string. While it doesn’t support separate flags, you can use inline flags within the pattern\nitself. For more details about Rust’s regex syntax and capabilities, check out the Rust regex documentation.\nNote\nOnly a subset of the Regex engine is actually supported. This is due to certain features like lookahead and lookaround\nassertions not being feasible to use in an LR(1) grammar, as well as certain flags being unnecessary for tree-sitter. However,\nplenty of features are supported by default:\nCharacter classes\nCharacter ranges\nCharacter sets\nQuantifiers\nAlternation\nGrouping\nUnicode character escapes\nUnicode property escapes\nSequences : seq(rule1, rule2, ...) — This function creates a rule that matches any number of other rules, one after\nanother. It is analogous to simply writing multiple symbols next to each other in EBNF notation.\nAlternatives : choice(rule1, rule2, ...) — This function creates a rule that matches one of a set of possible\nrules. The order of the arguments does not matter. This is analogous to the | (pipe) operator in EBNF notation.\nRepetitions : repeat(rule) — This function creates a rule that matches zero-or-more occurrences of a given rule.\nIt is analogous to the {x} (curly brace) syntax in EBNF notation.\nRepetitions : repeat1(rule) — This function creates a rule that matches one-or-more occurrences of a given rule.\nThe previous repeat rule is implemented in repeat1 but is included because it is very commonly used.\nOptions : optional(rule) — This function creates a rule that matches zero or one occurrence of a given rule.\nIt is analogous to the [x] (square bracket) syntax in EBNF notation.\nPrecedence : prec(number, rule) — This function marks the given rule with a numerical precedence, which will be\nused to resolve LR(1) Conflicts at parser-generation time. When two rules overlap in a way that represents\neither a true ambiguity or a local ambiguity given one token of lookahead, Tree-sitter will try to resolve the conflict\nby matching the rule with the higher precedence. The default precedence of all rules is zero. This works similarly to the\nprecedence directives in Yacc grammars.\nThis function can also be used to assign lexical precedence to a given\ntoken, but it must be wrapped in a token call, such as token(prec(1, 'foo')). This reads as “the token foo has a\nlexical precedence of 1”. The purpose of lexical precedence is to solve the issue where multiple tokens can match the same\nset of characters, but one token should be preferred over the other. See Lexical Precedence vs Parse Precedence\nfor a more detailed explanation.\nLeft Associativity : prec.left([number], rule) — This function marks the given rule as left-associative (and optionally\napplies a numerical precedence). When an LR(1) conflict arises in which all the rules have the same numerical precedence,\nTree-sitter will consult the rules’ associativity. If there is a left-associative rule, Tree-sitter will prefer matching\na rule that ends earlier. This works similarly to associativity directives in Yacc grammars.\nRight Associativity : prec.right([number], rule) — This function is like prec.left, but it instructs Tree-sitter\nto prefer matching a rule that ends later.\nDynamic Precedence : prec.dynamic(number, rule) — This function is similar to prec, but the given numerical precedence\nis applied at runtime instead of at parser generation time. This is only necessary when handling a conflict dynamically\nusing the conflicts field in the grammar, and when there is a genuine ambiguity: multiple rules correctly match a given\npiece of code. In that event, Tree-sitter compares the total dynamic precedence associated with each rule, and selects the\none with the highest total. This is similar to dynamic precedence directives in Bison grammars.\nTokens : token(rule) — This function marks the given rule as producing only\na single token. Tree-sitter’s default is to treat each String or RegExp literal\nin the grammar as a separate token. Each token is matched separately by the lexer\nand returned as its own leaf node in the tree. The token function allows you to\nexpress a complex rule using the functions described above (rather than as a single\nregular expression) but still have Tree-sitter treat it as a single token.\nThe token function will only accept terminal rules, so token($.foo) will not work.\nYou can think of it as a shortcut for squashing complex rules of strings or regexes\ndown to a single token.\nImmediate Tokens : token.immediate(rule) — Usually, whitespace (and any other extras, such as comments) is optional\nbefore each token. This function means that the token will only match if there is no whitespace.\nAliases : alias(rule, name) — This function causes the given rule to appear with an alternative name in the syntax\ntree. If name is a symbol, as in alias($.foo, $.bar), then the aliased rule will appear as a named node\ncalled bar. And if name is a string literal, as in alias($.foo, 'bar'), then the aliased rule will appear as an\nanonymous node, as if the rule had been written as the simple string.\nField Names : field(name, rule) — This function assigns a field name to the child node(s) matched by the given\nrule. In the resulting syntax tree, you can then use that field name to access specific children.\nReserved Keywords : reserved(wordset, rule)  — This function will override the global reserved word set with the\none passed into the wordset parameter. This is useful for contextual keywords, such as if in JavaScript, which cannot\nbe used as a variable name in most contexts, but can be used as a property name.\nEnd of Input : eof() — This function creates a rule that matches the end of the input, without consuming any\ncharacters. It may only appear as the final symbol of a rule, and is useful when a rule should match either an explicit\nterminator (such as a newline) or the end of the file. Choice branches where other symbols follow eof() can never\nmatch, so they are dropped, and eof() is not allowed inside token().\nIn addition to the name and rules fields, grammars have a few other optional public fields that influence the behavior\nof the parser. Each of these fields is a function that accepts the grammar object ($) as its only parameter, like the\ngrammar rules themselves. These fields are:\nextras — an array of tokens that may appear anywhere in the language. This is often used for whitespace and\ncomments. The default value of extras is to accept whitespace. To control whitespace explicitly, specify\nextras: $ => [] in your grammar. See the section on using extras for more details.\ninline — an array of rule names that should be automatically removed from the grammar by replacing all of their\nusages with a copy of their definition. This is useful for rules that are used in multiple places but for which you don’t\nwant to create syntax tree nodes at runtime.\nconflicts — an array of arrays of rule names. Each inner array represents a set of rules that’s involved in an\nLR(1) conflict that is intended to exist in the grammar. When these conflicts occur at runtime, Tree-sitter will use\nthe GLR algorithm to explore all the possible interpretations. If multiple parses end up succeeding, Tree-sitter will\npick the subtree whose corresponding rule has the highest total dynamic precedence.\nexternals — an array of token names which can be returned by an\nexternal scanner. External scanners allow you to write custom C code which runs during the lexing\nprocess to handle lexical rules (e.g. Python’s indentation tokens) that cannot be described by regular expressions.\nprecedences — an array of arrays of strings, where each array of strings defines named precedence levels in descending\norder. These names can be used in the prec functions to define precedence relative only to other names in the array, rather\nthan globally. Can only be used with parse precedence, not lexical precedence.\nword — the name of a token that will match keywords to the\nkeyword extraction optimization.\nsupertypes — an array of rule names which should be considered to be ‘supertypes’ in the generated\nnode types file. Supertype rules are automatically hidden from the parse tree, regardless\nof whether their names start with an underscore. The main use case for supertypes is to group together multiple different\nkinds of nodes under a single abstract category, such as “expression” or “declaration”. See the section on using supertypes\nfor more details.\nreserved — similar in structure to the main rules property, an object of reserved word sets associated with an\narray of reserved rules. The reserved rule in the array must be a terminal token meaning it must be a string, regex, token,\nor terminal rule. The reserved rule must also exist and be used in the grammar, specifying arbitrary tokens will not work.\nThe first reserved word set in the object is the global word set, meaning it applies to every rule in every parse state.\nHowever, certain keywords are contextual, depending on the rule. For example, in JavaScript, keywords are typically not\nallowed as ordinary variables, however, they can be used as a property name. In this situation, the reserved function\nwould be used, and the word set to pass in would be the name of the word set that is declared in the reserved object that\ncorresponds to an empty array, signifying no keywords are reserved.\nAdvanced Parsing - Tree-sitter\nKeyboard shortcuts\nPress ← or → to navigate between chapters\nPress S or / to search in the book\nPress ? to show this help\nPress Esc to hide this help\nAuto\nLight\nRust\nCoal\nNavy\nAyu\nTree-sitter\nAdvanced Parsing\nEditing\nIn applications like text editors, you often need to re-parse a file after its source code has changed. Tree-sitter is designed\nto support this use case efficiently. There are two steps required. First, you must edit the syntax tree, which adjusts\nthe ranges of its nodes so that they stay in sync with the code.\ntypedef struct {\nuint32_t start_byte;\nuint32_t old_end_byte;\nuint32_t new_end_byte;\nTSPoint start_point;\nTSPoint old_end_point;\nTSPoint new_end_point;\n} TSInputEdit;\nvoid ts_tree_edit(TSTree *, const TSInputEdit *);\nThen, you can call ts_parser_parse again, passing in the old tree. This will create a new tree that internally shares\nstructure with the old tree.\nWhen you edit a syntax tree, the positions of its nodes will change. If you have stored any TSNode instances outside of\nthe TSTree, you must update their positions separately, using the same TSInputEdit value, in order to update their\ncached positions.\nvoid ts_node_edit(TSNode *, const TSInputEdit *);\nThis ts_node_edit function is only needed in the case where you have retrieved TSNode instances before editing the\ntree, and then after editing the tree, you want to continue to use those specific node instances. Often, you’ll just want\nto re-fetch nodes from the edited tree, in which case ts_node_edit is not needed.\nMulti-language Documents\nSometimes, different parts of a file may be written in different languages. For example, templating languages like EJS\nand ERB allow you to generate HTML by writing a mixture of HTML and another language like JavaScript or Ruby.\nTree-sitter handles these types of documents by allowing you to create a syntax tree based on the text in certain\nranges of a file.\ntypedef struct {\nTSPoint start_point;\nTSPoint end_point;\nuint32_t start_byte;\nuint32_t end_byte;\n} TSRange;\nvoid ts_parser_set_included_ranges(\nTSParser *self,\nconst TSRange *ranges,\nuint32_t range_count\n);\nFor example, consider this ERB document:\n<ul>\n<% people.each do |person| %>\n<li><%= person.name %></li>\n<% end %>\n</ul>\nConceptually, it can be represented by three syntax trees with overlapping ranges: an ERB syntax tree, a Ruby syntax tree,\nand an HTML syntax tree. You could generate these syntax trees with the following code:\n#include <string.h>\n#include <tree_sitter/api.h>\n// These functions are each implemented in their own repo.\nconst TSLanguage *tree_sitter_embedded_template(void);\nconst TSLanguage *tree_sitter_html(void);\nconst TSLanguage *tree_sitter_ruby(void);\nint main(int argc, const char **argv) {\nconst char *text = argv[1];\nunsigned len = strlen(text);\n// Parse the entire text as ERB.\nTSParser *parser = ts_parser_new();\nts_parser_set_language(parser, tree_sitter_embedded_template());\nTSTree *erb_tree = ts_parser_parse_string(parser, NULL, text, len);\nTSNode erb_root_node = ts_tree_root_node(erb_tree);\n// In the ERB syntax tree, find the ranges of the `content` nodes,\n// which represent the underlying HTML, and the `code` nodes, which\n// represent the interpolated Ruby.\nTSRange html_ranges[10];\nTSRange ruby_ranges[10];\nunsigned html_range_count = 0;\nunsigned ruby_range_count = 0;\nunsigned child_count = ts_node_child_count(erb_root_node);\nfor (unsigned i = 0; i < child_count; i++) {\nTSNode node = ts_node_child(erb_root_node, i);\nif (strcmp(ts_node_type(node), \"content\") == 0) {\nhtml_ranges[html_range_count++] = (TSRange) {\nts_node_start_point(node),\nts_node_end_point(node),\nts_node_start_byte(node),\nts_node_end_byte(node),\n};\n} else {\nTSNode code_node = ts_node_named_child(node, 0);\nruby_ranges[ruby_range_count++] = (TSRange) {\nts_node_start_point(code_node),\nts_node_end_point(code_node),\nts_node_start_byte(code_node),\nts_node_end_byte(code_node),\n};\n}\n}\n// Use the HTML ranges to parse the HTML.\nts_parser_set_language(parser, tree_sitter_html());\nts_parser_set_included_ranges(parser, html_ranges, html_range_count);\nTSTree *html_tree = ts_parser_parse_string(parser, NULL, text, len);\nTSNode html_root_node = ts_tree_root_node(html_tree);\n// Use the Ruby ranges to parse the Ruby.\nts_parser_set_language(parser, tree_sitter_ruby());\nts_parser_set_included_ranges(parser, ruby_ranges, ruby_range_count);\nTSTree *ruby_tree = ts_parser_parse_string(parser, NULL, text, len);\nTSNode ruby_root_node = ts_tree_root_node(ruby_tree);\n// Print all three trees.\nchar *erb_sexp = ts_node_string(erb_root_node);\nchar *html_sexp = ts_node_string(html_root_node);\nchar *ruby_sexp = ts_node_string(ruby_root_node);\nprintf(\"ERB: %s\\n\", erb_sexp);\nprintf(\"HTML: %s\\n\", html_sexp);\nprintf(\"Ruby: %s\\n\", ruby_sexp);\nreturn 0;\n}\nThis API allows for great flexibility in how languages can be composed. Tree-sitter is not responsible for mediating the\ninteractions between languages. Instead, you are free to do that using arbitrary application-specific logic.\nConcurrency\nTree-sitter supports multi-threaded use cases by making syntax trees very cheap to copy.\nTSTree *ts_tree_copy(const TSTree *);\nInternally, copying a syntax tree just entails incrementing an atomic reference count. Conceptually, it provides you a new\ntree which you can freely query, edit, reparse, or delete on a new thread while continuing to use the original tree on a\ndifferent thread.\nCaution\nIndividual TSTree instances are not thread safe; you must copy a tree if you want to use it on multiple threads simultaneously.\n    a   a\n    b   b\n```\n\nExample using dynamic-complete:\n\n```python\n>>> g = \"\"\"\n...     start: (A | B)+\n...     A    : \"a\" | \"ab\"\n...     B    : \"b\"\n... \"\"\"\n>>> p = Lark(g, ambiguity=\"explicit\", lexer=\"dynamic_complete\")\n>>> rich.print(p.parse(\"ab\"))\n_ambig\n├── start\n│   └── ab\n└── start\n    ├── a\n    └── b\n```\n\n(note: the dynamic-complete lexer can significantly affect the performance of the parser)\n\n## Rules\n\n**Syntax:**\n```html\n<name> : <items-to-match>  [-> <alias> ]\n       | ...\n```\n\nNames of rules and aliases are always in lowercase.\n\nRule definitions can be extended to the next line by using the OR operator (signified by a pipe: `|` ).\n\nAn alias is a name for the specific rule alternative. It affects tree construction.\n\n\nEach item is one of:\n\n* `rule`\n* `TERMINAL`\n* `\"string literal\"` or `/regexp literal/`\n* `(item item ..)` - Group items\n* `[item item ..]` - Maybe. Same as `(item item ..)?`, but when `maybe_placeholders=True`, generates `None` if there is no match.\n* `item?` - Zero or one instances of item (\"maybe\")\n* `item*` - Zero or more instances of item\n* `item+` - One or more instances of item\n* `item ~ n` - Exactly *n* instances of item\n* `item ~ n..m` - Between *n* to *m* instances of item (not recommended for wide ranges, due to performance issues)\n\nNote that all operators, including `~ n`, apply directly to the item on their left.\nFor instance `a ~ 2 b ~ 3` is parsed as `(a ~ 2) (b ~ 3)`.\n\n**Examples:**\n```perl\nhello_world: \"hello\" \"world\"\nmul: (mul \"*\")? number     //# Left-recursion is allowed and encouraged!\nexpr: expr operator expr\n    | value               //# Multi-line, belongs to expr\n\nfour_words: word ~ 4\n```\n\n### Priority\n\nLike terminals, rules can be assigned a priority. Rule priorities are signed\nintegers with a default value of 0.\n\nWhen using LALR, the highest priority rules are used to resolve collision errors.\n\nWhen using Earley, rule priorities are used to resolve ambiguity.\n\n<a name=\"dirs\"></a>\n## Directives\n\n### %ignore\n\nAll occurrences of the terminal will be ignored, and won't be part of the parse.\n\nUsing the `%ignore` directive results in a cleaner grammar.\n\nIt's especially important for the LALR(1) algorithm, because adding whitespace (or comments, or other extraneous elements) explicitly in the grammar, harms its predictive abilities, which are based on a lookahead of 1.\n\n**Syntax:**\n```html\n%ignore <TERMINAL>\n```\n**Examples:**\n```perl\n%ignore \" \"\n\nCOMMENT: \"#\" /[^\\n]/*\n%ignore COMMENT\n```\n### %import\n\nAllows one to import terminals and rules from lark grammars.\n\nWhen importing rules, all their dependencies will be imported into a namespace, to avoid collisions. To override any of their dependencies (e.g. like you would override methods when inheriting a class), use the ``%override`` directive.\n\n**Syntax:**\n```html\n%import <module>.<TERMINAL>\n%import <module>.<rule>\n%import <module>.<TERMINAL> -> <NEWTERMINAL>\n%import <module>.<rule> -> <newrule>\n%import <module> (<TERM1>, <TERM2>, <rule1>, <rule2>)\n```\n\nIf the module path is absolute, Lark will attempt to load it from the built-in directory (which currently contains `common.lark`, `lark.lark`, `python.lark`, and `unicode.lark`).\n\nIf the module path is relative, such as `.path.to.file`, Lark will attempt to load it from the current working directory. Grammars must have the `.lark` extension.\n\nThe rule or terminal can be imported under another name (an alias) with the `->` syntax.\n\n**Example:**\n```perl\n%import common.NUMBER\n\n%import .terminals_file (A, B, C)\n\n%import .rules_file.rule_a -> rule_b\n```\n\nNote that `%ignore` directives cannot be imported. Imported rules will abide by the `%ignore` directives declared in the main grammar.\n\n### %declare\n\nDeclare a terminal without defining it. Useful for plugins.\n\n### %override\n\nOverride a rule or terminals, affecting all references to it, even in imported grammars.\n\nUseful for implementing an inheritance pattern when importing grammars.\n\n**Example:**\n```perl\n%import my_grammar (start, number, NUMBER)\n\n// Add hex support to my_grammar\n%override number: NUMBER | /0x\\w+/\n```\n\n### %extend\n\nExtend the definition of a rule or terminal, e.g. add a new option on what it can match, like when separated with `|`.\n\nUseful for splitting up a definition of a complex rule with many different options over multiple files.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Starting from raw text, Stanza divides it into sentences and words, and then can recognize parts of speech and entities, do syntactic analysis, and more. Stanza brings state-of-the-art NLP models to languages of your choosing.\nTable of contents\nAbout\nGetting Started\nLicense\nMain Contributors\nCiting Stanza in papers\nLinks\nAbout\nStanza is a Python natural language analysis package. It contains tools, which can be used in a pipeline, to convert a string containing human language text into lists of sentences and words, to generate base forms of those words, their parts of speech and morphological features, to give a syntactic structure dependency parse, and to recognize named entities. The toolkit is designed to be parallel among more than 70 languages, using the Universal Dependencies formalism.\nStanza is built with highly accurate neural network components that also enable efficient training and evaluation with your own annotated data. The modules are built on top of the PyTorch library. You will get much faster performance if you run the software on a GPU-enabled machine.\nIn addition, Stanza includes a Python interface to the CoreNLP Java package and inherits additional functionality from there, such as constituency parsing, coreference resolution, and linguistic pattern matching. (However, you do not need to have CoreNLP to use any of the core, native Stanza functionality.)\nTo summarize, Stanza features:\nNative Python implementation requiring minimal efforts to set up;\nFull neural network pipeline for robust text analytics, including tokenization, multi-word token (MWT) expansion, lemmatization, part-of-speech (POS) and morphological features tagging, dependency parsing, and named entity recognition;\nPretrained neural models supporting 70 (human) languages;\nA stable, officially maintained Python interface to CoreNLP.\nBelow is an overview of Stanza’s neural network NLP pipeline:\nGetting Started\nWe strongly recommend installing Stanza with pip, which is as simple as:\npip install stanza\nTo see Stanza’s neural pipeline in action, you can launch the Python interactive interpreter, and try the following commands:\n>>> import stanza\n>>> stanza.download('en') # download English model\n>>> nlp = stanza.Pipeline('en') # initialize English neural pipeline\n>>> doc = nlp(\"Barack Obama was born in Hawaii.\") # run annotation over a sentence\nYou should be able to see all the annotations in the example by running the following commands:\n>>> print(doc)\n>>> print(doc.entities)\nFor more details on how to use the neural network pipeline, please see our Installation, Getting Started Guide, and Tutorials pages.\nAside from the neural pipeline, Stanza also provides the official Python wrapper for accessing the Java Stanford CoreNLP package. The input to the tokenizer is a unicode text, and the output is a\nDoc object. To construct a Doc object, you need a\nVocab instance, a sequence of word strings, and optionally a\nsequence of spaces booleans, which allow you to maintain alignment of the\ntokens into the original string.\nImportant note\nspaCy’s tokenization is non-destructive, which means that you’ll always be\nable to reconstruct the original input from the tokenized output. Whitespace\ninformation is preserved in the tokens and no information is added or removed\nduring tokenization. This is kind of a core principle of spaCy’s Doc object:\ndoc.text == input_text should always hold true.\nDuring processing, spaCy first tokenizes the text, i.e. segments it into\nwords, punctuation and so on. This is done by applying rules specific to each\nlanguage. For example, punctuation at the end of a sentence should be split off\n– whereas “U.K.” should remain one token. Each Doc consists of individual\ntokens, and we can iterate over them:\nEditable CodespaCy v3.7 · Python 3 · via Binder\nrun\n012345678910\nAppleislookingatbuyingU.K.startupfor$1billion\nFirst, the raw text is split on whitespace characters, similar to\ntext.split(' '). Then, the tokenizer processes the text from left to right. On\neach substring, it performs two checks:\nDoes the substring match a tokenizer exception rule? For example, “don’t”\ndoes not contain whitespace, but should be split into two tokens, “do” and\n“n’t”, while “U.K.” should always remain one token.\nCan a prefix, suffix or infix be split off? For example punctuation like\ncommas, periods, hyphens or quotes.\nIf there’s a match, the rule is applied and the tokenizer continues its loop,\nstarting with the newly split substrings. This way, spaCy can split complex,\nnested tokens like combinations of abbreviations and multiple punctuation\nmarks.\nTokenizer exception: Special-case rule to split a string into several\ntokens or prevent a token from being split when punctuation rules are\napplied.\nPrefix: Character(s) at the beginning, e.g. $, (, “, ¿.\nSuffix: Character(s) at the end, e.g. km, ), ”, !.\nInfix: Character(s) in between, e.g. -, --, /, ….\nWhile punctuation rules are usually pretty general, tokenizer exceptions\nstrongly depend on the specifics of the individual language. This is why each\navailable language has its own subclass, like\nEnglish or German, that loads in lists of hard-coded data and exception\nrules.\nAlgorithm details: How spaCy's tokenizer works¶\nspaCy introduces a novel tokenization algorithm that gives a better balance\nbetween performance, ease of definition and ease of alignment into the original\nstring.\nAfter consuming a prefix or suffix, we consult the special cases again. We want\nthe special cases to handle things like “don’t” in English, and we want the same\nrule to work for “(don’t)!“. We do this by splitting off the open bracket, then\nthe exclamation, then the closed bracket, and finally matching the special case.\nHere’s an implementation of the algorithm in Python optimized for readability\nrather than performance:\nThe algorithm can be summarized as follows:\nIterate over space-separated substrings.\nCheck whether we have an explicitly defined special case for this substring.\nIf we do, use it.\nLook for a token match. If there is a match, stop processing and keep this\ntoken.\nCheck whether we have an explicitly defined special case for this substring.\nIf we do, use it.\nOtherwise, try to consume one prefix. If we consumed a prefix, go back to #3,\nso that the token match and special cases always get priority.\nIf we didn’t consume a prefix, try to consume a suffix and then go back to\n#3.\nIf we can’t consume a prefix or a suffix, look for a URL match.\nIf there’s no URL match, then look for a special case.\nLook for “infixes” – stuff like hyphens etc. and split the substring into\ntokens on all infixes.\nOnce we can’t consume any more of the string, handle it as a single token.\nMake a final pass over the text to check for special cases that include\nspaces or that were missed due to the incremental processing of affixes.\nGlobal and language-specific tokenizer data is supplied via the language\ndata in spacy/lang. The tokenizer exceptions\ndefine special cases like “don’t” in English, which needs to be split into two\ntokens: {ORTH: \"do\"} and {ORTH: \"n't\", NORM: \"not\"}. The prefixes, suffixes\nand infixes mostly define punctuation rules – for example, when to split off\nperiods (at the end of a sentence), and when to leave tokens containing periods\nintact (abbreviations like “U.S.”).\nShould I change the language data or add custom tokenizer rules?¶\nTokenization rules that are specific to one language, but can be generalized\nacross that language, should ideally live in the language data in\nspacy/lang – we always appreciate pull requests!\nAnything that’s specific to a domain or text type – like financial trading\nabbreviations or Bavarian youth slang – should be added as a special case rule\nto your tokenizer instance. If you’re dealing with a lot of customizations, it\nmight make sense to create an entirely custom subclass.\nAdding special case tokenization rules\nMost domains have at least some idiosyncrasies that require custom tokenization\nrules. Why?\nUtt\nLink Grammar Parser\n===================\n***Version 5.13.2***\n\n![Main](https://github.com/opencog/link-grammar/actions/workflows/main.yml/badge.svg)\n![node.js](https://github.com/opencog/link-grammar/actions/workflows/bindings-js.yml/badge.svg)\n\nThe Link Grammar Parser exhibits the linguistic (natural language)\nstructure of English, Thai, Russian, Arabic, Persian and limited subsets\nof a half-dozen other languages. This structure is a graph of typed\nlinks (edges) between the words in a sentence. One may obtain the\nmore conventional HPSG (constituent) and dependency style parses\nfrom Link Grammar by applying a collection of rules to convert to\nthese different formats. This is possible because Link Grammar goes\na bit \"deeper\" into the \"syntactico-semantic\" structure of a sentence:\nit provides considerably more fine-grained and detailed information\nthan what is commonly available in conventional parsers.\n\nThe theory of Link Grammar parsing was originally developed in 1991\nby Davy Temperley, John Lafferty and Daniel Sleator, at the time\nprofessors of linguistics and computer science at the Carnegie Mellon\nUniversity.  The three initial publications on this theory provide the\nbest introduction and overview; since then, there have been hundreds\nof publications further exploring, examining and extending the ideas.\n\nAlthough based on the\n[original Carnegie-Mellon code base](https://www.link.cs.cmu.edu/link/),\nthe current Link Grammar package has dramatically evolved and is\nprofoundly different from earlier versions.  There have been innumerable\nbug fixes; performance has improved by several orders of magnitude.\nThe package is fully multi-threaded, fully UTF-8 enabled, and has been\nscrubbed for security, enabling cloud deployment.  Parse coverage of\nEnglish has been dramatically improved; other languages have been added\n(most notably, Thai and Russian). There is a raft of new features,\nincluding support for morphology, dialects, and a fine-grained weight\n(cost) system, allowing vector-embedding-like behaviour. There is a\nnew, sophisticated tokenizer tailored for morphology: it can offer\nalternative splittings for morphologically ambiguous words.\nDictionaries can be updated at run-time, enabling systems that perform\ncontinuous learning of grammar to also parse at the same time. That is,\ndictionary updates and parsing are mutually thread-safe. Classes of\nwords can be recognized with regexes. Random planar graph parsing is\nfully supported; this allows uniform sampling of the space of planar\ngraphs.  A detailed report of what has changed can be found in the\n[ChangeLog](ChangeLog).\n\nThis code is released under the LGPL license, making it freely\navailable for both private and commercial use, with few restrictions.\nThe terms of the license are given in the LICENSE file included with\nthis software.\n\nPlease see the\n[main web page](https://opencog.github.io/link-grammar-website/)\nfor more information.  This version is a continuation of the\n[original CMU parser](http://www.link.cs.cmu.edu/link).\n\n### New!\nAs of version 5.9.0, the system include an experimental system for\ngenerating sentences. These are specified using a \"fill in the blanks\"\nAPI, where words are substituted into wild-card locations, whenever the\nresult is a grammatically valid sentence. Additional details are in\nthe man page: `man link-generator` (in the `man` subdirectory).\n\nThis generator is used in the\n[OpenCog Language Learning](https://github.com/opencog/learn)\nproject, which aims to automatically learn Link Grammars from corpora,\nusing brand-new and innovative information theoretic techniques,\nsomewhat similar to those found in artificial neural nets (deep\nlearning), but using explicitly symbolic representations.\n\nQuick Overview\n---------------\nThe parser includes API's in various different programming languages,\nas well as a handy command-line tool for playing with it.  Here's some\ntypical output:\n```\nlinkparser> This is a test!\n\tLinkage 1, cost vector = (UNUSED=0 DIS= 0.00 LEN=6)\n\n    +-------------Xp------------+\n    +----->WV----->+---Ost--+   |\n    +---Wd---+-Ss*b+  +Ds**c+   |\n    |        |     |  |     |   |\nLEFT-WALL this.p is.v a  test.n !\n\n(S (NP this.p) (VP is.v (NP a test.n)) !)\n\n            LEFT-WALL    0.000  Wd+ hWV+ Xp+\n               this.p    0.000  Wd- Ss*b+\n                 is.v    0.000  Ss- dWV- O*t+\n                    a    0.000  Ds**c+\n               test.n    0.000  Ds**c- Os-\n                    !    0.000  Xp- RW+\n           RIGHT-WALL    0.000  RW-\n\n```\nThis rather busy display illustrates many interesting things. For\nexample, the `Ss*b` link connects the verb and the subject, and\nindicates that the subject is singular.  Likewise, the `Ost` link\nconnects the verb and the object, and also indicates that the object\nis singular. The `WV` (verb-wall) link points at the head-verb of\nthe sentence, while the `Wd` link points at the head-noun. The `Xp`\nlink connects to the trailing punctuation. The `Ds**c` link connects\nthe noun to the determiner: it again confirms that the noun is singular,\nand also that the noun starts with a consonant. (The `PH` link, not\nrequired here, is used to force phonetic agreement, distinguishing\n'a' from 'an').  These link types are documented in the\n[English Link Documentation](https://opencog.github.io/link-grammar-website/dict/index.html).\n\nThe bottom of the display is a listing of the \"disjuncts\" used for\neach word. The disjuncts are simply a list of the connectors that\nwere employed to form the links. They are particularly interesting\nbecause they serve as an extremely fine-grained form of a \"part of\nspeech\".  Thus, for example: the disjunct `S- O+` indicates a\ntransitive verb: its a verb that takes both a subject and an object.\nThe additional markup above indicates that 'is' is not only being used\nas a transitive verb, but it also indicates finer details: a transitive\nverb that took a singular subject, and was used (is usable as) the head\nverb of a sentence.  The floating-point value is the \"cost\" of the\ndisjunct; it very roughly captures the idea of the log-probability\nof this particular grammatical usage.  Much as parts-of-speech correlate\nwith word-meanings, so also fine-grains parts-of-speech correlate with\nmuch finer distinctions and gradations of meaning.\n\nThe link-grammar parser also supports morphological analysis. Here is\nan example in Russian:\n```\nlinkparser> это теста\n\tLinkage 1, cost vector = (UNUSED=0 DIS= 0.00 LEN=4)\n\n             +-----MVAip-----+\n    +---Wd---+       +-LLCAG-+\n    |        |       |       |\nLEFT-WALL это.msi тест.= =а.ndnpi\n```\n\nThe `LL` link connects the stem 'тест' to the suffix 'а'. The `MVA`\nlink connects only to the suffix, because, in Russian, it is the\nsuffixes that carry all of the syntactic structure, and not the stems.\nThe Russian lexis is\n[documented here](https://opencog.github.io/link-grammar-website/russian/doc/).\n\nThe Thai dictionary is now fully developed, effectively covering the\nentire language.  \"body\": \"Hypothesis: translation in unrestricted grammars may be solved with dependent translation.\\n\\nAs we do in dependent logic in relative meta logic (when probability of single statement depends on probability of other statement, including recursively).\\n\\nTranslation changes depending on physical or abstract referent (or resolution of meaning of the word).\\n\\nAnd sometimes multiple resolutions of meaning are intentional as in irony, paradoxes as so on.\\n\\nAll of paradoxes are links and fundamental laws, where we link something that is opposite or contradictory, but enviably connected.\\n\\nSo may there there is a way to deterministically translate between all languages, including natural languages.\\n\\nWe also need to make sure we precisely record any imprecision of any statement.\\n\\nLike for example `person` is any person, `white person` is `any white person`, where `white` can reference anything white about that person, like `any person with a white skin` or `any person fully painted white` or `any person mostly white` and so on.\\n\\nBut as long as we make more concrete description the range of possible values gets smaller.\\n\\nThat means for example when we use associative model with type system defined as fractal like:\\nType -> SubType\\nSubType -> SubType\\nSubType -> Value.\\n\\nWe actually still get type, subtype and value as types, but on each step we make them much more narrow.\\n\\nSo it looks like there should be one to one match between natural language and formal type system.\\n\\nSo we always work with ranges, and by calculating frequencies of language corpus we can have some probabilities which more specific type or description is most likely.\\n\\nYet for best translation (most likely and more correct) we should prefer such translation, which survives the round trip.\\n\\nFor example:\\n\\n`белый` <-> `white`\\n\\n`белый человек` <-> `white person`\\n\\nIn both languages these are highly likely.\\n\\nAnd this example actually survives round trip, so that is the translation we should end up with using by default.\\n\\nIn programming language it may mean:\\n\\n```\\nstruct Person {\\n   Color color = Color.White;\\n}\\n```\\n\\nAnd so on.\\n\\nWe also can see how Person is usually described on GitHub, and in the internet and so on, and if we have knowledge about corpus, we can have some probabilities on what to include.\\n\\nWe can also use the language description for requirements that will adjust requirements.\\n\\nSo when we define enough dependent details about anything in a language, we just specify a more concrete type, set or category.\\n\\nThat is the vision.\\n\\nWe should start by supporting full translation of something simple via meta language see best practices of https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language\\n\\nBy simple I mean http://helloworldcollection.de, and https://rosettacode.org/wiki/Rosetta_Code\\n\\nSo once we take top 20-30 most used programming languages and support parsing all of them into meta language and back (basic roundtrip CST survival), we should also support translation from meta language expression to meta language expression, where we still in meta language, yet convert one abstraction to another (equivalent translation, with different levels of abstractions), yet at the same time we support exactly all concepts of each such language separately.\\n\\nFor example we can have function with no return value and no argument in both C, C#, C++ and so on, they match 1 to 1.\\n\\nYet we clearly have dependent expressions in languages, for example in `printf(\\\"Hello World!\\\\n\\\");` we have `printf` function depended on its import via `#include <stdio.h>`.\\n\\nYet effect of `printf(\\\"Hello World!\\\\n\\\");` is equivalent to effect of `System.Console.WriteLine(\\\"Hello, World!\\\");`.\\n\\nYet main function C depends only on file, yet in C# function depends also on class.\\n\\nSo if we select configuration of translation as `same effect` we do `meta language` -> `meta language` translation/transformation first, and only after we translatated from C expression in `meta language` to equivalent expression  of C# `meta language` we can do materialization or formatting or translation from meta language to C#.\\n\\nIf `literal` translation configuration we can preserve source code <stdio.h>\\n\\nmain()\\n{\\n    /* print \\\"Hello World!\\\" into console followed by new line symbol by function call */\\n    printf(\\\"Hello World!\\\\n\\\");\\n}\\n```\\n\\ngoes to\\n\\n```\\n/* Scrolling is mapped block by block, so blocks of different sizes stay aligned.\\n  - Lines that map to each other get matching colours, as in Compiler Explorer.\\n- **Comment and identifier language selectors on both sides.** The option checkboxes are now below the editors.\\n- **Comments are translated.** A shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`) is used both to detect a comment's language and to translate it.\\n  - `// Привет мир` → `// Hello world`.\\n  - «Привет» is now detected as Russian.\\n  - «Как хорошо покакать?» translates to \\\"How good to poop?\\\" (free prose translation).\\n- **Deeper grammars.**\\n  - Prose reads as `Prose > Sentence > Word`, with concepts and parts of speech.\\n  - Comments and strings are read with their own grammars (code in prose, prose in code). Long texts are stored once and referred to by id. Use `--shallow` for the plain tree.\\n- **A more general meta language.** `print` is a call to the library function `print-line`.\\n- **Assembly and intermediate languages.** NASM, GNU as, ARM64, LLVM IR, WebAssembly text, CIL and JVM bytecode are written and read back.\\n- **Language versions.** `javascript@es5`, `php@5`, `csharp@5`, `python@2`, `python@3.5`, `lua@5.1`, `java@1.4`, `swift@1` and `scala@2.9` are available. `registerLanguageVersion` adds a version of your own.\\n- **More tasks and corpora.**\\n  - 22 Rosetta Code tasks go through all 33 programming languages and the 7 machine targets.\\n  - 33 of the 34 programs of the Hello World Collection are read.\\n  - `check-equivalence` checks that a translation does what its source does.\\n- **Debugging and research.**\\n  - `--trace` prints the tree after every stage, and the web app logs translations and editor-sync events with `?debug`.\\n  - formal-ai was tried on six tasks; its failures are reported as link-assistant/formal-ai#1641 and link-assistant/formal-ai#1642.\\n\\n### Screenshots\\n\\nLine mapping in the linked Monaco editors:\\n\\n![mapping](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-mapping.png?raw=true)\\n\\nComment and identifier language selectors on both sides:\\n\\n![selectors](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-selectors.png?raw=true)\\n\\n![style](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-style.png?raw=true)\\n\\n### Tests\\n\\n- JavaScript: `npm test` passes 1823 tests, with 1 skipped (shellcheck is not on the PATH locally).\\n  - Tests touched by this PR include `layout`, `comments`, `prose`, `nesting`, `language-versions`, `machine-dialects`, `hello-world-dialects`, `identifiers` and `ranking`. Summary\\n\\nFixes #12\\n\\nThis PR covers every point of issue 12: the web demo, the meta-language view, rules and settings stored as Links Notation instead of JSON, skins, a case study, debug output, upstream reports, and an audit of earlier issues. The JavaScript and Rust versions behave the same.\\n\\nThe case study (data, timeline, requirements, root causes, solutions, audit) is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-12/README.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-12-6c3cea9725cc/docs/case-studies/issue-12/README.md).\\n\\n## Requirements → implementation → verification\\n\\n| # | Requirement | Done in | Checked by |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| 1 | Content of any size; the title and inputs don't jump | `styles.css`: fixed control heights, pickers of fixed width, the example note on its own line of fixed height, panes between `--pane-min` and `--pane-max` | E2E `keepsTheLayoutStill`: the title and pickers stay at the same position for a 1-line and a 30-line text |\\n| 2 | Optional Monaco editor, highlighted from our meta language | `CodeEditor.js`, `monaco.js`, `highlight.js`; a \\\"Text editor\\\" setting (plain or Monaco). Monaco loads only when chosen | E2E `editsInMonaco`; `js/tests/universal-app-issue-12.test.js` |\\n| 3 | Left and right panes always the same height | `.pane` grid rows stretch to the same height; Monaco reports its content height | E2E `keepsTheLayoutStill`, `editsInMonaco` |\\n| 4 | \\\"How it works\\\" moved down | `App.js`: a full-width `about-panel` below the translator | Screenshots |\\n| 5 | Word wrap on/off | `#word-wrap` switch plus a setting; Monaco `wordWrap` | E2E `wrapsLongLines` |\\n| 6 | Rules on their own tab | Rules tab (`RulesEditor.js`, with rows and the Links Notation text); the Translate tab shows a note while rules are active | E2E `detectsAndTranslatesPartially`, `editsRulesAsLinksNotation` |\\n| 7 | Every element aligned | One control height, one corner radius, labels on one baseline, a square swap button, an options row that wraps on narrow screens | Screenshots (desktop, mobile, dark, glass) |\\n| 8 | No JSON by default; When standard input isn't ready yet, `readFileSync(0)` throws `EAGAIN` (for example `(sleep 1; echo 'print(1)') | universal-translator translate python javascript -`), and a reader that closes early (`| head`) caused an unhandled `EPIPE`. Now `readStandardInput` waits through `EAGAIN`, and `EPIPE` ends the CLI quietly. The test `js/tests/cli-pipes.test.js` uses real shell pipes; it fails before the fix and passes after.\\n- **P9**: `coverage` and `detect` printed JSON by default, against requirement 8. They now print indented Links Notation in both CLIs; `--json` still prints JSON.\\n\\nNot done in this PR.

Every one found is fixed in this pull request. The full case study is in [`dev/log/issues/10/pulls/11/README.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-10-ac0b270fdd45/dev/log/issues/10/pulls/11/README.md). A read-only `preview-check` job renders the images on pull requests. Container steps use `bash`. Preview images regenerated. Rejected findings print `path:line`. (ca695ee, 9e800cf) |\\n| `finds nothing in the tracked scripts and hooks` failed on Node, Bun and Deno (run 45649688140) | The job pins ShellCheck 0.11, but the test runs the runner's ShellCheck 0.9, which reports SC2015 for `[ ] && echo \\\\|\\\\| true` | The trace helpers use an `if` statement, which both versions accept (e4364a2, 0ba9e7c) |\\n| Deno failed `rejects a syntax error in js/tests/nested/check.test.js` on every run since the fixture was added (runs 45646051898 to 45652861265) | The Deno leg ran the gate on the runner's preinstalled Node. On Node 20 and 22, `node --check` exits 0 for an untyped `.js` file that uses `export`, even with a syntax error; Node 24 reports it. The repository supports Node 20 and later, so the gate itself had a false negative | Untyped `.js` files are checked through stdin as CommonJS, then as an ES module (822375b). The fixture also fails on git errors (727f3bf) |\\n| CodeQL `Analyze` failed at \\\"Uploading results\\\" (run 45649687987) | A transient GitHub outage; no analysis exists for that commit | No code change; the next run uploads normally |\\n\\n## False negatives (green while broken)\\n\\n- Lint warnings were filtered to changed lines and never failed. Now any warning fails (13780da), and the eight hidden warnings are fixed (c60ff67).\\n- `cargo doc` never ran (two broken intra-doc links), and Cargo's own warnings passed Clippy (f96e27f).\\n- The syntax gate checked only `scripts/*.mjs`, not `js/` (9cf89c5). On Node 20 and 22 it also passed untyped `.js` files with ESM syntax errors (822375b).\\n- Change detection skipped every check for shell scripts, Dockerfiles, CSS and similar files (cfa3ab1).\\n- Shell scripts called by workflows were never linted. They now go through ShellCheck (fb74d84).\\n- `npm audit --audit-level=high` passed moderate advisories in silence. There is now a full advisory report and a live deprecation check (26ab768).\\n- CodeQL uploaded alerts but never failed the run, and it skipped `examples/` (09789a0).\\n- **Desktop app skins were broken on `file://`.** Vite only warned that `node:fs/promises` was externalized, and every skin failed in Electron with `readFile is not a function`. Theme files are now bundled. A new `file://` e2e reproduces the problem, and any Vite warning fails the build (4aab2bf).\\n\\n## False positives\\n\\n- The status gate compared fork pull requests with `refs/heads/<branch>` instead of `refs/pull/N/head` (150e131).\\n- The budget wrapper could kill a command up to 1 s before its budget ended (1088b33).\\n- The common library translations step had a smaller budget than its shorter sibling, so its 70% warning fired on ordinary slow runners (e674adc).\\n\\n## Warnings removed\\n\\n- Node 20 deprecation and DEP0040/DEP0169 from `actions/cache@v4`: moved to v6 (f367b67).\\n- Deprecated secretlint preset (f367b67).\\n- Deprecated ESLint 9: moved to ESLint 10 (c60ff67).\\n- `npm warn deprecated glob@7/inflight/boolean/rimraf@2` in the example app (2a65e53).\\n- Line-limit warnings for `parser.js` (1498 lines) and `release.yml` (1425 lines) (908917b, 3b015c9).\\n- Vite chunk-size and externalized-module warnings (4aab2bf).\\n- Native translation budget warning (e674adc).\\n- `actions/checkout` and `actions/setup-node` moved to v7, as the templates use (f58ba7e).\\n- Dependency Review warned that `npm/human-signals` (through `command-stream` and `execa`) has an OpenSSF Scorecard of 2.8, below the default 3. Scorecards are still listed in the summary, but a low one no longer warns, as in the template (ac9e65c).\\n\\n## Template best practices and upstream reports\\n\\nThe parts the [JS pipeline template](https://github.com/link-foundation/js-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template) already did better were ported:\\n\\n- changed-files lint scope;\\n- `HEAD_REF` in the status gate;\\n- the budget wrapper (identical except the `trace` helper, which avoids SC2015 on the runner's ShellCheck 0.9);\\n- the ShellCheck job;\\n- the npm audit report;\\n- the CodeQL result gate;\\n- lockfile-loaded release helpers;\\n- the example app overrides;\\n- Node 24 pinned in every test leg;\\n- the Dependency Review scorecard settings.\\n\\nThree problems also exist in the template and are reported there with a reproduction, workaround and fix:\\n\\n- link-foundation/js-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template#319: the CodeQL gate fails forever on a dismissed alert, and its failures do not name a location.\\n- link-foundation/js-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template#320: the dry run fails when no changeset is pending.\\n- link-foundation/js-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template#321: the syntax gate passes untyped `.js` files with ESM syntax errors on Node 20 and 22.\\n\\nA code search found these steps only in the JS template, so the other language templates are not affected.\\n\\n## How to reproduce and verify\\n\\n- Preview selectors: `js/tests/universal-app.test.js` (\\\"waits for preview selectors that the app renders\\\") checks that every selector the preview script waits for exists in the app source. With the old gate and Node 22 first on `PATH`, `deno test -A js/tests/javascript-syntax.test.js` fails with \\\"Expected 0 to be 1\\\", as in CI. `experiments/issue-10/node-check-untyped-esm.sh` shows the Node behaviour.\\n- Budget wrapper and timeouts: `js/tests/ci-timeouts.test.js` and `js/tests/run-with-budget-warning.test.js`.\\n\\nDebug output is off by default: `DEBUG=1` prints release script stack traces, `BUDGET_VERBOSE=1` and `PIPELINE_STATUS_VERBOSE=1` trace the budget wrapper and the status gate, `VITE_ALLOW_WARNINGS=true` lets a local Vite build finish despite warnings, and `CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` picks the browser for the `file://` Summary\\n\\nFixes #8.\\n\\n### Comparison wordings (the reported bug)\\n\\n`Если n меньше или равно 1, сделать это:` and `больше или равно` now translate, along with the \\\"obvious variations\\\" in every natural language:\\n\\n- Russian: `либо`, `не больше`, `<=`, `≤`.\\n- English: `at most`, `is less than or equal to`, and the symbols.\\n\\nPython `pass` now reads as \\\"do nothing\\\".\\n\\nReproduce on `main`:\\n\\n```bash\\nprintf 'Если n меньше или равно 1, сделать это:\\\\n  Ничего не делать\\\\n' | npx universal-translator translate russian python\\n# main: error · this branch: if n <= 1:\\\\n    pass\\n```\\n\\n### Partial translation by default; all-or-nothing on request\\n\\n- `translatePartial` translates what reads and keeps every unread part as a target-language comment with its error. For example, `// untranslated (line 2): …` is followed by the original line.\\n- `parsePartial` / the `coverage` command count the read lines and the missing parts.\\n- The CLI defaults to partial and has `--all-or-nothing`. The server takes `allOrNothing` and answers `{output, complete, errors, coverage, detected}`. The web demo has an \\\"All or nothing\\\" checkbox.\\n\\n### Source language detection\\n\\n`detectLanguage` scores each language as `100 × how much of the text its grammar reads`, plus evidence from the language's own syntax tables and templates. It needs no model or dependency.\\n\\n- CLI: `translate auto <to>` and the `detect` command.\\n- Server: `from: \\\"auto\\\"`.\\n- Web demo: \\\"Auto-detect\\\" is the default source language.\\n\\n### Rules as data at every stage\\n\\n`createTranslator({ rules })`, `--rules file.json`, the server's `rules` and the web editor all accept the same JSON, with one list per stage:\\n\\n- `source`: text before reading;\\n- `templates`: more wordings per natural-language template;\\n- `names`: a meta → meta renaming layer;\\n- `output`: text after writing.\\n\\nEach rule can be plain text or a regex, and can be limited to one language. Rules are validated with clear errors.\\n\\n### Visual rules editor\\n\\nThe web demo has a table per stage, a JSON import/export view, and a list of untranslated parts.\\n\\n![Partial translation](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-8-a666e1cbe6e5/docs/screenshots/issue-8/partial-translation.png?raw=true)\\n![Rules editor](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-8-a666e1cbe6e5/docs/screenshots/issue-8/rules-editor.png?raw=true)\\n\\n### Rosetta Code\\n\\n`node scripts/rosetta-code.mjs all`:\\n\\n- loads every programming and draft task (1772) through the MediaWiki API;\\n- keeps the solutions in our 32 languages in a git-ignored cache;\\n- sorts the tasks from the simplest meaning (median solution length, then how many languages solve it);\\n- reads them partially and writes a report of the missing lines and parts per task and per language.\\n\\nThe first full run reads **508,806 of 1,292,095 lines (39.4%)** over 1782 tasks ([report](docs/case-studies/issue-8/data/rosetta-code/README.md)).\\n\\nThe run also found a real bug. JS `Parser.next()` read past the end of the tokens, so the Ada reader looped forever on a cut text like `procedure P is`. It now throws \\\"Unexpected end of program\\\", as Rust already did, and a regression test covers it.\\n\\nTranslating *every* Rosetta Code solution is the issue's long-term goal, and this PR does not reach it. It adds the loading, ordering, partial mode and measurements the issue asks for, so the remaining ~60% of lines can be worked down task by task.\\n\\n### Rust parity\\n\\nThe Rust crate and CLI get the same features:\\n\\n- partial translation and `--all-or-nothing`;\\n- `auto` detection and the `detect` and `coverage` commands;\\n- `--rules`.\\n\\nOn the samples I compared, the Rust CLI's output matched the JS byte for byte. The Rust crate has no HTTP server, so the server changes are JS-only.\\n\\n### Case study\\n\\n[docs/case-studies/issue-8](docs/case-studies/issue-8/README.md) has:\\n\\n- the issue data and a timeline;\\n- every requirement mapped to where it is done and how it is verified;\\n- the root causes, solutions and the libraries considered (Linguist, guesslang, highlight.js, franc/cld3, tree-sitter, ANTLR recovery, Blockly).\\n\\nNo upstream issue was needed: every root cause was in this repository.\\n\\n## Tests\\n\\n- `js/tests/issue-8.test.js`: wordings in every language, partial translation, CLI, coverage, detection, rules, server, and cut texts.\\n- `js/tests/rosetta-code.test.js`: offline fixture for extraction, sorting and counts.\\n- `rust/tests/issue_8.rs`: mirrors the JS tests.\\n- `examples/universal-app/e2e/translate.e2e.mjs`: auto-detect, the Russian example, partial output, a rule from the editor, and all-or-nothing.\\n\\n## Security note\\n\\nCodeQL flags `js/regex-injection` in `custom-rules.js`. Compiling the user's own pattern is the purpose of a `regex: true` rule, and on the command line the pattern comes from the user's own `--rules` file.\\n\\nThe HTTP server refuses regex rules by default, so remote clients cannot send ReDoS patterns. `createTranslationServer({ allowRegexRules: true })` opts in. Plain-text rules use no RegExp at all. Whether to dismiss the alert is left to the maintainers.\\n\\n### CodeQL note\\nCodeQL alert #5 (`js/regex-injection` at `js/src/translation/custom-rules.js:46`) was dismissed as *won't fix*: building a `RegExp` from `find` is the requested regex-rule feature. The server refuses regex rules unless `allowRegexRules` is set, and plain rules never build a It adds the meta language view, a language switch that does not fail, random examples, one entry per language with versions, semantic primes for every natural language, settings based on link-foundation/ui, concrete syntax trees by default, a separate comment language, a Standards editor, word standards of at most 1024 words with recursive Wikidata definitions, and a re-check of every issue 1 requirement.\\n\\nThe case study is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-6`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/tree/issue-6-c597ff1041d9/docs/case-studies/issue-6). The demo has a \\\"Show the meta language\\\" switch | `meta-notation.test.js`, `rust/tests/grammar.rs`, e2e |\\n| Changing the left language does not fail | The right text is translated into the newly chosen left language | e2e |\\n| Buttons generate random examples | Program, Function, Statement (Sentence is removed). #1\\n\\n## Summary\\n\\nThis PR adds a translator for programs. It does not match templates: it reads source text with per-language grammar tables and rewrites it through rules. It translates between **32 programming languages** (including **Lean 4** and **Rocq**), **three machine targets** (NASM x86-64, CIL, JVM/Jasmin) and **controlled versions of 30+ natural languages**. The JavaScript (`js/`) and Rust (`rust/`) implementations write byte-identical output for every golden translation.\\n\\n```text\\nsource ──parser──▶ source tree ──understanding rules──▶ meta ──type inference──▶ typed meta\\n  ──meaning rules──▶ ──custom layers──▶ ──context rules──▶ ──emitter──▶ target text\\n  ──lowering──▶ stack machine ──▶ NASM / CIL / JVM (Jasmin)\\nNASM / CIL / JVM ──reader──▶ stack machine ──lifting──▶ meta\\ncontrolled natural text ──reader──▶ meta ──writer──▶ controlled natural text\\n```\\n\\n### Requirements gate (test-driven)\\n\\n`docs/case-studies/issue-1/requirements.lino` lists every requirement from the issue and its comments. `docs/case-studies/issue-1/rosetta-coverage.lino` lists the Rosetta Code algorithm types. `scripts/check-requirements.mjs` checks each requirement against the repository; for example, it compares the language lists of both implementations and checks that every task has a golden in every language. It fails CI (`Rust and cross-language translation` job, and `js/tests/requirements.test.js` under Node, Bun and Deno) unless every requirement is **done** or **blocked with a written reason**.\\n\\nThe gate caught real gaps during this work. The Rust implementation was missing 10 languages; that was fixed and the gate now passes.\\n\\n### Web demo\\n\\n![Web demo translating a Python function to Rust](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/screenshots/web-demo.png?raw=true)\\n\\n`examples/universal-app` is a React demo in which any programming or natural language can be translated to any other. You can paste a whole program, one function or one statement. The `web-e2e` job in `.github/workflows/example-app.yml` drives it in Chromium (`examples/universal-app/e2e/translate.e2e.mjs`) and takes the screenshot above.\\n\\n### Fragments: statements, functions or a whole program\\n\\n`translateFragment` / `parseFragment` (JS) and `translate_fragment` / `parse_fragment` (Rust), plus `universal-translator translate --fragment`, accept a statement, one or more functions, or a whole program. Each comes back as the same kind of fragment in the target. A fragment only has to be complete: a function must end with its closing. Otherwise the translator fails with the reason and the line, for example `The fragment is not complete: it ends before its closing (line 2)`. Goldens for every language are in `examples/programs/fragments/translated/` and are checked by `write-fragments.mjs --check`.\\n\\n### CLI, library, HTTP API and Docker\\n\\n- `universal-translator serve` starts an HTTP API (`GET /languages`, `POST /translate`). It reads `--port`/`--host`, then `PORT`/`HOST`, then `.lenv`, through lino-arguments.\\n- `js/src/index.js` (with types) and the `rust/` crate are the libraries.\\n- The `Dockerfile` image runs the CLI and the server. The release workflow builds it and smoke tests the CLI and the HTTP API.\\n\\n### Source layout and best practices\\n\\n- Sources are split into `src/meta` (shared types and trees), `src/formal` (programming languages, Lean, Rocq and machine code) and `src/natural` (human languages, with a reader and a writer), in both `js/` and `rust/`. The `source-layout` check rejects imports that point outwards from the meta layer.\\n- [`docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md) maps the associative technology stack, the code architecture principles and all 17 CI/CD best practices to evidence, or gives a reason when one does not apply. `cargo clippy -D warnings` now runs in CI.\\n- **Test coverage is required by CI.** `npm run test:coverage` replaces `npm test` in the Node.js job. It fails below 94% line, 91% branch or 95% function coverage of `js/src` and `bin`; current coverage is 95.4%, 92.1% and 96.5%. The Rust crate runs the same goldens, but CI does not measure its coverage.\\n\\n### Programming languages (32) and machine code\\n\\n| | |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Languages | JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Lua, PHP, C, C++, C#, Java, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Swift, Perl, Dart, Scala, Julia, R, Groovy, Objective-C, Nim, D, Pascal, Fortran, Ada, Visual Basic .NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave, Zig, **Lean 4, Rocq** |\\n| Dialects | Pascal, Fortran, Ada, VB.NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave and Zig have their own program layout. They are dialects of the shared parser and emitter (`js/src/formal/dialects/`, `rust/src/formal/dialects/`). Lean 4 programs use `partial def` and `IO`. Rocq programs are pure `Fixpoint`s over an output monad defined in a small runtime, and are evaluated with `Eval vm_compute`. |\\n| Machine targets | NASM, CIL and JVM are written through a named stack machine and read back by lifting, so machine code translates to every language and between targets. |\\n| Modes | context-dependent (default, adapts comments such as C \\\"function call\\\" → C# \\\"method call\\\"), literal, same-effect |\\n| Extensibility | Every stage and rule list is an option of `createGrammarTranslator`; custom meta → meta layers are supported. |\\n| Common library | `common-library/` (output operations only, one file per language), enabled with `--common-library` |\\n\\n### Controlled natural languages\\n\\n- Data lives in `data/natural/*.lino`; `js/src/natural/` and `rust/src/natural/` read and write the same texts byte for byte.\\n- Covers the 30 most spoken languages (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Marathi, Telugu, Turkish, Tamil, Vietnamese, Korean, Italian, Persian, Swahili, Tagalog, Thai, Polish, Ukrainian, Hausa, Gujarati, Punjabi, Dutch), each in a small controlled form (`cnl-default`).\\n- Profiles for the standards named in the issue:\\n  - ASD-STE100\\n  - Attempto Controlled English\\n  - Gellish (English and Dutch)\\n  - SBVR Structured English\\n  - Plain language (ISO 24495-1)\\n  - E-Prime\\n  - Basic English, VOA Special English and Globish\\n  - Minimal English, Minimal French and Minimal Polish, built on the **65 semantic primes** of NSM (`data/natural/semantic-primes.lino`)\\n- `checkText` and the `check-words` command enforce each standard's rules: sentence length, allowed first words, forbidden words such as \\\"to be\\\" in E-Prime or \\\"shall\\\" in plain language, vocabulary limits, and Gellish relation phrases.\\n- Translations run natural → meta → any programming or machine language, and back: `universal-translator translate russian python`, `translate python spanish`.\\n- Every example program is written in every natural language and profile under `examples/programs/natural/`. Each text is read back to the same meaning and checked against its standard.\\n\\n### Rosetta Code and Hello World\\n\\n18 tasks in `examples/programs/` are translated to all 32 languages, the 3 machine targets and every natural language, then run natively:\\n\\n- hello world\\n- factorial\\n- greatest common divisor\\n- FizzBuzz\\n- sum of squares\\n- Fibonacci\\n- Ackermann\\n- Towers of Hanoi\\n- leap year\\n- sum of digits\\n- hailstone\\n- 99 bottles\\n- primality by trial division\\n- mutual recursion\\n- perfect numbers\\n- sieve of Eratosthenes\\n- bubble sort\\n- sum and product of an array\\n\\nAlgorithm types covered (from `rosetta-coverage.lino`): output, integer arithmetic, conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion (including mutual recursion), number theory, text concatenation, and **integer arrays** (new: array values in the meta language, all 32 languages, NASM/CIL/JVM and natural-language sentences).\\n\\n**Blocked, with reasons recorded in `rosetta-coverage.lino`.** These are not presented as done. Rosetta Code has more than 1,300 tasks, and these types need values the meta language does not have yet:\\n\\n| Type | Why it is blocked |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| floating-point | Machine targets and the meta language use 64-bit integers only |\\n| string manipulation | Text can be printed and concatenated, but not indexed or transformed |\\n| higher-order functions | Functions are top-level declarations only |\\n| data structures | Records, maps, stacks and queues need compound values |\\n| input/output | Programs only write to standard output, which is what the native checks compare |\\n| objects and concurrency | Not supported |\\n\\n**Classes as fragments** are also **blocked** (`class-fragments` in the gate) for the same reason: the meta language has no objects or classes, so a class has no meaning to translate yet.\\n\\nThe gate reports `rosetta-algorithm-types` and `class-fragments` as **BLOCKED** with these reasons. Every other requirement is **DONE**.\\n\\n## Verification\\n\\n- **`npm test` (Node, Bun, Deno) and `cargo test`.** Every task is translated to every language, machine target and natural language and compared with the goldens in `examples/programs/translated` and `examples/programs/natural`.\\n- **`examples/programs/verify-native.mjs --require-all [--common-library]`.** The `native-translation` CI job compiles or runs each translation with its real toolchain and compares the output with the JavaScript original. The toolchains include Lean 4 (elan), Rocq (opam), fpc, gnat, gfortran, octave, zig, nim, ldc, Objective-C, Swift, Kotlin, Scala, .NET and Jasmin.\\n- **`experiments/verify-syntax-exchange.sh`.** The JS and Rust command lines list the same 32 languages and write identical output.\\n- **`node scripts/check-requirements.mjs`.** The requirements gate described above.\\n- **`npm run test:coverage`.** The coverage gate described above.\\n- **`web-e2e`.** The browser test of the demo.\\n- **`--trace`.** Logs each pipeline stage.\\n\\n### CI reliability (native translation job)\\n\\n- Toolchain archives are cached. Each download attempt is capped at 3 minutes and falls back to a mirror: Google's Maven Central mirror for Groovy and `zig.linus.dev` for Zig, all checked by SHA-256. This fixes a run where the step hung on a stalled download.\\n- `verify-native.mjs` runs its checks in parallel worker processes.\\n- `js/tests/ci-timeouts.test.js` keeps each job's step budgets within 70% of its backstop.\\n- Budgets are sized for slower runners. One run needed 330 s for all native translations and over 360 s for the common library translations, while a typical run needs about 220 s and 250 s. Every translation passed, but the 360 s budget ran out. The step budgets are now 540 s and 480 s, and the job backstop is 100 minutes so the budgets stay within 70% of it.\\n\\n### CodeQL\\n\\n- `js/incomplete-sanitization` flagged the Lean `s!\\\"…\\\"` brace escape, because it was chained after `escape()` where CodeQL cannot see that backslashes were already escaped. Brace escaping now happens inside `escape()` as the `escaped-braces` format. The output is unchanged, and a regression test in `js/tests/grammar.test.js` checks that `` `a\\\\\\\\b {c} ${name}` `` becomes `s!\\\"a\\\\\\\\b \\\\{c} {name}\\\"`.\\n- CodeQL still lists an older alert on `docs/case-studies/issue-3/original-format-release-notes.mjs`. That file came with the initial commit and is not part of this PR, and the CodeQL check passes.\\n\\nThe data files use Links Notation (`.lino`). The PR contains exactly one changeset (`.changeset/sharp-programs-translate.md`). much more narrow.\\n\\nSo it looks like there should be one to one match between natural language and formal type system.\\n\\nSo we always work with ranges, and by calculating frequencies of language corpus we can have some probabilities which more specific type or description is most likely.\\n\\nYet for best translation (most likely and more correct) we should prefer such translation, which Summary\\n\\nFixes #14\\n\\nThis PR addresses issue 14 and the requirements of earlier issues and pull requests that had not been delivered. Every change is made in both JavaScript and Rust, and the two command lines print byte-identical output. The full case study is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-14/`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/tree/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14):\\n\\n- `README.md`: timeline, the issue's requirements R1–R24, root causes and alternatives;\\n- `previous-requirements.md`: every earlier requirement with its status;\\n- `prior-art.md` and `architecture.md`;\\n- `requirements.lino`: CI fails while any requirement is neither done nor reported as blocked with a reason.\\n\\n### Issue 14 requirements\\n\\n- **A concrete syntax tree (CST) by default.** Whitespace and blank lines now survive a translation. The layout pass (`js/src/translation/layout.js`, `rust/src/layout.rs`) aligns the tokens of the output with those of the source and returns a `lineMap`. `--layout target` restores the emitter's own formatting.\\n  - `main`: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log(\\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n  - this branch: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n- **Monaco by default, with linked editors.**\\n  - Folding regions now work for every language.\\n  - Folding, selection, the cursor and scrolling are shared by both editors. Long texts are stored once and referred to by id.
