Formal AI's current\nsubstitution engine is an in-repository implementation in\n`rust/src/substitution.rs`, where `.lino` rules match and rewrite link patterns on\nCRUD events. The repository is useful for comparison and vocabulary, but its\ncode is not linked into the Formal AI runtime.\n\n## Development and orchestration components\n\nThese tools exercise or coordinate the system during development. They are not\nend-user runtime libraries.\n\n### Agent CLI\n\nRepository: [link-assistant/agent](https://github.com/link-assistant/agent)\n\nThe Agent CLI is an external development-time client for OpenAI-compatible\nmodel endpoints. Contributors use it against a running Formal AI server to\nprove that the symbolic agent loop can inspect a worktree, call tools, edit\nfiles, and verify its result through the same public protocol used by other\nclients.\n\n### Hive Mind\n\nRepository: [link-assistant/hive-mind](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind)\n\nHive Mind is development-time orchestration around issue-solving agents and\npull requests. It supplies tasks and coordinates repository work; Formal AI is\nthe system being driven. Hive Mind does not participate in knowledge storage,\nparsing, reasoning, or responses in a shipped Formal AI process.\n\n## Keeping this map accurate\n\nWhen an integration changes, update this guide from executable evidence:\n\n- `Cargo.toml` and its feature table define Rust runtime dependencies;\n- `package.json` defines the web bundle's direct packages;\n- `rust/src/link_store.rs`, `rust/src/coding/cst.rs`, `rust/src/document_formats.rs`,\n  `rust/src/calculation.rs`, `rust/src/main.rs`, and `js/i18n.js` show the integration\n  boundaries; and\n- compatibility or conceptual repositories must remain in the architecture\n  section until their code becomes an actual manifest dependency.\n\nThe project catalog in `data/seed/projects.lino` records a wider ecosystem for\ndiscovery. Catalog membership alone is not evidence that a component executes\ninside Formal AI.\n# meta-language\n\nA universal, self-describing meta language backed by a links network, implemented\nin **both Rust and JavaScript** with guaranteed feature parity between the two.\n\n[![Rust](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language/actions/workflows/rust.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language/actions/workflows/rust.yml)\n[![JavaScript](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language/actions/workflows/js.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language/actions/workflows/js.yml)\n[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/meta-language?label=crates.io&style=flat)](https://crates.io/crates/meta-language)\n[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/meta-language?label=npm&style=flat)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/meta-language)\n[![License: Unlicense](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Unlicense-blue.svg)](https://unlicense.org/)\n\n**Website:** <https://link-foundation.github.io/meta-language> — project\ndescription, an interactive WebAssembly demo, and the full\n[Rust API documentation](https://link-foundation.github.io/meta-language/api/).\n\n## Vision\n\n[`docs/vision.md`](docs/vision.md) is the authoritative specification of the\ntarget meta-language is built toward: one common language of links for\ngrammars, syntax trees, semantics and transformations, native merged grammars\nfor every language, and full JavaScript, Rust, Lean and Rocq translation. It\ndescribes that target, not the current state; the generated\n[requirement ledger](docs/issue-195-requirement-ledger.md) reports what is\nverified today. Where another document disagrees with the vision, the vision is\nthe contract.\n\n## Repository layout\n\nNo language implementation lives at the repository root. Each language has its own\nself-contained folder with its own `src/`, `tests/`, `scripts/`, `README.md`, and\nbadges, and its own CI/CD workflow.\n\n| Path | Contents |\n| --- | --- |\n| [`rust/`](rust/README.md) | Rust crate `meta-language` — the reference implementation. Built and tested by [`.github/workflows/rust.yml`](.github/workflows/rust.yml). |\n| [`js/`](js/README.md) | JavaScript package `meta-language`. Built and tested by [`.github/workflows/js.yml`](.github/workflows/js.yml). |\n| [`parity/`](parity/language-features.lino) | Cross-language feature manifest. Every feature must be present in both languages (see [Feature parity](#feature-parity)). |\n| [`docs/`](docs) | Shared documentation: the grammar subsystem, fidelity matrices, the project website source, and per-issue case studies. |\n| [`.github/`](.github/workflows) | Shared CI/CD workflows (`rust.yml`, `js.yml`). |\n\nDeclarative, recursive network translation and its template syntax are\ndocumented in [`docs/translation-rules.md`](docs/translation-rules.md).\nThe shared executable query-plan IR plus registry-driven GraphQL and SQL\nlowering APIs are documented in [`docs/query-plans.md`](docs/query-plans.md).\nThe versioned JavaScript, Rust, Lean, and Rocq parser/emitter capability and\ntranslation boundaries are documented in\n[`docs/four-language-contracts.md`](docs/four-language-contracts.md).\nThe full issue #195 delivery target is defined by the executable\n[`parity/issue-195-requirements.lino`](parity/issue-195-requirements.lino)\nmanifest. Its generated evidence report and remaining per-runtime gaps are\ntracked in\n[`docs/issue-195-requirement-ledger.md`](docs/issue-195-requirement-ledger.md).\n\n## Quick start\n\n### Rust\n\n```bash\ncd rust\ncargo test --all-features\n```\n\n```rust\nuse meta_language::{LinkNetwork, ParseConfiguration};\n\nlet network = LinkNetwork::parse(\"alpha beta\", \"plain-text\", ParseConfiguration::default());\nassert!(network.verify_full_match(None).is_clean());\nassert_eq!(network.reconstruct_text(), \"alpha beta\");\n```\n\nSee [`rust/README.md`](rust/README.md) for the full API, CLI, grammar subsystem,\nand website build instructions.\n\n### JavaScript\n\n```bash\ncd js\nnpm ci\nnpm test\n```\n\n```js\nimport { LinkNetwork, ParseConfiguration } from 'meta-language';\n\nconst network = LinkNetwork.parse('alpha beta', 'txt', ParseConfiguration.default());\nconsole.log(network.reconstructText()); // alpha beta\n```\n\nSee [`js/README.md`](js/README.md) for the full JavaScript API.\n\n### Arbitrary file formats\n\nFiles that do not have a semantic parser can still be stored and transformed\nwithout UTF-8 loss. `LinkNetwork::parse_bytes` in Rust and\n`LinkNetwork.parseBytes` in JavaScript represent ordered byte chunks as tokens\nand retain the caller-supplied media type or format identifier. Calling\n`reconstruct_bytes` or `reconstructBytes` returns the original file exactly.\n\n## Feature parity\n\nThe core requirement of this project is that **every feature present in Rust is\nalso present in JavaScript, and vice versa**. This is encoded as data in\n[`parity/language-features.lino`](parity/language-features.lino) and enforced by\n[`js/scripts/check-js-rust-parity.mjs`](js/scripts/check-js-rust-parity.mjs):\n\n- The manifest lists each feature with its Rust and JavaScript implementation\n  status and the evidence files that prove it.\n- The checker verifies every evidence file exists and that the JavaScript API\n  operation registry covers every operation family and API style.\n- Both `rust.yml` and `js.yml` run the parity gate, so changing one language\n  without mirroring the change in the other fails CI in **both** workflows.\n\nRun the gate locally from either language folder:\n\n```bash\nnode js/scripts/check-js-rust-parity.mjs            # full check\nnode js/scripts/check-js-rust-parity.mjs --manifest-only\n```\n\n## Case study\n\nThe analysis, requirements breakdown, and solution plan for the multi-language\nrestructuring live in\n[`docs/case-studies/issue-163`](docs/case-studies/issue-163).\n\n## License\n\nReleased into the public domain under the [Unlicense](https://unlicense.org/).\nhttps://github.com/link-assistant/router/pull/775 closed 2026-11-16T07:51:15Z\nFixes #772. 3.1.\nSymbol\nMeaning\nExample\nS\nsentence\nthe man walked\nNP\nnoun phrase\na dog\nVP\nverb phrase\nsaw a park\nPP\nprepositional phrase\nwith a shown by the | and is an abbreviation for the two productions\nVP -> V NP and VP -> V NP PP.\nFigure 3.2: Recursive Descent Parser Demo: This tool allows you to watch the operation of\na recursive descent parser as it grows the parse tree and matches it against\nthe input words.\nNote\nYour Turn:\nTry developing a simple grammar of your own, using the\nrecursive descent parser application, nltk.app.rdparser(),\nshown in 3.2.\nIt comes already loaded with a sample grammar, but you can\nedit this as you please (using the Edit menu).\nChange the grammar, and the sentence to be parsed, and\nrun the parser using the autostep button.\nIf we parse the sentence The dog saw a man in the park using\nthe grammar shown in 3.1, we end up with two trees, similar to\nthose we saw for (3b):\n(9)\na.\nb.\nSince our grammar licenses two trees for this sentence, the sentence is\nsaid to be structurally ambiguous.  The ambiguity in question is called\na prepositional phrase attachment ambiguity, as we saw earlier in this chapter.\nAs you may recall, it is an ambiguity about attachment since the\nPP in the park needs to be attached to one of two places\nin the tree: either as a child of VP or else as a child of NP.\nWhen the PP is attached to VP, the intended interpretation\nis that the seeing event happened\nin the park.  However, if the PP is attached to NP,\nthen it was the man who was in the park, and the agent of the seeing (the dog)\nmight have been sitting on the balcony of an apartment overlooking the\npark.\n3.2   Writing Your Own Grammars\nIf you are interested in experimenting with writing CFGs, you will\nfind it helpful to create and edit your grammar in a text\nfile, say mygrammar.cfg. You can then load it into NLTK and\nparse with it as follows:\n>>> grammar1 = nltk.data.load('file:mygrammar.cfg')\n>>> sent = \"Mary saw Bob\".split()\n>>> rd_parser = nltk.RecursiveDescentParser(grammar1)\n>>> for tree in rd_parser.parse(sent):\n...      print(tree)\nMake sure that you put a .cfg suffix on the filename, and that\nthere are no spaces in the string 'file:mygrammar.cfg'. If the\ncommand print(tree) produces no output, this is probably because\nyour sentence sent is not admitted by your grammar. In this case,\ncall the parser with tracing set to be on: rd_parser =\nnltk.RecursiveDescentParser(grammar1, trace=2). You can also check\nwhat productions are currently in the grammar with the command for p\nin grammar1.productions(): print(p).\nWhen you write CFGs for parsing in NLTK, you cannot combine\ngrammatical categories with lexical items on the righthand side of the\nsame production. Thus, a production such as PP -> 'of' NP is disallowed. In\naddition, you are not permitted to place multi-word lexical items on the\nrighthand side of a production. So rather than writing NP -> 'New\nYork', you have to resort to something like NP -> 'New_York'\ninstead.\n3.3   Recursion in Syntactic Structure\nA grammar is said to be recursive if a category occurring on the left hand\nside of a production also appears on\nthe righthand side of a production, as illustrated in 3.3.\nThe production Nom -> Adj Nom (where Nom is the\ncategory of nominals) involves direct recursion on the category\nNom, whereas indirect recursion on S arises from the\ncombination of two productions, namely S -> NP VP and VP -> V S.\ngrammar2 = nltk.CFG.fromstring(\"\"\"\nS  -> NP VP\nNP -> Det Nom | PropN\nNom -> Adj Nom | N\nVP -> V Adj | V NP | V S | V NP PP\nPP -> P NP\nPropN -> 'Buster' | 'Chatterer' | 'Joe'\nDet -> 'the' | 'a'\nN -> 'bear' | 'squirrel' | 'tree' | 'fish' | 'log'\nAdj  -> 'angry' | 'frightened' |  'little' | 'tall'\nV ->  'chased'  | 'saw' | 'said' | 'thought' | 'was' | 'put'\nP -> 'on'\n\"\"\")\nExample 3.3 (code_cfg2.py): Figure 3.3: A Recursive Context-Free Grammar\nTo see how recursion arises from this grammar, consider the following\ntrees.  (10a) involves nested nominal phrases,\nwhile (10b) contains nested sentences.\n(10)\na.\nb.\nWe've only illustrated two levels of recursion here, but there's\nno upper limit on the depth.  You can experiment with parsing\nsentences that involve more deeply nested structures.\nBeware that the RecursiveDescentParser is unable to handle\nleft-recursive productions of the form X -> X Y; we will\nreturn to this in 4.\n4   Parsing With Context Free Grammar\nA parser processes input sentences according to the\nproductions of a grammar, and builds one or more\nconstituent structures that conform to the grammar.\nA grammar is a declarative specification of well-formedness —\nit is actually just a string, not a program.\nA parser is a procedural interpretation of the grammar.\nIt searches through the space of trees licensed by a grammar\nto find one that has the required sentence along its fringe.\nA parser permits a grammar to be evaluated against\na collection of test sentences, helping linguists\nto discover mistakes in their grammatical analysis.\nA parser can serve as a model of psycholinguistic processing,\nhelping to explain the difficulties that humans have with processing\ncertain syntactic constructions.\nMany natural language applications involve parsing at some point;\nfor example, we would expect the natural language questions\nthe most items from the stack.  (A generalization of shift-reduce\nparser, a \"lookahead LR parser\", is commonly used in programming\nlanguage compilers.)\nThe advantage of shift-reduce parsers over recursive descent parsers\nis that they only build structure that corresponds to the words in the\ninput.  Furthermore, they only build each sub-structure once,\ne.g. NP(Det(the), N(man)) is only built and pushed onto the stack\na single time, regardless of whether it will later be used by the\nVP -> V NP PP reduction or the NP -> NP PP reduction.\n4.3   The Left-Corner Parser\nOne of the problems with the recursive descent parser is that it\ngoes into an infinite loop when it encounters a left-recursive production.\nThis is because it applies the grammar\nproductions blindly, without considering the actual input sentence.\nA left-corner parser is a hybrid between the bottom-up and top-down\napproaches we have seen.\nGrammar grammar1 allows us to produce the following parse of John saw\nMary:\n(11)\nRecall that the grammar (defined in 3.3) has the following productions for expanding NP:\n(12)\na.NP -> Det N\nb.NP -> Det N PP\nc.NP -> \"John\" | \"Mary\" | \"Bob\"\nSuppose we ask you to first look at tree (11), and then decide\nwhich of the NP productions you'd want a recursive descent parser to\napply first — obviously, (12c) is the right choice! How do you\nknow that it would be pointless to apply (12a) or (12b) instead? Because\nneither of these productions will derive a sequence whose first word is\nJohn.  That is, we can easily tell that in a successful\nparse of John saw Mary, the parser has to expand NP in\nsuch a way that NP derives the sequence John α. More\ngenerally, we say that a category B is a left-corner of\na tree rooted in A if  A ⇒*\nB α.\n(13)\nA left-corner parser is a top-down parser with bottom-up filtering.\nUnlike an ordinary recursive descent parser, it does not get trapped\nin left recursive productions.\nBefore starting its work, a left-corner parser preprocesses the\ncontext-free grammar to build a table where each row contains two\ncells, the first holding a non-terminal, and the second holding the\ncollection of possible left corners of that non-terminal. 4.1\nillustrates this for the grammar from grammar2.\nCategory\nLeft-Corners (pre-terminals)\nS\nNP\nNP\nDet, PropN\nVP\nV\nPP\nP\nTable 4.1:\nLeft-Corners in grammar2\nEach time a production is considered by the parser, it checks that the\nnext input word is compatible with at least one of the pre-terminal\ncategories in the left-corner table.\n4.4   Well-Formed Substring Tables\nThe simple parsers discussed above suffer from limitations in\nboth completeness and efficiency. In order to remedy these, we will\napply the algorithm design technique of dynamic programming to\nthe parsing problem.  As we saw in 4.7,\ndynamic programming stores intermediate results and re-uses them when\nappropriate, achieving significant efficiency gains. This technique\ncan be applied to syntactic parsing, allowing us to store\npartial solutions to the parsing task and then look them up as\nnecessary in order to efficiently arrive at a complete solution.\nThis approach to parsing is known as chart parsing.  We introduce\nthe main idea in this section; see the online materials available for\nthis chapter for more implementation details.\nDynamic programming allows us to build the PP in my pajamas\njust once.  The first time we build it we save it in a table, then we look it\nup when we need to use it as a subconstituent of either the object NP or\nthe higher VP. This table is known as a\n## Overview\n\nRML (Relative Meta-Logic, formerly Associative-Dependent Logic / ADL) is a minimal probabilistic logic system built on top of [LiNo (Links Notation)](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation). It supports [many-valued logics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Many-valued_logic) from unary (1-valued) through continuous probabilistic ([fuzzy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_logic)), allowing you to:\n\n- Define terms\n- Assign probabilities (truth values) to logical expressions\n- Redefine logical operators with different semantics\n- Configure truth value ranges: `[0, 1]` or `[-1, 1]` (balanced/symmetric)\n- Configure logic valence: 2-valued ([Boolean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra)), 3-valued ([ternary/Kleene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic)), N-valued, or continuous\n- Use and redefine truth constants: `true`, `false`, `unknown`, `undefined`\n- Use and redefine Belnap operators: `both...and` (contradiction/avg) and `neither...nor` (gap/product)\n- Resolve paradoxical statements (e.g. the [liar paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liar_paradox))\n- Perform decimal-precision arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`) — `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3`, not `0.30000000000000004`\n- Query the truth value of complex expressions\n- Define dependent types as links — universe hierarchy, Pi-types, lambdas, type queries\n- Combine types with probabilistic logic in a unified framework\n- Delegate domain-specific decision blocks through evaluator plugins, including\n  `(domain automatic-sequences (theorem thue-morse-cube-free))`\n- Reuse the evaluator as a library, including a meta-expression adapter that accepts selected interpretations and explicit dependencies while keeping underspecified claims partial\n- Export the simply typed LiNo fragment to Isabelle/HOL source for external certification experiments\n\n## Supported Logic Types\n\n![F0C5A9A4-B56E-4B64-8B7E-CC3A650EDAF7_1_201_a](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b54e3aaa-8645-4067-8051-6299745a2a3b)\n\n| Valence | Name | Truth Values (in `[0, 1]`) | Truth Values (in `[-1, 1]`) | Reference |\n|---------|------|---------------------------|----------------------------|-----------|\n| 1 | Unary (trivial) | `{any}` (no quantization) | `{any}` (no quantization) | [Many-valued logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Many-valued_logic) |\n| 2 | Binary / [Boolean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra) | `{0, 1}` (false, true) | `{-1, 1}` (false, true) | [Classical logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_logic) |\n| 3 | Ternary / [Three-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic) | `{0, 0.5, 1}` (false, unknown, true) | `{-1, 0, 1}` (false, unknown, true) | [Kleene logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic#Kleene_and_Priest_logics), [Łukasiewicz [Four-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-valued_logic) | `{0, ⅓, ⅔, 1}` | `{-1, -⅓, ⅓, 1}` | [Belnap's four-valued logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-valued_logic#Belnap) |\n| 5 | [Finite-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite-valued_logic) / N-valued | N evenly-spaced levels | N evenly-spaced levels | [Many-valued logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Many-valued_logic), [Finite-valued logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite-valued_logic) |\n| 0/∞ | Continuous / [Probabilistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_logic) / [Fuzzy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_logic) | Any value in `[0, 1]` | Any value in `[-1, 1]` | [Probabilistic logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_logic) (probability logic), [Fuzzy logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzy_logic), [Infinite-valued logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-valued_logic), [Łukasiewicz ∞-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81ukasiewicz_logic) |\n\n## Quick Start\n\n### JavaScript\n\n```bash\ncd js\nnpm install\nnode src/rml-links.mjs ../examples/demo.lino\nnode src/rml-links.mjs export lean ../examples/lean-export-basic.lino -o out.lean\n```\n\nThe library is also published to npm as\n[`relative-meta-logic`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/relative-meta-logic)\n(`npm install relative-meta-logic`), which provides the `rml`, `rml-check`,\n`rml-meta`, and `rml-lsp` commands. Releases are automated; see\n[`docs/RELEASING.md`](./docs/RELEASING.md).\n\nEditor integration is available through the stdio language server; see\n[`docs/LANGUAGE_SERVER.md`](./docs/LANGUAGE_SERVER.md) for Neovim and Helix\nsetup, and [`vscode/`](./vscode/) for an installable VS Code extension with\n`.lino` syntax highlighting and LSP-backed diagnostics, hover,\ngo-to-definition, and completion.\n\n### Rust\n\n```bash\ncd rust\ncargo run -- ../examples/demo.lino\ncargo run -- export lean ../examples/lean-export-basic.lino -o out.lean\n```\n\nFor a dependency-free Rust probability API that builds for WebAssembly, see\nthe [probability core and weighted-evidence example](./rust/README.md#probability-core).\n\n### Docker\n### Queries\n\n```lino\n(? <expression>)\n```\n\nQueries are evaluated and their truth value is printed to stdout.\n\n#### Type Queries\n\n```lino\n# Type check: (expr of Type) — returns 1 (true) or 0 (false)\n(? (zero of Natural))            # -> 1\n(? (Natural of Type))            # -> 1\n\n# Type inference: (type of expr) — returns the type name\n(? (type of zero))               # -> Natural\n```\n\n#### Paradox Resolution in the Type System\n\nIn classical type theory, `Type : Type` leads to [Russell's paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell%27s_paradox). ADL handles this differently — paradoxes are resolved to the midpoint truth value (0.5), not rejected:\n\n```lino\n(Type: Type Type)\n(s: s is s)\n((s = false) has probability 0.5)\n(? (s = false))                  # -> 0.5 (paradox resolves to midpoint)\n(? (not (s = false)))            # -> 0.5 (fixed point of negation)\n(? (Type of Type))               # -> 1   (self-referential type works)\n```\n\nThis means ADL can serve as a **meta-theory** for both classical and non-classical type systems, since it can express and reason about constructs that would be inconsistent in traditional frameworks.\n\n## Built-in Operators\nSpa: se duerme\nSwe: man sover\nTha: นอนหลับ\nUrd: کوی سوتا ہے\nmkCl\nNP -> V -> Cl\nshe [The vision](../vision.md#grammar-import-conversion-and-reverse-conversion)\nrequires the complete import, export and round-trip system in this pull request\nand in both runtime packages. The stage links below are historical references,\nnot ownership or permission to defer unfinished work.\n\nOwned by [F1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/F1-grammar-subsystem-docs.md);\nstage owners: [B1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B1-bnf-importer.md)\nthrough [B7](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B7-lark-gbnf-importer.md)\nfor importers, [C1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C1-bnf-ebnf-abnf-emitters.md)\nthrough [C3](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C3-gbnf-emitter.md) for\nemitters, and [F2](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/F2-grammar-format-fidelity-matrix.md)\nfor the fidelity matrix.\n\nImporters translate external grammar notations into the\n[`Grammar` IR](architecture.md). Emitters translate the IR back into a target\nnotation. The current branch already has the IR and native surface helpers; the\nformat-specific importer and emitter APIs are incomplete. The required APIs and\ncommand-line tools must be implemented and tested in both packages here.\n\n## Minimal example\n\n```text\nBNF, EBNF, ABNF, PEG, ANTLR, Lark, GBNF, or tree-sitter JSON\n  -> importer\n  -> Grammar { source_format: Some(...) }\n  -> emitter\n  -> target grammar notation\n```\n\nThe importer must preserve source order where possible, set `GrammarFormat`, and\nrepresent every source construct and its semantics as inspectable native links.\nThe emitter must consume only those links rather than re-reading the original\ntext. If a target format cannot express a feature directly, export needs a\nfaithful executable lowering or runtime encoding, with explicit reconstruction\nmetadata; a lossy report does not complete the conversion.\n\n## Format table\n\n| Format | Import owner | Emit owner | IR source tag |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| BNF | [B1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B1-bnf-importer.md) | [C1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C1-bnf-ebnf-abnf-emitters.md) | `GrammarFormat::Bnf` |\n| EBNF | [B2](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B2-ebnf-importer.md) | [C1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C1-bnf-ebnf-abnf-emitters.md) | `GrammarFormat::Ebnf` |\n| ABNF | [B3](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B3-abnf-importer.md) | [C1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C1-bnf-ebnf-abnf-emitters.md) | `GrammarFormat::Abnf` |\n| PEG | [B4](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B4-peg-importer.md) | [C2](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C2-peg-emitter.md) | `GrammarFormat::Peg` |\n| tree-sitter JSON | [B5](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B5-tree-sitter-json-importer.md) | [C7](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C7-tree-sitter-grammar-js-emitter.md) | `GrammarFormat::TreeSitter` |\n| ANTLR | [B6](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B6-antlr-importer.md) | required in this pull request | `GrammarFormat::Antlr` |\n| Lark and GBNF | [B7](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/B7-lark-gbnf-importer.md) | [C3](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C3-gbnf-emitter.md) for GBNF | `GrammarFormat::Lark`, `GrammarFormat::Gbnf` |\n\n## Fidelity\n\nFidelity is not a boolean property of the importer alone. It is the result of a\nround trip through the IR:\n\n```text\nsource notation -> Grammar -> target notation -> Grammar\n```\n\n[F2](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/F2-grammar-format-fidelity-matrix.md)\nowns the detailed [fidelity matrix](fidelity.md). This page only records the\nstage contract: each importer and emitter must preserve the relevant syntax and\nmeaning. An unsupported diagnostic or approximation is an honest indication of\nunfinished work, never passing round-trip evidence.\n\n## See also\n\n- [Authoring](authoring.md) for the native surface syntax.\n- [Translation](translation.md) for concept-aligned conversion between\n  notations.\n- [`src/grammar/mod.rs`](../../rust/src/grammar/mod.rs) for the `GrammarFormat`\n  variants shared by importers and emitters.\n# Grammar architecture\n\n> This document is subordinate to the authoritative\n> [vision and architecture specification](../vision.md). It describes one\n> subsystem as it exists today; where the two disagree, the vision is the\n> contract and this document is a defect to fix.\n\nOwned by [F1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/F1-grammar-subsystem-docs.md);\narchitecture anchor for [A1](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/A1-grammar-ir.md),\n[A3](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/A3-grammar-concept-ontology.md),\nand [C6](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C6-concept-aligned-translation.md).\n\nThe grammar layer uses one intermediate representation for every grammar-facing\nfeature. The core types live in [`src/grammar/mod.rs`](../../rust/src/grammar/mod.rs):\n\n| Type | Role |\n| --- | --- |\n| `Grammar` | Ordered collection of rules, optional start rule, and optional source format. |\n| `GrammarRule` | Named rule with an expression, `RuleKind`, optional concept, and optional documentation. |\n| `GrammarExpr` | Expression algebra for terminals, non-terminals, sequences, choices, repetition, predicates, captures, character classes, and empty expressions. |\n| `RuleKind` | Parse participation marker: normal, atomic, silent, or token. |\n| `GrammarFormat` | Source or target notation tag such as `MetaLanguage`, `Bnf`, `Ebnf`, `Abnf`, `Peg`, `Antlr`, `Lark`, `Gbnf`, `TreeSitter`, or `Inferred`. |\n\n## Minimal example\n\nThe rustdoc example on [`src/grammar/mod.rs`](../../rust/src/grammar/mod.rs) is the\ndoctested reference for building a grammar, encoding it as links, and decoding it\nback. The invariant is:\n\n```text\nGrammar::from_links(Grammar::to_links(grammar)) == grammar\n```\n\nIn code, use `Grammar::builder()` for rules and `Grammar::expr()` for expression\nconstructors. Then pass the value through `LinksEncoder` and `LinksDecoder`.\n\n## Grammar as links\n\nA grammar is data in the network. The links codec in\n[`src/grammar/links.rs`](../../rust/src/grammar/links.rs) implements `ToLinks` and\n`FromLinks` for `Grammar`. Each encoded grammar node is inserted with\n`LinkType::Grammar` from [`src/link_network.rs`](../../rust/src/link_network.rs) and a\nstable term such as `grammar::grammar`, `grammar::rule`, or\n`grammar::expression::sequence`.\n\nThe self-description root in\n[`src/self_description.rs`](../../rust/src/self_description.rs) declares the\n`grammar` root as `LinkType::Grammar` with references to `language` and\n`relation link`. That makes grammar structure part of the same self-describing\nnetwork as links, references, concepts, fields, regions, and objects.\n\nBecause grammar data is encoded as ordinary links:\n\n- Link projections can include or hide grammar links according to normal network\n  rules.\n- Grammar data can be serialized through the existing links codec and LiNo\n  helpers.\n- Other stages can accept a `Grammar` value, a grammar root link, or a serialized\n  links network without inventing a parallel storage path.\n\n## Pipeline\n\n```text\n                            +--------------------+\n                            | authoring surface  | A2, E4\n                            +----------+---------+\n                                       |\n                            +----------v---------+\n                            | external importers | B1-B7\n                            +----------+---------+\n                                       |\n                                       v\n+------------------+        +--------------------+        +------------------+\n| example corpora  +------->| Grammar IR links   +------->| emitters         |\n| and observations | D1,D5,D6| A1                 | C1-C3  | BNF/EBNF/etc.   |\n+------------------+        +---------+----------+        +------------------+\n                                      |\n                +---------------------+----------------------+\n                |                     |                      |\n                v                     v                      v\n        parser codegen          concept translation     runtime parser\n        C4, C5, E5              A3, C6                 E1, E2\n```\n\nThe rule for new work is simple: parse or infer into the IR first, then emit,\ntranslate, generate code, or run from that IR. This keeps every front end and\nback end comparable.\n\n## Concept alignment\n\nGrammar concepts in [`src/grammar/concepts.rs`](../../rust/src/grammar/concepts.rs)\nname constructs such as rules, terminals, non-terminals, sequences, choices, and\nrepetition. [A3](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/A3-grammar-concept-ontology.md)\nowns the full ontology. [C6](../case-studies/issue-93/proposed-issues/C6-concept-aligned-translation.md)\nuses that ontology so translation can preserve meaning even when two notations\nspell a construct differently.\n\nThis mirrors the document-format path described in\n[`docs/cross-format-fidelity.md`](../cross-format-fidelity.md): parse into a\nshared concept layer, then render in the target format with a faithful lowering\nor runtime encoding where direct spelling is impossible. A lossy fallback is an\nidentified gap against the [vision](../vision.md), not complete conversion.\n\n## See also\n\n- [Authoring](authoring.md) for the native surface syntax.\n- [Import and export](import-export.md) for external grammar notations.\n- [Translation](translation.md) for concept-aligned grammar conversion.\n- [CLI and runtime](cli-and-runtime.md) for running grammars through user-facing\n  commands and parser registration.\n# Bulk grammar pipeline\n\n[`js/scripts/run-grammar-bulk-pipeline.mjs`](../../js/scripts/run-grammar-bulk-pipeline.mjs)\nhandles every language in\n[the language catalog](../../parity/language-grammar-inventory.lino) that has\na grammar. That is 57 languages\n([I195-GRAMMAR-BULK-PIPELINE](../vision.md#native-merged-grammars)). For each\nlanguage, in its own process with a memory limit and a timeout, it runs these\nstages:\n\n1. **tree-sitter import.** The pipeline imports the pinned tree-sitter\n   `grammar.json` natively, without the generated parser:\n   - A source pinned in [`parity/grammars/sources.lino`](../../parity/grammars/sources.lino)\n     is imported the way the shipped native grammar is, with its reviewed\n     names and native scanner (see [native grammars](native-grammars.md)).\n   - Any other grammar comes from the crate `rust/Cargo.lock` pins, or from the\n     upstream revision of a vendored parser.\n2. **grammars-v4 import.** The pipeline imports the pinned\n   [antlr/grammars-v4](https://github.com/antlr/grammars-v4) grammar listed in\n   [`parity/grammars-v4-sources.lino`](../../parity/grammars-v4-sources.lino).\n   A language without one has a note there instead. ANTLR has no start rule,\n   so the import starts at the `<entry-point>` that the `desc.xml` beside the\n   grammar names. grammars-v4 runs its own tests from that rule. Without a\n   `desc.xml`, the first parser rule is the start rule.\n3. **compile and parse.** Both grammars are compiled on the native executor\n   and parse the catalog's sample source. The rows of the tree-sitter tree are\n   compared with the oracle rows in\n   [`parity/fixtures/default-cst-expected.lino`](../../parity/fixtures/default-cst-expected.lino).\n4. **merge.** The grammars that imported are merged with `mergeGrammars`.\n\nA failing language does not fail the run. It becomes a matrix row that lists\nits missing features, each with the stage it failed in:\n\n- unsupported constructs;\n- undefined rules;\n- compile errors;\n- rejected samples, with the position and the expected tokens;\n- rows that differ from the oracle;\n- stages that timed out.\n\nCI's `Bulk Grammar Pipeline` job in [`ci.yml`](../../.github/workflows/ci.yml)\nruns every language. It writes the Markdown matrix to the job summary and\nuploads both the Links Notation and the Markdown matrix as the `grammar-bulk-matrix`\nartifact. The job runs alongside the JavaScript and Rust workflows and does\nnot delay either of them.\n\n```sh\ncargo fetch --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml   # the registry grammar.json files\nnode js/scripts/run-grammar-bulk-pipeline.mjs --out-dir grammar-bulk --jobs 4\nnode js/scripts/run-grammar-bulk-pipeline.mjs --out-dir grammar-bulk --only JSON,INI\n```\n\nUpstream grammars are fetched at their pinned revisions into\n`GRAMMAR_BULK_CACHE`, which defaults to a directory under the system temporary\ndirectory. [`js/tests/grammar-bulk-pipeline.test.js`](../../js/tests/grammar-bulk-pipeline.test.js)\nchecks two things without downloading anything:\n\n- every catalog language has a pinned source;\n- a row runs every stage on the pinned C grammar, and the matrix lists every\n  missing feature.\n\n## What the matrix has driven so far\n\n- **A token over an extra.** Under `(matching longest)`, a `token(...)` and a\n  terminal are lexed over a separator or a silent extra rule that matches the\n  same text. tree-sitter does the same: it shifts a valid token before it\n  reduces the same text to an extra. This lets the tree-sitter INI and CSV\n  grammars take their line breaks. Both runtimes do this, and\n  [`parity/fixtures/grammar-token-over-extra.lino`](../../parity/fixtures/grammar-token-over-extra.lino)\n  records the cases.\n- **ANTLR alternative labels.** In `expr # Label`, the label names the context\n  class ANTLR generates for the alternative; it is not syntax. Both importers\n  keep the alternative and add `alternative Label` to the rule's doc. Before\n  this, every grammars-v4 grammar that labels its alternatives (Rust among\n  them) failed to import.\n- **ANTLR `~` over a set.** `~` complements a set and matches one character\n  outside it. The set can be a character class, a one-character literal, a\n  range, or an alternation of these. `~` over anything else stays a negative\n  lookahead. Before this, `~'\"'` imported as a zero-width lookahead, so the\n  grammars-v4 CSV `STRING` rule rejected every quoted field. The shared fixture\n  [`set-complement.g4`](../../rust/tests/fixtures/grammar/antlr/set-complement.g4)\n  checks this in both importers.\n- **ANTLR left recursion, surrogates and numbered channels.**\n  - *Left recursion.* ANTLR resolves a left-recursive rule by alternative\n    order. The importers give each alternative that starts or ends with the\n    rule a `precedence` form, where earlier alternatives bind tighter.\n    `<assoc=right>` makes an alternative right-associative. Other alternative\n    options join the rule's doc.\n  - *Surrogates.* ANTLR reads `\\uD800`-`\\uDFFF` in a set as UTF-16\n    surrogates. Text here is code points, so a set keeps only the scalar\n    values it names.\n  - *Numbered channels.* `-> channel(2)` puts a token on a numbered channel.\n  - *Before this,* the JavaScript, Java, TypeScript, PHP, Lua and Solidity\n    grammars failed to import.\n  - *Coverage.* The shared fixture\n    [`precedence.g4`](../../rust/tests/fixtures/grammar/antlr/precedence.g4)\n    checks all three in both importers.\n- **ANTLR `caseInsensitive` and rule preludes.**\n  - *Case.* `options { caseInsensitive = true; }` makes the lexer match\n    literals, ranges and sets in either case. A rule's own `options` block can\n    turn it off for that rule. A literal becomes a case-insensitive terminal.\n    A range or set also gets the other case of each character it lists, and\n    of the ASCII letters in its ranges.\n  - *Preludes.* `returns [...]`, `locals [...]` and `throws A, B` declare\n    target-language values. Like actions, they are added to the rule's doc.\n    Other rule options are added to the doc too.\n  - *Before this,* the PHP and Swift grammars failed to import.\n  - *Coverage.* The shared fixture\n    [`case-insensitive.g4`](../../rust/tests/fixtures/grammar/antlr/case-insensitive.g4)\n    checks both in both importers.\n- **grammars-v4 entry points.** The pipeline once started each grammar at its\n  first parser rule. TypeScriptParser.g4 begins with\n  `initializer : '=' singleExpression`, so the TypeScript sample was rejected\n  at its end, where `=` was expected. Starting at the `desc.xml` entry point\n  (`program`) lets the sample parse.\n- **ANTLR `-> type(NAME)`.** The command gives a lexer rule's tokens the type\n  `NAME`, so a parser rule that asks for `NAME` also takes them. Both\n  importers add the rule as one more alternative of `NAME`; if `NAME` is only\n  declared in `tokens { ... }`, they define it from the retyped rules. The\n  doc of `NAME` lists each rule that retypes into it. Before this, the R\n  grammar named tokens that no rule defined. The shared fixture\n  [`retype.g4`](../../rust/tests/fixtures/grammar/antlr/retype.g4) checks this\n  in both importers.\n{\n  \"name\": \"meta-language\",\n  \"version\": \"1.1.0\",\n The invariant is:\n\n```text\nGrammar::from_links(Grammar::to_links(grammar)) == grammar\n```\n\nIn code, use `Grammar::builder()` for rules and `Grammar::expr()` for expression\nconstructors. Then pass the value through `LinksEncoder` and `LinksDecoder`.\n\n## Grammar as links\n\nA grammar is data in the network. The links codec in\n[`src/grammar/links.rs`](../../rust/src/grammar/links.rs) implements `ToLinks` and\n`FromLinks` for `Grammar`. Each encoded grammar node is inserted with\n`LinkType::Grammar` from [`src/link_network.rs`](../../rust/src/link_network.rs) and a\nstable term such as `grammar::grammar`, `grammar::rule`, or\n`grammar::expression::sequence`.\n\nThe self-description root in\n[`src/self_description.rs`](../../rust/src/self_description.rs) declares the\n`grammar` root as `LinkType::Grammar` with references to `language` and\n`relation link`. That makes grammar structure part of the same self-describing\nnetwork as links, references, concepts, fields, regions, and objects.\n\nBecause grammar data is encoded as ordinary links:\n\n- Link projections can include or hide grammar links according to normal network\n  rules.\n- Grammar data can be serialized through the existing links codec and LiNo\n  helpers.\n- Other stages can accept a `Grammar` value, a grammar root link, or a serialized\n  links network without inventing a parallel storage path.\n\n## Pipeline\n\n```text\n                            +--------------------+\n                            | authoring surface  | A2, E4\n                            +----------+---------+\n                                       |\n                            +----------v---------+\n                            | external importers | B1-B7\n                            +----------+---------+\n                                       |\n                                       v\n+------------------+        +--------------------+        +------------------+\n| example corpora  +------->| Grammar IR links   +------->| emitters         |\n| and observations | D1,D5,D6| A1                 | C1-C3  | BNF/EBNF/etc.   |\n+------------------+        +---------+----------+        +------------------+\n                                      |\n                +---------------------+----------------------+\n                |                     |                      |\n                v                     v                      v\n        parser codegen          concept translation     runtime parser\n        C4, C5, E5              A3, C6                 E1, E2\n```\n\nThe rule for new work is simple: parse or infer into the IR first, then emit,\ntranslate, generate code, or run from that IR. This repository already uses its\nprobability core for ranking. Their archived\nquotes and prior evidence must be reconciled with the final PR diff and CI.\n# Concrete syntax in the translation pipeline\n\nThe default readers retain a concrete source record in `sourceTree.syntax`.\nIts token and trivia leaves partition the original text:\nquotes, comment markers, whitespace, line endings, directives and file headers\nremain present. `reconstructConcrete(sourceTree.syntax)` in JavaScript, or\n`reconstruct_concrete` in Rust, concatenates those leaves to reproduce the input.\n\nRanges are half-open UTF-8 byte offsets in both implementations. A production\nrecords its grammar rule, the concept it produces and its source range. Productions\nare views over the shared token stream, so a transformation can retain its source\nwithout copying the entire text into every node. Synthetic indentation and\nend-of-file tokens consume no source bytes.\n\nThe `parsed` trace callback receives this record for formal languages, controlled\nnatural languages and all seven machine formats. A decorator around the formal\n`parse` stage also receives it before understanding rules derive a meta program.\nNo tracing is enabled by default. Existing custom readers remain replaceable\nthrough the stage API.\n\n```js\nimport {\n  createTranslator,\n  reconstructConcrete,\n} from '@link-foundation/universal-translator';\n\nconst translator = createTranslator({\n  trace(stage, tree) {\n    if (stage === 'parsed') {\n      console.log(reconstructConcrete(tree.syntax));\n    }\n  },\n});\ntranslator.translate('const x = 1;\\r\\n', 'javascript', 'python');\n```\n\nThe semantic view remains responsible for understanding and lowering operations;\nthe concrete record owns their original spelling. This follows the separation\nbetween source tokens and rewrites in\n[ANTLR's token stream rewriter](https://github.com/antlr/antlr4/blob/master/runtime/Java/src/org/antlr/v4/runtime/TokenStreamRewriter.java)\nand the explicit source ranges used by\n[tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/using-parsers/3-advanced-parsing.html).\n\n`translator.parsePartial(source, language).syntax` in JavaScript, or\n`translator.parse_partial(source, language)?.syntax` in Rust, also retains\nincomplete input, including unclosed literals and unsupported constructs. Its\n`productions` describe accepted fragments; its `errors` contain unread byte\nranges and diagnostic messages. Whitespace-only and empty inputs have a complete\nrecord with no productions or errors. The original CRLF endings and indentation\nremain intact even though fragment recovery dedents its semantic inputs.\n\nThe formal parser records its actual grammar tokens and production methods.\nLine-oriented readers and recovery use lossless word/symbol leaves and layout\ntrivia; accepted semantic concepts have `source-lines` production views. A\nconcept assembled from separate instruction ranges has separate views rather\nthan claiming ownership of the instructions between them. Recovery's `fragment`\nviews describe accepted parts, while unread parts appear only in `errors`.\n\nGrammar import/update and exact subline ranges through every semantic rewrite\nremain tracked work in issue 16. Retaining the concrete source alone does not\nestablish a semantic mapping between two translated programs.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Define it or fix the spelling.`;\n      diagnostics.push({ kind: 'undefined-non-terminal', severity: 'error', rule: rule.name, message, name, referencedIn: rule.name });\n    }\n  }\n  return diagnostics;\n}\n\nfunction checkLeftRecursion(rules, nullability) {\n  const graph = leftReferenceGraph(rules, nullability);\n  const diagnostics = [];\n  const seenCycles = new Set();\n  const visit = (target, current, seenRules, path) => {\n    for (const next of graph.get(current) ?? Weak keys release them with the parse or transformed program.\nconst origins = new WeakMap();\nconst commentRecords = new WeakMap();\n\nexport const commentOrigins = (texts) => commentRecords.get(texts) ?? [];\n\nexport function trackComments(texts, positions) {\n  commentRecords.set(texts, positions.slice());\n  return texts;\n}\n\nexport function pushComment(texts, text, origin) {\n  const positions = commentRecords.get(texts) ?? new Array(texts.length);\n  positions[texts.length] = origin;\n  texts.push(text);\n  commentRecords.set(texts, positions);\n  return texts;\n}\n\nexport function attachComments(tree, key, comments) {\n  const nodes = comments.filter(({ kind }) => kind === 'Comment');\n  tree[key] = trackComments(\n    nodes.map(({ text }) => text),\n    nodes.map(sourceOrigin)\n  );\n  return tree;\n}\n\nexport const sourceOrigin = (tree) => origins.get(tree);\n\nexport function withOrigin(tree, origin) {\n  if (tree && origin) {\n    origins.set(tree, origin);\n  }\n  return tree;\n}\n\nexport function inheritOrigin(tree, source) {\n  if (tree && source) {\n    for (const key of ['comments', 'mainComments']) {\n      if (Array.isArray(tree[key]) && Array.isArray(source[key])) {\n        trackComments(tree[key], commentOrigins(source[key]));\n      }\n    }\n  }\n  return withOrigin(tree, sourceOrigin(source));\n}\n\nexport const mapOrigins = (items, change) =>\n  items.map((item, index) => inheritOrigin(change(item, index), item));\n\nexport function combineOrigins(items) {\n  const found = items.filter(Boolean);\n  if (!found.length) {\n    return undefined;\n  }\n  return {\n    source: found[0].source,\n    lines: [\n      ...new Set(\n        found.flatMap((origin) =>\n          origin.source === found[0].source ? Its\n    // inherited range still needs the same child-ownership pass as raw nodes.\n    const own = location\n      ? locate(location.start, location.end)\n      : sourceOrigin(value);\n    if (!own) {\n      return;\n    }\n    const first = own.lines[0];\n    const last = own.lines.at(-1);\n    const lines = new Set(own.lines);\n    // A block header owns its punctuation, while nested statements own their\n    // individual lines. Shared boundary lines can belong to several nodes.\n    const exclude = (child) => {\n      if (!child || typeof child !== 'object') {\n        return;\n      }\n      if (statements.has(child.kind)) {\n        // A lifted command can lie outside the consuming statement's own\n        // span. Those lines belong exclusively to the consuming statement.\n        for (const origin of expressionOrigins(child)) {\n          const owned = origin.range\n            ? Array.from(\n                { length: origin.range[1] - origin.range[0] + 1 },\n                (_, index) => origin.range[0] + index\n              )\n            : origin.lines;\n          for (const line of owned) {\n            if (line !== first && line !== last) {\n              lines.delete(line);\n            }\n          }\n        }\n      } else {\n        Object.values(child).forEach(exclude);\n      }\n    };\n    if (containers.has(value.kind) || statements.has(value.kind)) {\n      Object.values(value).forEach(exclude);\n    }\n    withOrigin(value, { ...own, source, lines: [...lines] });\n  };\n  visit(tree);\n}\n\n// A fragment is parsed inside its language's executable wrapper. A group of lines on both sides is one band per run of lines.\nexport function connectorPaths(link, span, width, active) {\n  const middle = width / 2;\n  const paths = [];\n  for (const group of link.groups) {\n    const [left, right] = group.lines.map(runs);\n    const count = Math.max(left.length, right.length);\n    for (let at = 0; at < count; at += 1) {\n      const from = left[Math.min(at, left.length - 1)];\n      const to = right[Math.min(at, right.length - 1)];\n      const a = span(0, ...from);\n      const b = span(1, ...to);\n      if (!a || !b) {\n        continue;\n      }\n      paths.push({\n        colour: group.colour,\n        active: group === active,\n        d: [\n          `M0 ${a.top}`,\n          `C${middle} ${a.top} ${middle} ${b.top} ${width} ${b.top}`,\n          `L${width} ${b.bottom}`,\n          `C${middle} ${b.bottom} ${middle} ${a.bottom} 0 ${a.bottom}`,\n          'Z',\n        ].join(' '),\n      });\n    }\n  }\n  return paths;\n}\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

It does not match templates: it reads source text with per-language grammar tables and rewrites it through rules. It translates between **32 programming languages** (including **Lean 4** and **Rocq**), **three machine targets** (NASM x86-64, CIL, JVM/Jasmin) and **controlled versions of 30+ natural languages**. The JavaScript (`js/`) and Rust (`rust/`) implementations write byte-identical output for every golden translation.\\n\\n```text\\nsource ──parser──▶ source tree ──understanding rules──▶ meta ──type inference──▶ typed meta\\n  ──meaning rules──▶ ──custom layers──▶ ──context rules──▶ ──emitter──▶ target text\\n  ──lowering──▶ stack machine ──▶ NASM / CIL / JVM (Jasmin)\\nNASM / CIL / JVM ──reader──▶ stack machine ──lifting──▶ meta\\ncontrolled natural text ──reader──▶ meta ──writer──▶ controlled natural text\\n```\\n\\n### Requirements gate (test-driven)\\n\\n`docs/case-studies/issue-1/requirements.lino` lists every requirement from the issue and its comments. `docs/case-studies/issue-1/rosetta-coverage.lino` lists the Rosetta Code algorithm types. `scripts/check-requirements.mjs` checks each requirement against the repository; for example, it compares the language lists of both implementations and checks that every task has a golden in every language. It fails CI (`Rust and cross-language translation` job, and `js/tests/requirements.test.js` under Node, Bun and Deno) unless every requirement is **done** or **blocked with a written reason**.\\n\\nThe gate caught real gaps during this work. The Rust implementation was missing 10 languages; that was fixed and the gate now passes.\\n\\n### Web demo\\n\\n![Web demo translating a Python function to Rust](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/screenshots/web-demo.png?raw=true)\\n\\n`examples/universal-app` is a React demo in which any programming or natural language can be translated to any other. You can paste a whole program, one function or one statement. The `web-e2e` job in `.github/workflows/example-app.yml` drives it in Chromium (`examples/universal-app/e2e/translate.e2e.mjs`) and takes the screenshot above.\\n\\n### Fragments: statements, functions or a whole program\\n\\n`translateFragment` / `parseFragment` (JS) and `translate_fragment` / `parse_fragment` (Rust), plus `universal-translator translate --fragment`, accept a statement, one or more functions, or a whole program. Each comes back as the same kind of fragment in the target. A fragment only has to be complete: a function must end with its closing. Otherwise the translator fails with the reason and the line, for example `The fragment is not complete: it ends before its closing (line 2)`. Goldens for every language are in `examples/programs/fragments/translated/` and are checked by `write-fragments.mjs --check`.\\n\\n### CLI, library, HTTP API and Docker\\n\\n- `universal-translator serve` starts an HTTP API (`GET /languages`, `POST /translate`). It reads `--port`/`--host`, then `PORT`/`HOST`, then `.lenv`, through lino-arguments.\\n- `js/src/index.js` (with types) and the `rust/` crate are the libraries.\\n- The `Dockerfile` image runs the CLI and the server. The release workflow builds it and smoke tests the CLI and the HTTP API.\\n\\n### Source layout and best practices\\n\\n- Sources are split into `src/meta` (shared types and trees), `src/formal` (programming languages, Lean, Rocq and machine code) and `src/natural` (human languages, with a reader and a writer), in both `js/` and `rust/`. The `source-layout` check rejects imports that point outwards from the meta layer.\\n- [`docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md) maps the associative technology stack, the code architecture principles and all 17 CI/CD best practices to evidence, or gives a reason when one does not apply. `cargo clippy -D warnings` now runs in CI.\\n- **Test coverage is required by CI.** `npm run test:coverage` replaces `npm test` in the Node.js job. It fails below 94% line, 91% branch or 95% function coverage of `js/src` and `bin`; current coverage is 95.4%, 92.1% and 96.5%. The Rust crate runs the same goldens, but CI does not measure its coverage.\\n\\n### Programming languages (32) and machine code\\n\\n| | |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Languages | JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Lua, PHP, C, C++, C#, Java, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Swift, Perl, Dart, Scala, Julia, R, Groovy, Objective-C, Nim, D, Pascal, Fortran, Ada, Visual Basic .NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave, Zig, **Lean 4, Rocq** |\\n| Dialects | Pascal, Fortran, Ada, VB.NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave and Zig have their own program layout. They are dialects of the shared parser and emitter (`js/src/formal/dialects/`, `rust/src/formal/dialects/`). Lean 4 programs use `partial def` and `IO`. Rocq programs are pure `Fixpoint`s over an output monad defined in a small runtime, and are evaluated with `Eval vm_compute`. |\\n| Machine targets | NASM, CIL and JVM are written through a named stack machine and read back by lifting, so machine code translates to every language and between targets. |\\n| Modes | context-dependent (default, adapts comments such as C \\\"function call\\\" → C# \\\"method call\\\"), literal, same-effect |\\n| Extensibility | Every stage and rule list is an option of `createGrammarTranslator`; custom meta → meta layers are supported. |\\n| Common library | `common-library/` (output operations only, one file per language), enabled with `--common-library` |\\n\\n### Controlled natural languages\\n\\n- Data lives in `data/natural/*.lino`; `js/src/natural/` and `rust/src/natural/` read and write the same texts byte for byte.\\n- Covers the 30 most spoken languages (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Marathi, Telugu, Turkish, Tamil, Vietnamese, Korean, Italian, Persian, Swahili, Tagalog, Thai, Polish, Ukrainian, Hausa, Gujarati, Punjabi, Dutch), each in a small controlled form (`cnl-default`).\\n- Profiles for the standards named in the issue:\\n  - ASD-STE100\\n  - Attempto Controlled English\\n  - Gellish (English and Dutch)\\n  - SBVR Structured English\\n  - Plain language (ISO 24495-1)\\n  - E-Prime\\n  - Basic English, VOA Special English and Globish\\n  - Minimal English, Minimal French and Minimal Polish, built on the **65 semantic primes** of NSM (`data/natural/semantic-primes.lino`)\\n- `checkText` and the `check-words` command enforce each standard's rules: sentence length, allowed first words, forbidden words such as \\\"to be\\\" in E-Prime or \\\"shall\\\" in plain language, vocabulary limits, and Gellish relation phrases.\\n- Translations run natural → meta → any programming or machine language, and back: `universal-translator translate russian python`, `translate python spanish`.\\n- Every example program is written in every natural language and profile under `examples/programs/natural/`. Each text is read back to the same meaning and checked against its standard.\\n\\n### Rosetta Code and Hello World\\n\\n18 tasks in `examples/programs/` are translated to all 32 languages, the 3 machine targets and every natural language, then run natively:\\n\\n- hello world\\n- factorial\\n- greatest common divisor\\n- FizzBuzz\\n- sum of squares\\n- Fibonacci\\n- Ackermann\\n- Towers of Hanoi\\n- leap year\\n- sum of digits\\n- hailstone\\n- 99 bottles\\n- primality by trial division\\n- mutual recursion\\n- perfect numbers\\n- sieve of Eratosthenes\\n- bubble sort\\n- sum and product of an array\\n\\nAlgorithm types covered (from `rosetta-coverage.lino`): output, integer arithmetic, conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion (including mutual recursion), number theory, text concatenation, and **integer arrays** (new: array values in the meta language, all 32 languages, NASM/CIL/JVM and natural-language sentences).\\n\\n**Blocked, with reasons recorded in `rosetta-coverage.lino`.** These are not presented as done. Rosetta Code has more than 1,300 tasks, and these types need values the meta language does not have yet:\\n\\n| Type | Why it is blocked |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| floating-point | Machine targets and the meta language use 64-bit integers only |\\n| string manipulation | Text can be printed and concatenated, but not indexed or transformed |\\n| higher-order functions | Functions are top-level declarations only |\\n| data structures | Records, maps, stacks and queues need compound values |\\n| input/output | Programs only write to standard output, which is what the native checks compare |\\n| objects and concurrency | Not supported |\\n\\n**Classes as fragments** are also **blocked** (`class-fragments` in the gate) for the same reason: the meta language has no objects or classes, so a class has no meaning to translate yet.\\n\\nThe gate reports `rosetta-algorithm-types` and `class-fragments` as **BLOCKED** with these reasons. Every other requirement is **DONE**.\\n\\n## Verification\\n\\n- **`npm test` (Node, Bun, Deno) and `cargo test`.** Every task is translated to every language, machine target and natural language and compared with the goldens in `examples/programs/translated` and `examples/programs/natural`.\\n- **`examples/programs/verify-native.mjs --require-all [--common-library]`.** The `native-translation` CI job compiles or runs each translation with its real toolchain and compares the output with the JavaScript original. All-or-nothing\n// translation throws the whole text away for that one part. Partial\n// translation keeps everything it can read and marks the rest.\n//\n// The text is cut into parts along its own layout, so the method needs no\n// grammar of its own and works for every language:\n//\n// 1. A part starts at a line and may end before any later line that is\n//    indented no deeper than its first line, unless that line only closes\n//    or continues the part (`}`, `end`, `else`, ...).\n// 2. source wherever the target has\nthe same tokens: the spaces inside a line, the step of indentation, the\nblank lines, the blank lines around the code and the line ends. The broader question and query\ncriterion remains open while SQL/LINQ and other target families are implemented.\n\n## Representation and composition\n\n\"'`Question` is an expression with an `aspect` (`type`, `documentation`, `source`,\n`details`) and an ordinary expression as its `subject`. An `Evaluate` statement\nasks the question; other expression positions consume its answer. For example,\nPython `print(meaning.__doc__)` asks for documentation inside an output statement.\nThe controlled natural grammars have distinct question and answer phrases. The\nsame recursive expression reader handles their subject slots; these are not\nwhole-program examples or name-specific substitutions.\n\nPython readers recognize built-in `type`, the `__doc__` property, imported\n`inspect.getsource` (including module/member aliases), and IPython `meaning??`.\nDeclared names, parameters, and conflicting imports prevent mistaking a custom\nprocedure for a known reflection procedure. Detailed inspection writes the\nIPython `pinfo2` API and requires an entity name rather than evaluating an\narbitrary call through a string. JavaScript/TypeScript use their native function\nsource and prototype constructor operations, and a portable `__doc__` property.\nUnsupported aspects/targets report an error rather than guessing a replacement.\nNative type objects and source spellings belong to the target language.\n\n`Function.documentation` contains runtime text, separately from comments.\nPython'\"'s first plain string expression becomes this field; an f-string does not.\nJavaScript definitions carry it through an immediately following property\nassignment. Assignments after other statements stay in execution order. Natural\nfunction definitions carry an explicit documentation sentence whose quoted value\ncan span physical lines. An orphan documentation sentence, or a non-text value,\nis rejected.\n\n## Python edition experiment\n\nThe initial native check failed: Python 3.13+ cleans indentation in docstrings,\nwhile an earlier compiler retains it. These methods execute without an explicit foreach statement because the query itself must use foreach in order to return a result. These queries return a single value, not an IEnumerable collection. The full query\nand inherited language-coverage requirements remain open.\n\n## Shared meaning\n\n`Query` holds ordinary expressions for `source`, `condition` and `projection`,\na scoped range `variable`, and an `eager` evaluation flag. It can appear as an\nexpression in a binding, return or another query. `Evaluate(Query)` asks for the\nresult. This separates selection questions from the earlier introspection\n`Question` expression; SQL does not implement Python reflection.\n\nReaders recognize SQL `SELECT … FROM … [AS …] [WHERE …]`, C# LINQ\n`from … in … [where …] select …`, Python list/generator comprehensions, and\nsingle-parameter JavaScript/TypeScript `filter`/`map` chains. All 71 controlled\nnatural grammars compose their own expression slots into question and answer\nforms. The 30 base languages have native phrases; restricted profiles derive\nclauses from their own allowed loop/condition/result vocabulary. Minimal profiles\nuse quoted technical operation tags. No vocabulary limits are expanded.\n\nSQL is listed as a query target separately from the 33 imperative grammars and\nseven machine dialects. Its reader preserves quoted identifier case and SQL\nstring escaping; its writer rejects imperative programs and common-library\nmode. The public capability flag prevents old algorithm-coverage tests from\nclaiming that a query language implements imperative entry points.\n\n## Evaluation, types and scope\n\nC# query expressions enumerate lazily. `ToArray()` materializes their results;\nthis is described by Microsoft's [query execution documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/get-started/introduction-to-linq-queries).\nPython list comprehensions are eager while generator expressions defer their\nbodies, as documented in the [Python expression reference](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#generator-expressions).\nThe native example changes a source row between construction and enumeration\nto make this distinction observable. SQL output rejects a deferred iterator,\nand JavaScript output rejects deferred queries until it has a lazy writer.\n\nEager filter/map chains with function calls remain nested query expressions:\nall filtering effects finish before projection effects start. Combining\nside-effect-free predicates and projections is supported for ordinary data\nrecords. Arbitrary getters, custom iterators and overloaded operations still\nneed additional semantic modeling.\n\nCollection types retain the projected element and evaluation strategy as\n`array<element>` or `sequence<element>`. C# emits inferred query bindings with\n`var`, typed array/enumerable function returns, and expression-position array\nconstructors. A local range variable receives the source element type, rather\nthan inheriting an unrelated outer binding's type. Free-variable rewrites stop\nat nested binders while still traversing their source expressions. C# receives\nfresh range names where its local-name rules require them.\n\n## Reproduction and evidence\n\n- `experiments/issue-16-queries.mjs` exercises four source grammars against four\n  targets and records explicit unsupported evaluation strategies.\n- `experiments/issue-16-query-typing.mjs` records binding, function-return and\n  nested-scope translations.\n- `js/tests/queries.test.js` checks registration/detection, formal round trips,\n  all natural grammars, vocabulary constraints, eager/deferred strategies,\n  quoted SQL names, collection types, scope, filter/map side effects and native\n  SQLite/Python/Node agreement.\n- `rust/tests/queries.rs` covers the matching shared representation, formal and\n  natural round trips, strategy rejection, collection types and scopes.\n- `examples/queries/verify-native.mjs` compiles the generated C# methods and\n  bindings and compares finite results across four native runtimes. Comments directly above a function belong to that function.\nfunction collectItems(items) {\n  const program = node('Program', {\n    comments: [],\n    imports: [],\n    functions: [],\n    main: block(),\n  });\n  let pending = [];\n  const append = (trivia) => {\n    for (const item of trivia.filter(({ kind }) => kind === 'Comment')) {\n      pushComment(program.comments, item.text, sourceOrigin(item));\n    }\n  };\n  for (const item of items) {\n    if (item.kind === 'Comment' || item.kind === 'Blank') {\n      pending.push(item);\n      continue;\n    }\n    const isFirstCode =\n      program.imports.length +\n        program.functions.length +\n        program.main.statements.length ===\n      0;\n    if (isFirstCode) {\n      // Comments before the last empty line describe the file; the ones\n      // after it (all of them without an empty line) describe the first item.\n      const split = pending.findLastIndex(({ kind }) => kind === 'Blank');\n      append(pending.slice(0, Math.max(split, 0)));\n      pending = pending.slice(split + 1);\n    }\n    // An empty line after a function is kept only where the source has one.\n    const previous = program.functions.at(-1);\n    if (previous && previous.blankAfter === undefined) {\n      previous.blankAfter = pending.some(({ kind }) => kind === 'Blank');\n    }\n    if (item.kind === 'Import') {\n      // An import keeps no comments: the ones above it describe the file.\n      append(pending);\n      program.imports.push(item.text);\n    } else if (item.kind === 'Function') {\n      program.functions.push(\n        attachComments(inheritOrigin({ ...item }, item), 'comments', pending)\n      );\n    } else {\n      program.main.statements.push(...pending, item);\n    }\n    pending = [];\n  }\n  program.main.statements.push(...pending);\n  program.main = block(layout(program.main.statements));\n  return program;\n}\n\nconst isExitSuccess = (statement) =>\n  statement?.kind === 'Return' &&\n  statement.value?.kind === 'Number' &&\n  statement.value.value === 0;\n\n// Collect functions, the entry point and file comments into a Program. The\n// body of `main` becomes the program's main block.\nexport function findEntryPoint(source, { from } = {}) {\n  const program = unqualifyClassCalls(\n    collectItems(flattenClasses(source.items)),\n    source.items\n  );\n  const own = from && languageSyntax(from).mainName;\n  const entry = program.functions.find(\n    (item) => entryNames.has(item.name) || item.name === own\n  );\n  if (!entry) {\n    return program;\n  }\n  const leftovers = program.main.statements.filter(\n    (statement) =>\n      !isCallTo(statement, entry.name) && !isPythonMainGuard(statement)\n  );\n  const statements = [...leftovers, ...entry.body.statements];\n  // `return 0;` at the end of C's main is the default exit status.\n  if (isExitSuccess(statements.at(-1))) {\n    statements.pop();\n  }\n  return inheritOrigin(\n    {\n      ...program,\n      functions: program.functions.filter((item) => item !== entry),\n      main: block(statements),\n      mainComments: entry.comments,\n    },\n    program\n  );\n}\n\n// The output procedures of each language, described as data.\nconst lineCalls = new Set([\n  'console.log',\n  'print',\n  'puts',\n  'System.Console.WriteLine',\n  'Console.WriteLine',\n  'System.out.println',\n  'fmt.Println',\n  'println',\n  'Console.Out.WriteLine',\n]);\nconst textCalls = new Set([\n  'System.Console.Write',\n  'Console.Write',\n  'System.out.print',\n  'fmt.Print',\n  'process.stdout.write',\n  'sys.stdout.write',\n  'io.write',\n]);\nconst formatCalls = {\n  printf: 'percent',\n  'fmt.Printf': 'percent',\n  'println!': 'braces',\n  'print!': 'braces',\n};\n\nfunction joinWithSpaces(values, separator = text(' ')) {\n  if (values.length === 1) {\n    return values[0];\n  }\n  const parts = [];\n  values.forEach((value, index) => {\n    if (index > 0) {\n      parts.push(separator);\n    }\n    parts.push(value);\n  });\n  return node('Interpolation', { parts });\n}\n\nfunction readFormat(format, values, style) {\n  const pattern =\n    style === 'percent'\n      ? /%(?:l{0,2}d|i|s|c|v|t|%|(?:\\.\\d+)?l?[fgeG])/g\n      : /\\{\\{|\\}\\}|\\{\\}/g;\n  const parts = [];\n  let last = 0;\n  let index = 0;\n  for (const match of format.matchAll(pattern)) {\n    if (match.index > last) {\n      parts.push(text(format.slice(last, match.index)));\n    }\n    if (match[0] === '%%') {\n      parts.push(text('%'));\n    } else if (match[0] === '{{') {\n      parts.push(text('{'));\n    } else if (match[0] === '}}') {\n      parts.push(text('}'));\n    } else {\n      parts.push(values[index++]);\n    }\n    last = match.index + match[0].length;\n  }\n  if (last < format.length) {\n    parts.push(text(format.slice(last)));\n  }\n  return parts;\n}\n\nexport function partsToValue(parts) {\n  const merged = [];\n  for (const part of parts) {\n    if (part.kind === 'Text' && merged.at(-1)?.kind === 'Text') {\n      merged[merged.length - 1] = text(merged.at(-1).value + part.value);\n    } else if (!(part.kind === 'Text' && part.value === '')) {\n      merged.push(part);\n    }\n  }\n  if (merged.length === 0) {\n    return text('');\n  }\n  // A format with a single placeholder prints just that value.\n  if (merged.length === 1) {\n    return merged[0];\n  }\n  return node('Interpolation', { parts: merged });\n}\n\nfunction withoutTrailingNewline(parts) {\n  const last = parts.at(-1);\n  if (last?.kind === 'Text' && last.value.endsWith('\\n')) {\n    return {\n      parts: [...parts.slice(0, -1), text(last.value.slice(0, -1))],\n      newline: true,\n    };\n  }\n  return { parts, newline: false };\n}\n\nfunction streamParts(expression) {\n  if (expression.kind === 'Binary' && expression.operator === 'stream') {\n    return [...streamParts(expression.left), expression.right];\n  }\n  return [expression];\n}\n\nconst knownPrint = (callee) =>\n  lineCalls.has(callee) ||\n  textCalls.has(callee) ||\n  Object.hasOwn(formatCalls, callee) ||\n  callee === 'echo';\n\n// Which kind of output procedure a call names: 'line' when it ends the line,\n// 'text' when the text carries its own line ends.\nfunction printKind(callee, { printCalls: own, print: renamed }) {\n  // A version of one's own may give the line output another name.\n  if (renamed?.line === callee && !knownPrint(callee)) {\n    return 'line';\n  }\n  if (own) {\n    return own.line.includes(callee)\n      ? 'line'\n      : own.text.includes(callee)\n        ? 'text'\n        : undefined;\n  }\n  if (lineCalls.has(callee)) {\n    return 'line';\n  }\n  return textCalls.has(callee) || callee === 'echo' ? 'text' : undefined;\n}\n\n// Python's print(..., sep=, end=) and Swift's print(..., separator:,\n// terminator:): an empty end keeps the line open (\"\" reads as an empty\n// interpolation where quotes interpolate), and any other end is printed\n// after the values, so `end=\"!\"` is not lost.\nfunction printLine(values, named) {\n  const separator = named.sep ?? named.separator;\n  const joined = values.length ? joinWithSpaces(values, separator) : text('');\n  const end = named.end ?? named.terminator;\n  if (end === undefined) {\n    return node('Print', { value: joined, newline: true });\n  }\n  const empty =\n    (end.kind === 'Text' && end.value === '') ||\n    (end.kind === 'Interpolation' && end.parts.length === 0);\n  if (empty) {\n    return node('Print', { value: joined, newline: false });\n  }\n  const flat = [joined, end].flatMap((value) =>\n    value.kind === 'Interpolation' ? value.parts : [value]\n  );\n  const { parts, newline } = withoutTrailingNewline(flat);\n  return node('Print', { value: partsToValue(parts), newline });\n}\n\nfunction printFromCall(call, syntax) {\n  const kind = printKind(call.callee, syntax);\n  const values = call.arguments.filter(\n    (value) => value.kind !== 'NamedArgument'\n  );\n  const named = Object.fromEntries(\n    call.arguments\n      .filter((value) => value.kind === 'NamedArgument')\n      .map((value) => [value.name, value.value])\n  );\n  // D's writeln prints its arguments one after another, without spaces.\n  if (kind === 'line' && syntax.printCalls?.adjacent) {\n    const flat = values.flatMap((value) =>\n      value.kind === 'Interpolation' ? value.parts : [value]\n    );\n    return node('Print', { value: partsToValue(flat), newline: true });\n  }\n  if (kind === 'line') {\n    return printLine(values, named);\n  }\n  if (kind === 'text') {\n    const flat = values.flatMap((value) =>\n      value.kind === 'Interpolation' ? value.parts : [value]\n    );\n    const { parts, newline } = withoutTrailingNewline(flat);\n    return node('Print', { value: partsToValue(parts), newline });\n  }\n  const style = Object.hasOwn(formatCalls, call.callee)\n    ? formatCalls[call.callee]\n    : undefined;\n  if (style && values[0]?.kind === 'Text') {\n    const { parts, newline } = withoutTrailingNewline(\n      readFormat(values[0].value, values.slice(1), style)\n    );\n    return node('Print', {\n      value: partsToValue(parts),\n      newline: newline || call.callee === 'println!',\n    });\n  }\n  return undefined;\n}\n\n// Replace each known output procedure with the Print concept.\nexport function recognizePrint(program, { from } = {}) {\n  const syntax = from ? languageSyntax(from) : {};\n  return rewrite(program, (current) => {\n    if (current.kind !== 'Evaluate') {\n      return current;\n    }\n    const expression = current.expression;\n    if (expression.kind === 'Call') {\n      return printFromCall(expression, syntax) ?? current;\n    }\n    if (expression.kind === 'Binary' && expression.operator === 'stream') {\n      const [stream, ...values] = streamParts(expression);\n      if (stream.kind === 'Name' && /cout$/.test(stream.name)) {\n        const endsLine =\n          values.at(-1)?.kind === 'Name' && /endl$/.test(values.at(-1).name);\n        const { parts, newline } = withoutTrailingNewline(\n          endsLine ?
