A variable read before its first\n// assignment (`x = x + 1`, or `if x > 0` above `x = 0`) is not declared\n// there: it comes from outside, as in a statement translated on its own.\nexport function declareOnFirstAssignment(program) {\n  const declareIn = (body, known) => {\n    const scope = new Set(known);\n    const read = new Set();\n    const visitBlock = (current) => ({\n      ...current,\n      statements: mapOrigins(current.statements, visitStatement),\n    });\n    const visitStatement = (statement) => {\n      if (statement.kind === 'If') {\n        addReadNames(statement.condition, read);\n        return {\n          ...statement,\n          then: visitBlock(statement.then),\n          otherwise:\n            statement.otherwise &&\n            (statement.otherwise.kind === 'Block'\n              ? visitBlock(statement.otherwise)\n              : visitStatement(statement.otherwise)),\n        };\n      }\n      if (statement.kind === 'While') {\n        addReadNames(statement.condition, read);\n        return { ...statement, body: visitBlock(statement.body) };\n      }\n      if (statement.kind === 'CountingLoop') {\n        addReadNames([statement.start, statement.end], read);\n        scope.add(statement.variable);\n        return { ...statement, body: visitBlock(statement.body) };\n      }\n      if (statement.kind === 'ForEach') {\n        addReadNames(statement.array, read);\n        scope.add(statement.variable);\n        return { ...statement, body: visitBlock(statement.body) };\n      }\n      // The value is read before the variable is assigned.\n      addReadNames(statement, read);\n      if (\n        statement.kind === 'Assignment' &&\n        statement.operator === '=' &&\n        !scope.has(statement.name) &&\n        !read.has(statement.name)\n      ) {\n        scope.add(statement.name);\n        // A Python hint (`total: int = 0`) gives the declared type.\n        return node('Declaration', {\n          name: statement.name,\n          ...(statement.type ? { type: statement.type } : {}),\n          value: statement.value,\n          mutable: true,\n        });\n      }\n      if (statement.kind === 'Declaration') {\n        scope.add(statement.name);\n      }\n      return statement;\n    };\n    return visitBlock(body);\n  };\n  return {\n    ...program,\n    functions: mapOrigins(program.functions, (item) => ({\n      ...item,\n      body: declareIn(\n        item.body,\n        item.parameters.map((parameter) => parameter.name)\n      ),\n    })),\n    main: declareIn(program.main, []),\n  };\n}\n\n// A variable is mutable exactly when the program assigns it again. An array\n// whose elements the program assigns is marked too: Rust, Swift and Nim\n// declare it like a mutable variable.\nexport function inferMutability(program) {\n  const assigned = new Set();\n  const stored = new Set();\n  rewrite(program, (current) => {\n    if (current.kind === 'Assignment') {\n      assigned.add(current.name);\n    }\n    if (current.kind === 'IndexAssignment') {\n      stored.add(current.name);\n    }\n    if (current.kind === 'Call') {\n      const mutator =\n        /^(.*)\\.(?:push|pop|shift|unshift|splice|sort|reverse|append|extend|insert|remove|clear)$/u.exec(\n          current.callee\n        );\n      if (mutator) {\n        stored.add(mutator[1]);\n      }\n    }\n    return current;\n  });\n  return rewrite(program, (current) => {\n    if (current.kind !== 'Declaration') {\n      return current;\n    }\n    const marked = { ...current, mutable: assigned.has(current.name) };\n    delete marked.elementsAssigned;\n    if (stored.has(current.name)) {\n      marked.elementsAssigned = true;\n    }\n    return marked;\n  });\n}\n\nexport function dropSourceDetails(program) {\n  return rewrite(program, (current) => {\n    if (current.kind === 'Return' && current.implicit) {\n      const rest = { ...current };\n      delete rest.implicit;\n      return rest;\n    }\n    return current;\n  });\n}\n\nconst compoundMeanings = {\n  '+=': 'add',\n  '-=': 'subtract',\n  '*=': 'multiply',\n  '/=': 'divide',\n  '%=': 'remainder',\n};\n\n// `x += v` means `x = x + v`; the meta language keeps only the plain form.\n// `/=` divides like the language's `/`.\nexport function expandCompoundAssignment(program, { from } = {}) {\n  const meanings = {\n    ...compoundMeanings,\n    '/=': from ? It is a detail of the\n// source language (see copyReassignedParameters), not part of the meaning.\nexport function dropParameterCopies(program) {\n  return {\n    ...program,\n    functions: mapOrigins(program.functions, (item) => {\n      const statements = [...item.body.statements];\n      let parameters = item.parameters;\n      const copiedParameter = (statement) =>\n        statement?.kind === 'Declaration' &&\n        statement.value?.kind === 'Name' &&\n        parameters.find(\n          ({ name }) =>\n            name === statement.value.name &&\n            (name === statement.name ||\n              copyName(statement.name) === neutralName(name))\n        );\n      for (\n        let parameter = copiedParameter(statements[0]);\n        parameter;\n        parameter = copiedParameter(statements[0])\n      ) {\n        const copy = statements.shift().name;\n        parameters = parameters.map((current) =>\n          current === parameter ? { ...current, name: copy } : current\n        );\n      }\n      return {\n        ...item,\n        parameters,\n        body: { ...item.body, statements },\n      };\n    }),\n  };\n}\n\n// The neutral name of the parameter that a copy named `name` is made from.\nconst copyName = (name) => ['initial', ...nameWords(name)].join('-');\n\n// Languages without an integer division operator call a library procedure:\n// JavaScript writes `Math.trunc(a / b)`, Perl `int(a / b)`, PHP\n// `intdiv(a, b)`, Julia `div(a, b)` and Groovy `a.intdiv(b)`. The language description names its spelling.\nconst integerDivisionSpellings = [\n  { wrapper: 'Math.trunc' },\n  { wrapper: '~~' },\n  { wrapper: 'int' },\n  { call: 'intdiv' },\n];\n\nfunction integerDivision(call, { wrapper, call: callee, method }) {\n  const [first, second] = call.arguments;\n  const divide = (left, right) =>\n    node('Binary', { operator: 'divide', left, right });\n  if (\n    call.callee === wrapper &&\n    call.arguments.length === 1 &&\n    first.kind === 'Binary' &&\n    ['divide', 'realDivide'].includes(first.operator)\n  ) {\n    return { ...first, operator: 'divide' };\n  }\n  if (call.callee === callee && call.arguments.length === 2) {\n    return divide(first, second);\n  }\n  if (method && call.callee === `.${method}` && call.arguments.length === 2) {\n    return divide(first, second);\n  }\n  // a.intdiv(b) with a named receiver reads as the callee \"a.intdiv\".\n  if (\n    method &&\n    call.callee.endsWith(`.${method}`) &&\n    call.arguments.length === 1\n  ) {\n    return divide(\n      { kind: 'Name', name: call.callee.slice(0, -method.length - 1) },\n      first\n    );\n  }\n  return undefined;\n}\n\n// The spellings of the language a program is read from, in every version\n// of it: Lua 5.1 writes `math.floor(a / b)` for Lua 5.3's `a // b`.\nfunction ownIntegerDivisions(from) {\n  if (!from) {\n    return [];\n  }\n  const { id } = splitVersion(from);\n  return [\n    languageSyntax(id),\n    ...versionsOf(id).map(({ version }) => languageSyntax(`${id}@${version}`)),\n  ]\n    .map(({ integerDivision }) => integerDivision)\n    .filter(Boolean);\n}\n\nexport function integerDivisionCalls(program, { from } = {}) {\n  const spellings = [...ownIntegerDivisions(from), ...integerDivisionSpellings];\n  return rewrite(program, (current) => {\n    if (current.kind !== 'Call') {\n      return current;\n    }\n    for (const spelling of spellings) {\n      const divided = integerDivision(current, spelling);\n      if (divided) {\n        return divided;\n      }\n    }\n    return current;\n  });\n}\n\n// `greatest_common_divisor` and `greatestCommonDivisor` are one name.\nexport function neutralNames(program) {\n  return renameDeclared(program, neutralName);\n}\n\n// `i = a; while (i < b) { ...; i += 1 }` is the counting loop `for i in a..b`\n// written at a lower level, as languages without a counting loop over a\n// computed range (R, for example) spell it. The others write the counting loop\n// over a fresh index whose body starts by reading the element,\n//\n//   for index in 0..len(a): x = a[index]; ...\n//\n// and the rule that reads a program raises that loop back to a ForEach, so\n// that every language round-trips to the same meta program.\n\nimport { block, node, number, rewrite, walk } from './tree.js';\nimport { inheritOrigin } from '../translation/source-origins.js';\n\n// The names a function body and its parameters already use.\nexport function usedNames(body, parameters = []) {\n  const used = new Set(parameters.map((parameter) => parameter.name));\n  walk(body, (current) => {\n    for (const key of ['name', 'variable']) {\n      if (typeof current[key] === 'string') {\n        used.add(current[key]);\n      }\n    }\n  });\n  return used;\n}\n\n// A name for a loop index that is not in `used`.\nexport function freshName(used) {\n  const candidates = ['index', 'position', 'slot', 'place'];\n  return (\n    candidates.find((candidate) => !used.has(candidate)) ??\n    [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]\n      .map((count) => `index-${count}`)\n      .find((candidate) => !used.has(candidate))\n  );\n}\n\nconst mentions = (tree, identifier) => {\n  let found = false;\n  walk(tree, (current) => {\n    if (current.kind === 'Name' && current.name === identifier) {\n      found = true;\n    }\n  });\n  return found;\n};\n\n// Whether a tree assigns or declares the name, or stores into the array of\n// that name.\nconst changes = (tree, identifier) => {\n  let found = false;\n  walk(tree, (current) => {\n    if (\n      ['Assignment', 'Declaration', 'IndexAssignment'].includes(current.kind) &&\n      current.name === identifier\n    ) {\n      found = true;\n    }\n  });\n  return found;\n};\n\n// A loop that changes its own variable or the array it reads is written as\n// a counting loop everywhere: the loop variable is read-only in many\n// languages and the array may not change while it is being read.\nexport const isPlain = (loop) =>\n  !changes(loop.body, loop.variable) && !changes(loop.body, loop.array.name);\n\n// The ForEach written out as a counting loop over the index.\nfunction lowered(loop, index, body) {\n  const { variable, array } = loop;\n  const element = node('Declaration', {\n    name: variable,\n    type: 'integer',\n    value: node('Index', { array, index: node('Name', { name: index }) }),\n    mutable: changes(loop.body, variable),\n  });\n  return node('CountingLoop', {\n    variable: index,\n    start: number(0),\n    end: node('Length', { array, type: 'integer' }),\n    body: block([element, ...body.statements]),\n  });\n}\n\n// Every ForEach the `keep` test refuses becomes a counting loop. The index\n// differs from every name of the function and from the index of the loops\n// around it.\nexport function lowerForEach(program, keep) {\n  const expand = (tree, used, around) => {\n    if (Array.isArray(tree)) {\n      return tree.map((item) => expand(item, used, around));\n    }\n    if (!tree || typeof tree !== 'object' || !tree.kind) {\n      return tree;\n    }\n    if (tree.kind === 'ForEach' && !keep(tree)) {\n      const index = freshName(new Set([...used, ...around]));\n      return inheritOrigin(\n        lowered(\n          tree,\n          index,\n          expand(tree.body, used, new Set([...around, index]))\n        ),\n        tree\n      );\n    }\n    return inheritOrigin(\n      Object.fromEntries(\n        Object.entries(tree).map(([key, value]) => [\n          key,\n          value && typeof value === 'object'\n            ? expand(value, used, around)\n            : value,\n        ])\n      ),\n      tree\n    );\n  };\n  const inside = (body, parameters = []) =>\n    expand(body, usedNames(body, parameters), new Set());\n  return {\n    ...program,\n    functions: program.functions.map((item) =>\n      inheritOrigin(\n        {\n          ...item,\n          body: inside(item.body, item.parameters),\n        },\n        item\n      )\n    ),\n    main: inside(program.main),\n  };\n}\n\n// `for index in 0..len(a): x = a[index]; ...` where the index is used for\n// nothing else is the loop `for x in a`.\nfunction raised(counting) {\n  const [first, ...rest] = counting.body.statements;\n  const { variable, start, end } = counting;\n  const array = end.kind === 'Length' ? end.array : undefined;\n  const reads = first?.value;\n  if (\n    !array ||\n    start.kind !== 'Number' ||\n    start.value !== 0 ||\n    first?.kind !== 'Declaration' ||\n    reads?.kind !== 'Index' ||\n    reads.array.name !== array.name ||\n    reads.index.kind !== 'Name' ||\n    reads.index.name !== variable\n  ) {\n    return undefined;\n  }\n  const remaining = block(rest);\n  return mentions(remaining, variable) || changes(remaining, array.name)\n    ? undefined\n    : node('ForEach', { variable: first.name, array, body: remaining });\n}\n\nexport function raiseForEach(program) {\n  return rewrite(program, (current) =>\n    current.kind === 'CountingLoop' ? A section starts at an anchor\n// <a name=\"...\"></a> and ends at the next one.\nexport function extractSections(html) {\n  const result = new Map();\n  const parts = html.split(/<a name=\"[^\"]*\"><\\/a>/).slice(1);\n  for (const part of parts) {\n    const heading = /<h2>([^<]*)<\\/h2>/.exec(part);\n    const program = /<pre[^>]*>([\\s\\S]*?)<\\/pre>/.exec(part);\n    if (heading && program) {\n      const text = decodeEntities(stripTags(program[1]));\n      result.set(decodeEntities(heading[1]), text.replace(/^\\n+/, ''));\n    }\n  }\n  return result;\n}\n\n// language id -> [{ section, program }] for the sections the table names.\nexport function extractPrograms(html) {\n  const all = extractSections(html);\n  const programs = {};\n  for (const [id, names] of Object.entries(sections)) {\n    programs[id] = names\n      .filter((name) => all.has(name))\n      .map((name) => ({ section: name, program: all.get(name) }));\n  }\n  return programs;\n}\n\n// Whether robots.txt lets automated clients read the page. A missing file\n// (404) allows everything.\nexport function robotsAllow(robots) {\n  let applies = false;\n  for (const raw of robots.split('\\n')) {\n    const line = raw.replace(/#.*/, '').trim();\n    const [field, ...rest] = line.split(':');\n    const value = rest.join(':').trim();\n    if (/^user-agent$/i.test(field)) {\n      applies = value === '*' || agent.includes(value.toLowerCase());\n    } else if (applies && /^disallow$/i.test(field) && value === '/') {\n      return false;\n    }\n  }\n  return true;\n}\n\nasync function download() {\n  const robots = await fetch(`${source}robots.txt`, {\n    headers: { 'user-agent': agent },\n  });\n  if (robots.ok && !robotsAllow(await robots.text())) {\n    throw new Error('robots.txt disallows the Hello World Collection');\n  }\n  const response = await fetch(source, { headers: { 'user-agent': agent } });\n  if (!response.ok) {\n    throw new Error(`${source} answered ${response.status}`);\n  }\n  const html = await response.text();\n  mkdirSync(dataFolder, { recursive: true });\n  writeFileSync(pageFile, html);\n  const date = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);\n  writeFileSync(\n    join(dataFolder, 'README.md'),\n    [\n      '# The Hello World Collection',\n      '',\n      `Source: ${source} (one HTML page, a section per language).`,\n      `Retrieved: ${date}, after /robots.txt allowed it (the site is served by`,\n      'GitHub Pages and has no robots.txt).',\n      '',\n      '- `index.html` is the raw page, unchanged.',\n      '- `programs.json` holds the programs extracted for the language ids of',\n      '  `js/src/formal/languages.js`, by `scripts/hello-world-collection.mjs`.',\n      '',\n## Summary\n\nFixes #16\nFixes #1\nFixes #2\nFixes #10\nFixes #6\nFixes #8\nFixes #12\nFixes #14\n\nThis draft addresses translation correctness and the unfinished requirements inherited from earlier issues. **The full acceptance criteria are not yet met; It does not match templates: it reads source text with per-language grammar tables and rewrites it through rules. It translates between **32 programming languages** (including **Lean 4** and **Rocq**), **three machine targets** (NASM x86-64, CIL, JVM/Jasmin) and **controlled versions of 30+ natural languages**. The JavaScript (`js/`) and Rust (`rust/`) implementations write byte-identical output for every golden translation.\\n\\n```text\\nsource ──parser──▶ source tree ──understanding rules──▶ meta ──type inference──▶ typed meta\\n  ──meaning rules──▶ ──custom layers──▶ ──context rules──▶ ──emitter──▶ target text\\n  ──lowering──▶ stack machine ──▶ NASM / CIL / JVM (Jasmin)\\nNASM / CIL / JVM ──reader──▶ stack machine ──lifting──▶ meta\\ncontrolled natural text ──reader──▶ meta ──writer──▶ controlled natural text\\n```\\n\\n### Requirements gate (test-driven)\\n\\n`docs/case-studies/issue-1/requirements.lino` lists every requirement from the issue and its comments. `docs/case-studies/issue-1/rosetta-coverage.lino` lists the Rosetta Code algorithm types. `scripts/check-requirements.mjs` checks each requirement against the repository; for example, it compares the language lists of both implementations and checks that every task has a golden in every language. It fails CI (`Rust and cross-language translation` job, and `js/tests/requirements.test.js` under Node, Bun and Deno) unless every requirement is **done** or **blocked with a written reason**.\\n\\nThe gate caught real gaps during this work. The Rust implementation was missing 10 languages; that was fixed and the gate now passes.\\n\\n### Web demo\\n\\n![Web demo translating a Python function to Rust](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/screenshots/web-demo.png?raw=true)\\n\\n`examples/universal-app` is a React demo in which any programming or natural language can be translated to any other. You can paste a whole program, one function or one statement. The `web-e2e` job in `.github/workflows/example-app.yml` drives it in Chromium (`examples/universal-app/e2e/translate.e2e.mjs`) and takes the screenshot above.\\n\\n### Fragments: statements, functions or a whole program\\n\\n`translateFragment` / `parseFragment` (JS) and `translate_fragment` / `parse_fragment` (Rust), plus `universal-translator translate --fragment`, accept a statement, one or more functions, or a whole program. Each comes back as the same kind of fragment in the target. A fragment only has to be complete: a function must end with its closing. Otherwise the translator fails with the reason and the line, for example `The fragment is not complete: it ends before its closing (line 2)`. Goldens for every language are in `examples/programs/fragments/translated/` and are checked by `write-fragments.mjs --check`.\\n\\n### CLI, library, HTTP API and Docker\\n\\n- `universal-translator serve` starts an HTTP API (`GET /languages`, `POST /translate`). It reads `--port`/`--host`, then `PORT`/`HOST`, then `.lenv`, through lino-arguments.\\n- `js/src/index.js` (with types) and the `rust/` crate are the libraries.\\n- The `Dockerfile` image runs the CLI and the server. The release workflow builds it and smoke tests the CLI and the HTTP API.\\n\\n### Source layout and best practices\\n\\n- Sources are split into `src/meta` (shared types and trees), `src/formal` (programming languages, Lean, Rocq and machine code) and `src/natural` (human languages, with a reader and a writer), in both `js/` and `rust/`. The `source-layout` check rejects imports that point outwards from the meta layer.\\n- [`docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md) maps the associative technology stack, the code architecture principles and all 17 CI/CD best practices to evidence, or gives a reason when one does not apply. `cargo clippy -D warnings` now runs in CI.\\n- **Test coverage is required by CI.** `npm run test:coverage` replaces `npm test` in the Node.js job. It fails below 94% line, 91% branch or 95% function coverage of `js/src` and `bin`; current coverage is 95.4%, 92.1% and 96.5%. The Rust crate runs the same goldens, but CI does not measure its coverage.\\n\\n### Programming languages (32) and machine code\\n\\n| | |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Languages | JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Lua, PHP, C, C++, C#, Java, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Swift, Perl, Dart, Scala, Julia, R, Groovy, Objective-C, Nim, D, Pascal, Fortran, Ada, Visual Basic .NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave, Zig, **Lean 4, Rocq** |\\n| Dialects | Pascal, Fortran, Ada, VB.NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave and Zig have their own program layout. They are dialects of the shared parser and emitter (`js/src/formal/dialects/`, `rust/src/formal/dialects/`). Lean 4 programs use `partial def` and `IO`. Rocq programs are pure `Fixpoint`s over an output monad defined in a small runtime, and are evaluated with `Eval vm_compute`. |\\n| Machine targets | NASM, CIL and JVM are written through a named stack machine and read back by lifting, so machine code translates to every language and between targets. |\\n| Modes | context-dependent (default, adapts comments such as C \\\"function call\\\" → C# \\\"method call\\\"), literal, same-effect |\\n| Extensibility | Every stage and rule list is an option of `createGrammarTranslator`; custom meta → meta layers are supported. |\\n| Common library | `common-library/` (output operations only, one file per language), enabled with `--common-library` |\\n\\n### Controlled natural languages\\n\\n- Data lives in `data/natural/*.lino`; `js/src/natural/` and `rust/src/natural/` read and write the same texts byte for byte.\\n- Covers the 30 most spoken languages (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Marathi, Telugu, Turkish, Tamil, Vietnamese, Korean, Italian, Persian, Swahili, Tagalog, Thai, Polish, Ukrainian, Hausa, Gujarati, Punjabi, Dutch), each in a small controlled form (`cnl-default`).\\n- Profiles for the standards named in the issue:\\n  - ASD-STE100\\n  - Attempto Controlled English\\n  - Gellish (English and Dutch)\\n  - SBVR Structured English\\n  - Plain language (ISO 24495-1)\\n  - E-Prime\\n  - Basic English, VOA Special English and Globish\\n  - Minimal English, Minimal French and Minimal Polish, built on the **65 semantic primes** of NSM (`data/natural/semantic-primes.lino`)\\n- `checkText` and the `check-words` command enforce each standard's rules: sentence length, allowed first words, forbidden words such as \\\"to be\\\" in E-Prime or \\\"shall\\\" in plain language, vocabulary limits, and Gellish relation phrases.\\n- Translations run natural → meta → any programming or machine language, and back: `universal-translator translate russian python`, `translate python spanish`.\\n- Every example program is written in every natural language and profile under `examples/programs/natural/`. Each text is read back to the same meaning and checked against its standard.\\n\\n### Rosetta Code and Hello World\\n\\n18 tasks in `examples/programs/` are translated to all 32 languages, the 3 machine targets and every natural language, then run natively:\\n\\n- hello world\\n- factorial\\n- greatest common divisor\\n- FizzBuzz\\n- sum of squares\\n- Fibonacci\\n- Ackermann\\n- Towers of Hanoi\\n- leap year\\n- sum of digits\\n- hailstone\\n- 99 bottles\\n- primality by trial division\\n- mutual recursion\\n- perfect numbers\\n- sieve of Eratosthenes\\n- bubble sort\\n- sum and product of an array\\n\\nAlgorithm types covered (from `rosetta-coverage.lino`): output, integer arithmetic, conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion (including mutual recursion), number theory, text concatenation, and **integer arrays** (new: array values in the meta language, all 32 languages, NASM/CIL/JVM and natural-language sentences).\\n\\n**Blocked, with reasons recorded in `rosetta-coverage.lino`.** These are not presented as done. Rosetta Code has more than 1,300 tasks, and these types need values the meta language does not have yet:\\n\\n| Type | Why it is blocked |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| floating-point | Machine targets and the meta language use 64-bit integers only |\\n| string manipulation | Text can be printed and concatenated, but not indexed or transformed |\\n| higher-order functions | Functions are top-level declarations only |\\n| data structures | Records, maps, stacks and queues need compound values |\\n| input/output | Programs only write to standard output, which is what the native checks compare |\\n| objects and concurrency | Not supported |\\n\\n**Classes as fragments** are also **blocked** (`class-fragments` in the gate) for the same reason: the meta language has no objects or classes, so a class has no meaning to translate yet.\\n\\nThe gate reports `rosetta-algorithm-types` and `class-fragments` as **BLOCKED** with these reasons. Every other requirement is **DONE**.\\n\\n## Verification\\n\\n- **`npm test` (Node, Bun, Deno) and `cargo test`.** Every task is translated to every language, machine target and natural language and compared with the goldens in `examples/programs/translated` and `examples/programs/natural`.\\n- **`examples/programs/verify-native.mjs --require-all [--common-library]`.** The `native-translation` CI job compiles or runs each translation with its real toolchain and compares the output with the JavaScript original. The toolchains include Lean 4 (elan), Rocq (opam), fpc, gnat, gfortran, octave, zig, nim, ldc, Objective-C, Swift, Kotlin, Scala, .NET and Jasmin.\\n- **`experiments/verify-syntax-exchange.sh`.** The JS and Rust command lines list the same 32 languages and write identical output.\\n- **`node scripts/check-requirements.mjs`.** The requirements gate described above.\\n- **`npm run test:coverage`.** The coverage gate described above.\\n- **`web-e2e`.** The browser test of the demo.\\n- **`--trace`.** Logs each pipeline stage.\\n\\n### CI reliability (native translation job)\\n\\n- Toolchain archives are cached. Each download attempt is capped at 3 minutes and falls back to a mirror: Google's Maven Central mirror for Groovy and `zig.linus.dev` for Zig, all checked by SHA-256. This fixes a run where the step hung on a stalled download.\\n- `verify-native.mjs` runs its checks in parallel worker processes.\\n- `js/tests/ci-timeouts.test.js` keeps each job's step budgets within 70% of its backstop.\\n- Budgets are sized for slower runners. One run needed 330 s for all native translations and over 360 s for the common library translations, while a typical run needs about 220 s and 250 s. Every translation passed, but the 360 s budget ran out. The step budgets are now 540 s and 480 s, and the job backstop is 100 minutes so the budgets stay within 70% of it.\\n\\n### CodeQL\\n\\n- `js/incomplete-sanitization` flagged the Lean `s!\\\"…\\\"` brace escape, because it was chained after `escape()` where CodeQL cannot see that backslashes were already escaped. Summary\\n\\nFixes #14\\n\\nThis PR addresses issue 14 and the requirements of earlier issues and pull requests that had not been delivered. Every change is made in both JavaScript and Rust, and the two command lines print byte-identical output. The full case study is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-14/`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/tree/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14):\\n\\n- `README.md`: timeline, the issue's requirements R1–R24, root causes and alternatives;\\n- `previous-requirements.md`: every earlier requirement with its status;\\n- `prior-art.md` and `architecture.md`;\\n- `requirements.lino`: CI fails while any requirement is neither done nor reported as blocked with a reason.\\n\\n### Issue 14 requirements\\n\\n- **A concrete syntax tree (CST) by default.** Whitespace and blank lines now survive a translation. The layout pass (`js/src/translation/layout.js`, `rust/src/layout.rs`) aligns the tokens of the output with those of the source and returns a `lineMap`. `--layout target` restores the emitter's own formatting.\\n  - `main`: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log(\\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n  - this branch: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n- **Monaco by default, with linked editors.**\\n  - Folding regions now work for every language.\\n  - Folding, selection, the cursor and scrolling are shared by both editors. Scrolling is mapped block by block, so blocks of different sizes stay aligned.\\n  - Lines that map to each other get matching colours, as in Compiler Explorer.\\n- **Comment and identifier language selectors on both sides.** The option checkboxes are now below the editors.\\n- **Comments are translated.** A shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`) is used both to detect a comment's language and to translate it.\\n  - `// Привет мир` → `// Hello world`.\\n  - «Привет» is now detected as Russian.\\n  - «Как хорошо покакать?» translates to \\\"How good to poop?\\\" (free prose translation).\\n- **Deeper grammars.**\\n  - Prose reads as `Prose > Sentence > Word`, with concepts and parts of speech.\\n  - Comments and strings are read with their own grammars (code in prose, prose in code). Long texts are stored once and referred to by id. Use `--shallow` for the plain tree.\\n- **A more general meta language.** `print` is a call to the library function `print-line`.\\n- **Assembly and intermediate languages.** NASM, GNU as, ARM64, LLVM IR, WebAssembly text, CIL and JVM bytecode are written and read back.\\n- **Language versions.** `javascript@es5`, `php@5`, `csharp@5`, `python@2`, `python@3.5`, `lua@5.1`, `java@1.4`, `swift@1` and `scala@2.9` are available. `registerLanguageVersion` adds a version of your own.\\n- **More tasks and corpora.**\\n  - 22 Rosetta Code tasks go through all 33 programming languages and the 7 machine targets.\\n  - 33 of the 34 programs of the Hello World Collection are read.\\n  - `check-equivalence` checks that a translation does what its source does.\\n- **Debugging and research.**\\n  - `--trace` prints the tree after every stage, and the web app logs translations and editor-sync events with `?debug`.\\n  - formal-ai was tried on six tasks; its failures are reported as link-assistant/formal-ai#1641 and link-assistant/formal-ai#1642.\\n\\n### Screenshots\\n\\nLine mapping in the linked Monaco editors:\\n\\n![mapping](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-mapping.png?raw=true)\\n\\nComment and identifier language selectors on both sides:\\n\\n![selectors](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-selectors.png?raw=true)\\n\\n![style](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-style.png?raw=true)\\n\\n### Tests\\n\\n- JavaScript: `npm test` passes 1823 tests, with 1 skipped (shellcheck is not on the PATH locally).\\n  - Tests touched by this PR include `layout`, `comments`, `prose`, `nesting`, `language-versions`, `machine-dialects`, `hello-world-dialects`, `identifiers` and `ranking`. The web app has unit tests and end-to-end tests.\\n  - `npm run lint` and `node scripts/check-requirements.mjs` pass.\\n- Rust: every JavaScript test above has a twin under `rust/tests/` (for example `layout.rs`, `prose.rs`, `nesting.rs`, `language_versions.rs` and `hello_world_dialects.rs`).\\n  - `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo fmt` pass.\\n  - The full `cargo test` runs in CI.\\n\\n### Still open or blocked\\n\\nThese items are tracked in `docs/case-studies/issue-14/previous-requirements.md` (\\\"Concise list: everything still open\\\"). None of them is claimed as done.\\n\\n1. **Blocked:**\\n   - The Objective-C program of the Hello World Collection is Portable Object Compiler code that clang rejects.\\n   - Publishing the unscoped npm name `universal-translator` needs the owner's npm account. `npm view universal-translator version` gives `E404`.\\n   - The JavaScript CLI loads Meta Language from an environment variable until link-foundation/meta-language#230 is released.\\n   - The upstream process fix link-assistant/hive-mind#3929 is still open.\\n   - `Example app` on `main` needs `RELEASE_PR_TOKEN`; it passes on this PR.\\n2. **Partial:**\\n   - Rosetta Code: 22 tasks, not the whole set. Summary\\n\\nFixes #14\\n\\nThis PR addresses issue 14 and the requirements of earlier issues and pull requests that had not been delivered. Every change is made in both JavaScript and Rust, and the two command lines print byte-identical output. The full case study is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-14/`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/tree/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14):\\n\\n- `README.md`: timeline, the issue's requirements R1–R24, root causes and alternatives;\\n- `previous-requirements.md`: every earlier requirement with its status;\\n- `prior-art.md` and `architecture.md`;\\n- `requirements.lino`: CI fails while any requirement is neither done nor reported as blocked with a reason.\\n\\n### Issue 14 requirements\\n\\n- **A concrete syntax tree (CST) by default.** Whitespace and blank lines now survive a translation. The layout pass (`js/src/translation/layout.js`, `rust/src/layout.rs`) aligns the tokens of the output with those of the source and returns a `lineMap`. `--layout target` restores the emitter's own formatting.\\n  - `main`: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log(\\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n  - this branch: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n- **Monaco by default, with linked editors.**\\n  - Folding regions now work for every language.\\n  - Folding, selection, the cursor and scrolling are shared by both editors. Scrolling is mapped block by block, so blocks of different sizes stay aligned.\\n  - Lines that map to each other get matching colours, as in Compiler Explorer.\\n- **Comment and identifier language selectors on both sides.** The option checkboxes are now below the editors.\\n- **Comments are translated.** A shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`) is used both to detect a comment's language and to translate it.\\n  - `// Привет мир` → `// Hello world`.\\n  - «Привет» is now detected as Russian.\\n  - «Как хорошо покакать?» translates to \\\"How good to poop?\\\" (free prose translation).\\n- **Deeper grammars.**\\n  - Prose reads as `Prose > Sentence > Word`, with concepts and parts of speech.\\n  - Comments and strings are read with their own grammars (code in prose, prose in code). Long texts are stored once and referred to by id. Summary\\n\\nFixes #14\\n\\nThis PR addresses issue 14 and the requirements of earlier issues and pull requests that had not been delivered. Every change is made in both JavaScript and Rust, and the two command lines print byte-identical output. The full case study is in [`docs/case-studies/issue-14/`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/tree/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14):\\n\\n- `README.md`: timeline, the issue's requirements R1–R24, root causes and alternatives;\\n- `previous-requirements.md`: every earlier requirement with its status;\\n- `prior-art.md` and `architecture.md`;\\n- `requirements.lino`: CI fails while any requirement is neither done nor reported as blocked with a reason.\\n\\n### Issue 14 requirements\\n\\n- **A concrete syntax tree (CST) by default.** Whitespace and blank lines now survive a translation. The layout pass (`js/src/translation/layout.js`, `rust/src/layout.rs`) aligns the tokens of the output with those of the source and returns a `lineMap`. `--layout target` restores the emitter's own formatting.\\n  - `main`: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log(\\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n  - this branch: `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");` → `console.log( \\\"Hello World!\\\");`\\n- **Monaco by default, with linked editors.**\\n  - Folding regions now work for every language.\\n  - Folding, selection, the cursor and scrolling are shared by both editors. Scrolling is mapped block by block, so blocks of different sizes stay aligned.\\n  - Lines that map to each other get matching colours, as in Compiler Explorer.\\n- **Comment and identifier language selectors on both sides.** The option checkboxes are now below the editors.\\n- **Comments are translated.** A shared multilingual vocabulary (`data/natural/vocabulary.lino`) is used both to detect a comment's language and to translate it.\\n  - `// Привет мир` → `// Hello world`.\\n  - «Привет» is now detected as Russian.\\n  - «Как хорошо покакать?» translates to \\\"How good to poop?\\\" (free prose translation).\\n- **Deeper grammars.**\\n  - Prose reads as `Prose > Sentence > Word`, with concepts and parts of speech.\\n  - Comments and strings are read with their own grammars (code in prose, prose in code). Long texts are stored once and referred to by id. Use `--shallow` for the plain tree.\\n- **A more general meta language.** `print` is a call to the library function `print-line`.\\n- **Assembly and intermediate languages.** NASM, GNU as, ARM64, LLVM IR, WebAssembly text, CIL and JVM bytecode are written and read back.\\n- **Language versions.** `javascript@es5`, `php@5`, `csharp@5`, `python@2`, `python@3.5`, `lua@5.1`, `java@1.4`, `swift@1` and `scala@2.9` are available. `registerLanguageVersion` adds a version of your own.\\n- **More tasks and corpora.**\\n  - 22 Rosetta Code tasks go through all 33 programming languages and the 7 machine targets.\\n  - 33 of the 34 programs of the Hello World Collection are read.\\n  - `check-equivalence` checks that a translation does what its source does.\\n- **Debugging and research.**\\n  - `--trace` prints the tree after every stage, and the web app logs translations and editor-sync events with `?debug`.\\n  - formal-ai was tried on six tasks; its failures are reported as link-assistant/formal-ai#1641 and link-assistant/formal-ai#1642.\\n\\n### Screenshots\\n\\nLine mapping in the linked Monaco editors:\\n\\n![mapping](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-mapping.png?raw=true)\\n\\nComment and identifier language selectors on both sides:\\n\\n![selectors](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-selectors.png?raw=true)\\n\\n![style](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-14-213b02ae6953/docs/case-studies/issue-14/screenshots/app-style.png?raw=true)\\n\\n### Tests\\n\\n- JavaScript: `npm test` passes 1823 tests, with 1 skipped (shellcheck is not on the PATH locally).\\n  - Tests touched by this PR include `layout`, `comments`, `prose`, `nesting`, `language-versions`, `machine-dialects`, `hello-world-dialects`, `identifiers` and `ranking`. Summary\\n\\nFixes #8.\\n\\n### Comparison wordings (the reported bug)\\n\\n`Если n меньше или равно 1, сделать это:` and `больше или равно` now translate, along with the \\\"obvious variations\\\" in every natural language:\\n\\n- Russian: `либо`, `не больше`, `<=`, `≤`.\\n- English: `at most`, `is less than or equal to`, and the symbols.\\n\\nPython `pass` now reads as \\\"do nothing\\\".\\n\\nReproduce on `main`:\\n\\n```bash\\nprintf 'Если n меньше или равно 1, сделать это:\\\\n  Ничего не делать\\\\n' | npx universal-translator translate russian python\\n# main: error · this branch: if n <= 1:\\\\n    pass\\n```\\n\\n### Partial translation by default; all-or-nothing on request\\n\\n- `translatePartial` translates what reads and keeps every unread part as a target-language comment with its error. For example, `// untranslated (line 2): …` is followed by the original line.\\n- `parsePartial` / the `coverage` command count the read lines and the missing parts.\\n- The CLI defaults to partial and has `--all-or-nothing`. The server takes `allOrNothing` and answers `{output, complete, errors, coverage, detected}`. The web demo has an \\\"All or nothing\\\" checkbox.\\n\\n### Source language detection\\n\\n`detectLanguage` scores each language as `100 × how much of the text its grammar reads`, plus evidence from the language's own syntax tables and templates. It needs no model or dependency.\\n\\n- CLI: `translate auto <to>` and the `detect` command.\\n- Server: `from: \\\"auto\\\"`.\\n- Web demo: \\\"Auto-detect\\\" is the default source language.\\n\\n### Rules as data at every stage\\n\\n`createTranslator({ rules })`, `--rules file.json`, the server's `rules` and the web editor all accept the same JSON, with one list per stage:\\n\\n- `source`: text before reading;\\n- `templates`: more wordings per natural-language template;\\n- `names`: a meta → meta renaming layer;\\n- `output`: text after writing.\\n\\nEach rule can be plain text or a regex, and can be limited to one language. Rules are validated with clear errors.\\n\\n### Visual rules editor\\n\\nThe web demo has a table per stage, a JSON import/export view, and a list of untranslated parts.\\n\\n![Partial translation](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-8-a666e1cbe6e5/docs/screenshots/issue-8/partial-translation.png?raw=true)\\n![Rules editor](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-8-a666e1cbe6e5/docs/screenshots/issue-8/rules-editor.png?raw=true)\\n\\n### Rosetta Code\\n\\n`node scripts/rosetta-code.mjs all`:\\n\\n- loads every programming and draft task (1772) through the MediaWiki API;\\n- keeps the solutions in our 32 languages in a git-ignored cache;\\n- sorts the tasks from the simplest meaning (median solution length, then how many languages solve it);\\n- reads them partially and writes a report of the missing lines and parts per task and per language.\\n\\nThe first full run reads **508,806 of 1,292,095 lines (39.4%)** over 1782 tasks ([report](docs/case-studies/issue-8/data/rosetta-code/README.md)).\\n\\nThe run also found a real bug. JS `Parser.next()` read past the end of the tokens, so the Ada reader looped forever on a cut text like `procedure P is`. It now throws \\\"Unexpected end of program\\\", as Rust already did, and a regression test covers it.\\n\\nTranslating *every* Rosetta Code solution is the issue's long-term goal, and this PR does not reach it. It adds the loading, ordering, partial mode and measurements the issue asks for, so the remaining ~60% of lines can be worked down task by task.\\n\\n### Rust parity\\n\\nThe Rust crate and CLI get the same features:\\n\\n- partial translation and `--all-or-nothing`;\\n- `auto` detection and the `detect` and `coverage` commands;\\n- `--rules`.\\n\\nOn the samples I compared, the Rust CLI's output matched the JS byte for byte. The Rust crate has no HTTP server, so the server changes are JS-only.\\n\\n### Case study\\n\\n[docs/case-studies/issue-8](docs/case-studies/issue-8/README.md) has:\\n\\n- the issue data and a timeline;\\n- every requirement mapped to where it is done and how it is verified;\\n- the root causes, solutions and the libraries considered (Linguist, guesslang, highlight.js, franc/cld3, tree-sitter, ANTLR recovery, Blockly).\\n\\nNo upstream issue was needed: every root cause was in this repository.\\n\\n## Tests\\n\\n- `js/tests/issue-8.test.js`: wordings in every language, partial translation, CLI, coverage, detection, rules, server, and cut texts.\\n- `js/tests/rosetta-code.test.js`: offline fixture for extraction, sorting and counts.\\n- `rust/tests/issue_8.rs`: mirrors the JS tests.\\n- `examples/universal-app/e2e/translate.e2e.mjs`: auto-detect, the Russian example, partial output, a rule from the editor, and all-or-nothing.\\n\\n## Security note\\n\\nCodeQL flags `js/regex-injection` in `custom-rules.js`. Compiling the user's own pattern is the purpose of a `regex: true` rule, and on the command line the pattern comes from the user's own `--rules` file.\\n\\nThe HTTP server refuses regex rules by default, so remote clients cannot send ReDoS patterns. `createTranslationServer({ allowRegexRules: true })` opts in. Plain-text rules use no RegExp at all. Whether to dismiss the alert is left to the maintainers.\\n\\n### CodeQL note\\nCodeQL alert #5 (`js/regex-injection` at `js/src/translation/custom-rules.js:46`) was dismissed as *won't fix*: building a `RegExp` from `find` is the requested regex-rule feature. #1\\n\\n## Summary\\n\\nThis PR adds a translator for programs. It does not match templates: it reads source text with per-language grammar tables and rewrites it through rules. It translates between **32 programming languages** (including **Lean 4** and **Rocq**), **three machine targets** (NASM x86-64, CIL, JVM/Jasmin) and **controlled versions of 30+ natural languages**. The JavaScript (`js/`) and Rust (`rust/`) implementations write byte-identical output for every golden translation.\\n\\n```text\\nsource ──parser──▶ source tree ──understanding rules──▶ meta ──type inference──▶ typed meta\\n  ──meaning rules──▶ ──custom layers──▶ ──context rules──▶ ──emitter──▶ target text\\n  ──lowering──▶ stack machine ──▶ NASM / CIL / JVM (Jasmin)\\nNASM / CIL / JVM ──reader──▶ stack machine ──lifting──▶ meta\\ncontrolled natural text ──reader──▶ meta ──writer──▶ controlled natural text\\n```\\n\\n### Requirements gate (test-driven)\\n\\n`docs/case-studies/issue-1/requirements.lino` lists every requirement from the issue and its comments. `docs/case-studies/issue-1/rosetta-coverage.lino` lists the Rosetta Code algorithm types. `scripts/check-requirements.mjs` checks each requirement against the repository; for example, it compares the language lists of both implementations and checks that every task has a golden in every language. It fails CI (`Rust and cross-language translation` job, and `js/tests/requirements.test.js` under Node, Bun and Deno) unless every requirement is **done** or **blocked with a written reason**.\\n\\nThe gate caught real gaps during this work. The Rust implementation was missing 10 languages; that was fixed and the gate now passes.\\n\\n### Web demo\\n\\n![Web demo translating a Python function to Rust](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/screenshots/web-demo.png?raw=true)\\n\\n`examples/universal-app` is a React demo in which any programming or natural language can be translated to any other. You can paste a whole program, one function or one statement. The `web-e2e` job in `.github/workflows/example-app.yml` drives it in Chromium (`examples/universal-app/e2e/translate.e2e.mjs`) and takes the screenshot above.\\n\\n### Fragments: statements, functions or a whole program\\n\\n`translateFragment` / `parseFragment` (JS) and `translate_fragment` / `parse_fragment` (Rust), plus `universal-translator translate --fragment`, accept a statement, one or more functions, or a whole program. Each comes back as the same kind of fragment in the target. A fragment only has to be complete: a function must end with its closing. Otherwise the translator fails with the reason and the line, for example `The fragment is not complete: it ends before its closing (line 2)`. Goldens for every language are in `examples/programs/fragments/translated/` and are checked by `write-fragments.mjs --check`.\\n\\n### CLI, library, HTTP API and Docker\\n\\n- `universal-translator serve` starts an HTTP API (`GET /languages`, `POST /translate`). It reads `--port`/`--host`, then `PORT`/`HOST`, then `.lenv`, through lino-arguments.\\n- `js/src/index.js` (with types) and the `rust/` crate are the libraries.\\n- The `Dockerfile` image runs the CLI and the server. The release workflow builds it and smoke tests the CLI and the HTTP API.\\n\\n### Source layout and best practices\\n\\n- Sources are split into `src/meta` (shared types and trees), `src/formal` (programming languages, Lean, Rocq and machine code) and `src/natural` (human languages, with a reader and a writer), in both `js/` and `rust/`. The `source-layout` check rejects imports that point outwards from the meta layer.\\n- [`docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md`](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/blob/issue-1-35d65b774bf6/docs/case-studies/issue-1/best-practices.md) maps the associative technology stack, the code architecture principles and all 17 CI/CD best practices to evidence, or gives a reason when one does not apply. `cargo clippy -D warnings` now runs in CI.\\n- **Test coverage is required by CI.** `npm run test:coverage` replaces `npm test` in the Node.js job. It fails below 94% line, 91% branch or 95% function coverage of `js/src` and `bin`; current coverage is 95.4%, 92.1% and 96.5%. The Rust crate runs the same goldens, but CI does not measure its coverage.\\n\\n### Programming languages (32) and machine code\\n\\n| | |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Languages | JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Lua, PHP, C, C++, C#, Java, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Swift, Perl, Dart, Scala, Julia, R, Groovy, Objective-C, Nim, D, Pascal, Fortran, Ada, Visual Basic .NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave, Zig, **Lean 4, Rocq** |\\n| Dialects | Pascal, Fortran, Ada, VB.NET, Bash, MATLAB/Octave and Zig have their own program layout. They are dialects of the shared parser and emitter (`js/src/formal/dialects/`, `rust/src/formal/dialects/`). Lean 4 programs use `partial def` and `IO`. Rocq programs are pure `Fixpoint`s over an output monad defined in a small runtime, and are evaluated with `Eval vm_compute`. |\\n| Machine targets | NASM, CIL and JVM are written through a named stack machine and read back by lifting, so machine code translates to every language and between targets. |\\n| Modes | context-dependent (default, adapts comments such as C \\\"function call\\\" → C# \\\"method call\\\"), literal, same-effect |\\n| Extensibility | Every stage and rule list is an option of `createGrammarTranslator`; custom meta → meta layers are supported. |\\n| Common library | `common-library/` (output operations only, one file per language), enabled with `--common-library` |\\n\\n### Controlled natural languages\\n\\n- Data lives in `data/natural/*.lino`; `js/src/natural/` and `rust/src/natural/` read and write the same texts byte for byte.\\n- Covers the 30 most spoken languages (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, German, Japanese, Marathi, Telugu, Turkish, Tamil, Vietnamese, Korean, Italian, Persian, Swahili, Tagalog, Thai, Polish, Ukrainian, Hausa, Gujarati, Punjabi, Dutch), each in a small controlled form (`cnl-default`).\\n- Profiles for the standards named in the issue:\\n  - ASD-STE100\\n  - Attempto Controlled English\\n  - Gellish (English and Dutch)\\n  - SBVR Structured English\\n  - Plain language (ISO 24495-1)\\n  - E-Prime\\n  - Basic English, VOA Special English and Globish\\n  - Minimal English, Minimal French and Minimal Polish, built on the **65 semantic primes** of NSM (`data/natural/semantic-primes.lino`)\\n- `checkText` and the `check-words` command enforce each standard's rules: sentence length, allowed first words, forbidden words such as \\\"to be\\\" in E-Prime or \\\"shall\\\" in plain language, vocabulary limits, and Gellish relation phrases.\\n- Translations run natural → meta → any programming or machine language, and back: `universal-translator translate russian python`, `translate python spanish`.\\n- Every example program is written in every natural language and profile under `examples/programs/natural/`. Each text is read back to the same meaning and checked against its standard.\\n\\n### Rosetta Code and Hello World\\n\\n18 tasks in `examples/programs/` are translated to all 32 languages, the 3 machine targets and every natural language, then run natively:\\n\\n- hello world\\n- factorial\\n- greatest common divisor\\n- FizzBuzz\\n- sum of squares\\n- Fibonacci\\n- Ackermann\\n- Towers of Hanoi\\n- leap year\\n- sum of digits\\n- hailstone\\n- 99 bottles\\n- primality by trial division\\n- mutual recursion\\n- perfect numbers\\n- sieve of Eratosthenes\\n- bubble sort\\n- sum and product of an array\\n\\nAlgorithm types covered (from `rosetta-coverage.lino`): output, integer arithmetic, conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion (including mutual recursion), number theory, text concatenation, and **integer arrays** (new: array values in the meta language, all 32 languages, NASM/CIL/JVM and natural-language sentences).\\n\\n**Blocked, with reasons recorded in `rosetta-coverage.lino`.** These are not presented as done. Rosetta Code has more than 1,300 tasks, and these types need values the meta language does not have yet:\\n\\n| Type | Why it is blocked |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| floating-point | Machine targets and the meta language use 64-bit integers only |\\n| string manipulation | Text can be printed and concatenated, but not indexed or transformed |\\n| higher-order functions | Functions are top-level declarations only |\\n| data structures | Records, maps, stacks and queues need compound values |\\n| input/output | Programs only write to standard output, which is what the native checks compare |\\n| objects and concurrency | Not supported |\\n\\n**Classes as fragments** are also **blocked** (`class-fragments` in the gate) for the same reason: the meta language has no objects or classes, so a class has no meaning to translate yet.\\n\\nThe gate reports `rosetta-algorithm-types` and `class-fragments` as **BLOCKED** with these reasons. Every other requirement is **DONE**.\\n\\n## Verification\\n\\n- **`npm test` (Node, Bun, Deno) and `cargo test`.** Every task is translated to every language, machine target and natural language and compared with the goldens in `examples/programs/translated` and `examples/programs/natural`.\\n- **`examples/programs/verify-native.mjs --require-all [--common-library]`.** The `native-translation` CI job compiles or runs each translation with its real toolchain and compares the output with the JavaScript original. The toolchains include Lean 4 (elan), Rocq (opam), fpc, gnat, gfortran, octave, zig, nim, ldc, Objective-C, Swift, Kotlin, Scala, .NET and Jasmin.\\n- **`experiments/verify-syntax-exchange.sh`.** The JS and Rust command lines list the same 32 languages and write identical output.\\n- **`node scripts/check-requirements.mjs`.** The requirements gate described above.\\n- **`npm run test:coverage`.** The coverage gate described above.\\n- **`web-e2e`.** The browser test of the demo.\\n- **`--trace`.** Logs each pipeline stage.\\n\\n### CI reliability (native translation job)\\n\\n- Toolchain archives are cached. Each download attempt is capped at 3 minutes and falls back to a mirror: Google's Maven Central mirror for Groovy and `zig.linus.dev` for Zig, all checked by SHA-256. This fixes a run where the step hung on a stalled download.\\n- `verify-native.mjs` runs its checks in parallel worker processes.\\n- `js/tests/ci-timeouts.test.js` keeps each job's step budgets within 70% of its backstop.\\n- Budgets are sized for slower runners. One run needed 330 s for all native translations and over 360 s for the common library translations, while a typical run needs about 220 s and 250 s. Every translation passed, but the 360 s budget ran out. The step budgets are now 540 s and 480 s, and the job backstop is 100 minutes so the budgets stay within 70% of it.\\n\\n### CodeQL\\n\\n- `js/incomplete-sanitization` flagged the Lean `s!\\\"…\\\"` brace escape, because it was chained after `escape()` where CodeQL cannot see that backslashes were already escaped. Brace escaping now happens inside `escape()` as the `escaped-braces` format. The output is unchanged, and a regression test in `js/tests/grammar.test.js` checks that `` `a\\\\\\\\b {c} ${name}` `` becomes `s!\\\"a\\\\\\\\b \\\\{c} {name}\\\"`.\\n- CodeQL still lists an older alert on `docs/case-studies/issue-3/original-format-release-notes.mjs`. That file came with the initial commit and is not part of this PR, and the CodeQL check passes.\\n\\nThe data files use Links Notation (`.lino`). The PR contains exactly one changeset (`.changeset/sharp-programs-translate.md`). The case study is in translation in unrestricted grammars may be solved with dependent translation.\\n\\nAs we do in dependent logic in relative meta logic (when probability of single statement depends on probability of other statement, including recursively).\\n\\nTranslation changes depending on physical or abstract referent (or resolution of meaning of the word).\\n\\nAnd sometimes multiple resolutions of meaning are intentional as in irony, paradoxes as so on.\\n\\nAll of paradoxes are links and fundamental laws, where we link something that is opposite or contradictory, but enviably connected.\\n\\nSo may there there is a way to deterministically translate between all languages, including natural languages.\\n\\nWe also need to make sure we precisely record any imprecision of any statement.\\n\\nLike for example `person` is any person, `white person` is `any white person`, where `white` can reference anything white about that person, like `any person with a white skin` or `any person fully painted white` or `any person mostly white` and so on.\\n\\nBut as long as we make more concrete description the range of possible values gets smaller.\\n\\nThat means for example when we use associative model with type system defined as fractal like:\\nType -> SubType\\nSubType -> SubType\\nSubType -> Value.\\n\\nWe actually still get type, subtype and value as types, but on each step we make them much more narrow.\\n\\nSo it looks like there should be one to one match between natural language and formal type system.\\n\\nSo we always work with ranges, and by calculating frequencies of language corpus we can have some probabilities which more specific type or description is most likely.\\n\\nYet for best translation (most likely and more correct) we should prefer such translation, which survives the round trip.\\n\\nFor example:\\n\\n`белый` <-> `white`\\n\\n`белый человек` <-> `white person`\\n\\nIn both languages these are highly likely.\\n\\nAnd this example actually survives round trip, so that is the translation we should end up with using by default.\\n\\nIn programming language it may mean:\\n\\n```\\nstruct Person {\\n   Color color = Color.White;\\n}\\n```\\n\\nAnd so on.\\n\\nWe also can see how Person is usually described on GitHub, and in the internet and so on, and if we have knowledge about corpus, we can have some probabilities on what to include.\\n\\nWe can also use the language description for requirements that will adjust requirements.\\n\\nSo when we define enough dependent details about anything in a language, we just specify a more concrete type, set or category.\\n\\nThat is the vision.\\n\\nWe should start by supporting full translation of something simple via meta language see best practices of concepts of each such language separately.\\n\\nFor example we can have function with no return value and no argument in both C, C#, C++ and so on, they match 1 to 1.\\n\\nYet we clearly have Blocks\nretain parameter names and statements. A scoped understanding rule recognizes\ndocumented operations on known library values, rather than matching a whole\nprogram or substituting a saved translation. Unknown messages remain explicit.\nParameters and local bindings shadow library class names.\n\nThe argument entry point becomes an array of process arguments, an integer\nargument count and an integer cursor. Pointer dereferences become ordinary\narray indexing. Prefix and postfix unit updates retain their distinct values.\nUnsupported pointer uses raise a diagnostic. Generated argument adapters are\nrecognized only with a verified library definition and the actual entry-point\nparameters.\n\nObjpak string sets carry an explicit ordering policy. The implementation models\n16 initial slots, the original signed-byte 32-bit string hash on the verified\nLinux/GCC platform, linear probing, growth before insertion above half occupancy\nand iteration by occupied slot. Growth is checked even for a duplicate value.\nSet aliases share identity, `add:` returns that same set and additions during\niteration can become visible. Rust uses shared interior mutability and borrows\nonly while obtaining the next item, so an iteration body can add values.\nString literals constructed through `String str:` stop at their first NUL.\n\nPython, JavaScript and Rust receive independently implemented helpers for that\npolicy. Objective-C uses the original native classes and a small argument\nadapter. Helper names avoid identifiers in the input. A reader binds a helper's\ncontract only when its complete definition matches and its declaration is at\nthe top level, outside comments and strings. Changing its implementation does\nnot retain the old contract. Concrete records preserve the complete definition\nas a library token and production, with UTF-8 ranges, rather than labelling its\nbytes as whitespace. This is an explicit library adapter, not a general reader\nfor arbitrary class implementations.\n\nAll 71 controlled natural grammars compose the new expressions using their own\nevaluation syntax and quoted operation names. Existing host\nheaders are not modified. Build logs and the exact revision/options stamp stay\nin the reusable temporary installation prefix.\n\nThe original\n[`set.m`](https://github.com/fkhannouf/objc/blob/983114f60a69d77fc82759e5ceb43ee6a20ed69b/src/objpak/set.m),\n[`ocstring.m`](https://github.com/fkhannouf/objc/blob/983114f60a69d77fc82759e5ceb43ee6a20ed69b/src/objpak/ocstring.m)\nand [`setseq.m`](https://github.com/fkhannouf/objc/blob/983114f60a69d77fc82759e5ceb43ee6a20ed69b/src/objpak/setseq.m)\nestablish the hash, insertion and live-iterator behavior. The emitted helpers implement the observed policy\nindependently; upstream library source is not included in distributed helpers.\n\n## Verification and limits\n\nThe native verifier compares stdout and successful process exit against real\nPOC execution for four independently parsed programs. Every child field is named, so\n//! conditions, actions, operands and arguments remain distinguishable.\n//!\n//! ```text\n//!   program (comments hi)\n//!     main\n//!       declaration x (mutable false) (type text)\n//!         value\n//!           text 'a b' (type text)\n//!       evaluate\n//!         expression\n//!           call print-line (library standard)\n//!             arguments\n//!               name x (type text)\n//! ```\n//!\n//! out.extend(letter.to_lowercase());\n        previous = Some(letter);\n    }\n    out\n}\n\nfn plain(text: &str) -> bool {\n    !text.is_empty()\n        && text\n            .chars()\n            .all(|it| it.is_alphanumeric() || \"_.+*/<>=!-\".contains(it))\n}\n\nfn atom(value: &Value) -> String {\n    match value {\n        Value::Bool(flag) => flag.to_string(),\n        Value::Number(number) => number.to_string(),\n        Value::Text(text) if plain(text) => text.clone(),\n        Value::Text(text) => format!(\"'{}'\", text.replace('\\'', \"''\")),\n        _ => \"right\",\n    \"start\",\n    \"end\",\n    \"step\",\n    \"length\",\n    \"fill\",\n    \"expression\",\n    \"subject\",\n    \"object\",\n    \"value\",\n    \"arguments\",\n    \"elements\",\n \"otherwise\",\n];\n\nfn rank(field: &str) -> usize {\n    CHILD_ORDER\n        .iter()\n        .position(|it| *it == field)\n        .unwrap_or(CHILD_ORDER.len())\n}\n\nfn scalar(value: &Value) -> bool {\n    !matches!(value, Value::List(_) | Value::Node(_))\n}\n\nfn empty(value: &Value) -> bool {\n    match value {\n        Value::List(items) => items.is_empty(),\n        Value::Node(node) => fields: Vec<(&String, &Value)> = node\n        .fields\n        .iter()\n        .filter(|(_, value)| match value {\n            _ if empty(value) => false,\n            Value::Node(_) => true,\n            Value::List(items) => !items.iter().all(scalar),\n            _ => false,\n        })\n        .collect();\n    // A stable sort keeps the fields of the same rank in name order.\n Every advisory, at any severity, becomes an\nannotation and a row in the step summary, so a green run states what it\naccepted. Pull requests and pushes fail at `high`, the same level as\n`dependency-review`: a moderate advisory with no patched release would\notherwise block every contributor. The weekly scheduled run also fails on a\nmoderate advisory that `npm audit fix` resolves without `--force`. Fix it with\n`npm update <package>` or an `overrides` entry. When only a breaking upgrade\nwould remove an advisory, the run stays green and keeps reporting it.\n\nThe same audit matrix looks up each locked package version in the npm registry,\nincluding optional and development dependencies. Live deprecations produce\nannotations on pull requests and fail the weekly run. Registry lookup failures\nfail every run. Use `DEPRECATED_FAIL=true node scripts/check-deprecated-packages.mjs package-lock.json`\nlocally to apply the scheduled policy to the current directory's lock.\n`js/tests/deprecated-packages.test.js` also fails when a committed lock records\na deprecated package. Deprecated dependencies are not allowlisted: replace or\noverride them. The desktop overrides and their probe are documented in\n[universal-app/compat](../examples/universal-app/compat/README.md).\n\nEvery dependency with an install script needs an explicit `allowScripts`\ndecision in its owning package manifest. Approvals pin the exact locked version\n(`\"esbuild@0.25.12\": true`), so a new release needs a new review; denials name\nthe package (`\"node-pty\": false`). The root denies command-stream's optional\nnode-pty adapter, because the release scripts only use its ordinary process\nAPI; Deno reads its own policy from `deno.json`, which denies it as well.\n`js/tests/issue-228-regressions.test.js` checks every entry of both npm locks,\nincluding optional platform-specific packages.\n\nRelease scripts load `command-stream` and `lino-arguments` from installed,\nlockfile-pinned development dependencies. Every node\n// is one line: its kind, its main value as a plain word and its other plain\n// fields as (name value) links. Every child field is named, so conditions,\n// actions, operands and arguments remain distinguishable at every depth.\n//\n//   program (comments hi)\n//     main\n//       declaration x (mutable false) (type text)\n//         value\n//           text 'a b' (type text)\n//       evaluate\n//         expression\n//           call print-line (library standard)\n//             arguments\n//               name x (type text)\n//\n// The program is written in its general form (see library.js): writing a\n// line or taking a length is a call to a procedure of the standard\n// library, like any other call.\n//\n// A block is written under its field name (main, body, then, otherwise).\n// Evaluate remains a statement containing an expression: a call used for\n// its effect cannot be confused with a call used as a value.\n// Links Notation keeps \"name:\" for links that define a unique name, and no\n// field name is unique here: \"value\", \"left\" or \"body\" appear again and\n// again. The full query\nand inherited language-coverage requirements remain open.\n\n## Shared meaning\n\n`Query` holds ordinary expressions for `source`, `condition` and `projection`,\na scoped range `variable`, and an `eager` evaluation flag. It can appear as an\nexpression in a binding, return or another query. `Evaluate(Query)` asks for the\nresult. This separates selection questions from the earlier introspection\n`Question` expression; SQL does not implement Python reflection.\n\nReaders recognize SQL `SELECT … FROM … [AS …] [WHERE …]`, C# LINQ\n`from … in … [where …] select …`, Python list/generator comprehensions, and\nsingle-parameter JavaScript/TypeScript `filter`/`map` chains. All 71 controlled\nnatural grammars compose their own expression slots into question and answer\nforms. The 30 base languages have native phrases; restricted profiles derive\nclauses from their own allowed loop/condition/result vocabulary. Minimal profiles\nuse quoted technical operation tags. No vocabulary limits are expanded.\n\nSQL is listed as a query target separately from the 33 imperative grammars and\nseven machine dialects. Its reader preserves quoted identifier case and SQL\nstring escaping; its writer rejects imperative programs and common-library\nmode. The public capability flag prevents old algorithm-coverage tests from\nclaiming that a query language implements imperative entry points.\n\n## Evaluation, types and scope\n\nC# query expressions enumerate lazily. `ToArray()` materializes their results;\nthis is described by Microsoft's [query execution documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/get-started/introduction-to-linq-queries).\nPython list comprehensions are eager while generator expressions defer their\nbodies, as documented in the [Python expression reference](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#generator-expressions).\nThe native example changes a source row between construction and enumeration\nto make this distinction observable. SQL output rejects a deferred iterator,\nand JavaScript output rejects deferred queries until it has a lazy writer.\n\nEager filter/map chains with function calls remain nested query expressions:\nall filtering effects finish before projection effects start. Combining\nside-effect-free predicates and projections is supported for ordinary data\nrecords. Arbitrary getters, custom iterators and overloaded operations still\nneed additional semantic modeling.\n\nCollection types retain the projected element and evaluation strategy as\n`array<element>` or `sequence<element>`. C# emits inferred query bindings with\n`var`, typed array/enumerable function returns, and expression-position array\nconstructors. A local range variable receives the source element type, rather\nthan inheriting an unrelated outer binding's type. Free-variable rewrites stop\nat nested binders while still traversing their source expressions. C# receives\nfresh range names where its local-name rules require them.\n\n## Reproduction and evidence\n\n- `experiments/issue-16-queries.mjs` exercises four source grammars against four\n  targets and records explicit unsupported evaluation strategies.\n- `experiments/issue-16-query-typing.mjs` records binding, function-return and\n  nested-scope translations.\n- `js/tests/queries.test.js` checks registration/detection, formal round trips,\n  all natural grammars, vocabulary constraints, eager/deferred strategies,\n  quoted SQL names, collection types, scope, filter/map side effects and native\n  SQLite/Python/Node agreement.\n- `rust/tests/queries.rs` covers the matching shared representation, formal and\n  natural round trips, strategy rejection, collection types and scopes.\n- `examples/queries/verify-native.mjs` compiles the generated C# methods and\n  bindings and compares finite results across four native runtimes. Imperative programs are deliberately rejected.\nimport { node } from '../../meta/tree.js';\nimport { query, rowMembers } from '../query-parser.js';\n\nconst identifier = (value) => `\"${value.replaceAll('\"', '\"\"')}\"`;\nconst table = (value) => value.split('.').map(identifier).join('.');\n\nconst parser = (Base) =>\n  class SqlParser extends Base {\n    primary() {\n      if (this.peek().quote === '\"') {\n        return node('Name', { name: this.next().value });\n      }\n      if (this.is('null')) {\n        throw new Error('SQL NULL expressions require three-valued logic');\n      }\n      return super.primary();\n    }\n\n    item() {\n      if (this.peek().type === 'comment') {\n        return super.item();\n      }\n      const expression = this.selection();\n      this.endStatement();\n      return node('Evaluate', { expression });\n    }\n\n    selection() {\n      this.expect('select');\n      const projection = this.accept('*') ? undefined : this.expression();\n      this.expect('from');\n      const source = super.postfix();\n      const variable = this.accept('as') ? this.expectName() : 'row';\n      const condition = this.accept('where') ? this.expression() : undefined;\n      return query(\n        source,\n        variable,\n        projection\n          ? rowMembers(projection, variable, true)\n          : node('Name', { name: variable }),\n        condition && rowMembers(condition, variable, true)\n      );\n    }\n  };\n\nconst emitter = (Base) =>\n  class SqlEmitter extends Base {\n    quote(value) {\n      return `'${value.replaceAll(\"'\", \"''\")}'`;\n    }\n\n    expression(expression, parent = 0) {\n      if (expression.kind === 'Query') {\n        const { source, variable, projection, condition } = expression;\n        if (!expression.eager) {\n          throw new Error(\n            'SQL selection execution cannot preserve a deferred iterator'\n          );\n        }\n        const relation =\n          source.kind === 'Name'\n            ? table(source.name)\n            : `(${this.expression(source)})`;\n        const selected =\n          projection.kind === 'Name' && projection.name === variable\n            ? '*'\n            : this.expression(projection);\n        const filtered =\n          condition.kind === 'Boolean' && condition.value\n            ? ''\n            : ` WHERE ${this.expression(condition)}`;\n        return `SELECT ${selected} FROM ${relation} AS ${identifier(variable)}${filtered}`;\n      }\n      if (\n        expression.kind === 'Index' &&\n        expression.index.kind === 'Text' &&\n        expression.array.kind === 'Name'\n      ) {\n        return `${identifier(expression.array.name)}.${identifier(expression.index.value)}`;\n      }\n      if (expression.kind === 'Name') {\n        return table(expression.name);\n      }\n      return super.expression(expression, parent);\n    }\n\n    program(program) {\n      if (\n        program.functions.length ||\n        program.main.statements.some(\n          (item) =>\n            !['Comment', 'Blank'].includes(item.kind) &&\n            (item.kind !== 'Evaluate' || item.expression.kind !== 'Query')\n        )\n      ) {\n        throw new Error('SQL requires selection queries');\n      }\n      this.comments(program);\n      for (const item of program.main.statements) {\n        this.statement(item);\n      }\n      return this.lines.join('\\n') + (this.lines.length ? Blocks\nretain parameter names and statements. A scoped understanding rule recognizes\ndocumented operations on known library values, rather than matching a whole\nprogram or substituting a saved translation. Unknown messages remain explicit.\nParameters and local bindings shadow library class names.\n\nThe argument entry point becomes an array of process arguments, an integer\nargument count and an integer cursor. Pointer dereferences become ordinary\narray indexing. Prefix and postfix unit updates retain their distinct values.\nUnsupported pointer uses raise a diagnostic. Generated argument adapters are\nrecognized only with a verified library definition and the actual entry-point\nparameters.\n\nObjpak string sets carry an explicit ordering policy. The implementation models\n16 initial slots, the original signed-byte 32-bit string hash on the verified\nLinux/GCC platform, linear probing, growth before insertion above half occupancy\nand iteration by occupied slot. Growth is checked even for a duplicate value.\nSet aliases share identity, `add:` returns that same set and additions during\niteration can become visible. Rust uses shared interior mutability and borrows\nonly while obtaining the next item, so an iteration body can add values.\nString literals constructed through `String str:` stop at their first NUL.\n\nPython, JavaScript and Rust receive independently implemented helpers for that\npolicy. Objective-C uses the original native classes and a small argument\nadapter. Helper names avoid identifiers in the input. A reader binds a helper's\ncontract only when its complete lexical definition matches and its declaration\nis at the top level, outside comments and strings. Matching retains Python\nblock structure, complete operators, joined numeric spellings and JavaScript\nreturn/update line-break semantics while allowing supported layout styles. Changing its implementation does\nnot retain the old contract. Concrete records preserve the complete definition\nas a library token and production, with UTF-8 ranges, rather than labelling its\nbytes as whitespace. This is an explicit library adapter, not a general reader\nfor arbitrary class implementations.\n\nAll 71 controlled natural grammars compose the new expressions using their own\nevaluation syntax and quoted operation names. The empty-set operation has an\nexplicit empty argument list, distinguishing it from a quoted text value.\nRestricted profile vocabularies are unchanged. Python editions without assignment\nexpressions and ECMAScript 5 reject constructs they cannot emit faithfully.\n\n## Original compiler and primary evidence\n\nThe finite native verifier builds the original toolchain without system\ninstallation:\n\n```sh\nbash experiments/build-objpak.sh\nnode examples/objpak/verify-native.mjs\n```\n\nThe source mirror is pinned to\n[`fkhannouf/objc` at 983114f](https://github.com/fkhannouf/objc/tree/983114f60a69d77fc82759e5ceb43ee6a20ed69b),\nand its generated-C bootstrap to\n[`fkhannouf/objc-bootstrap` at 5d2ffc1](https://github.com/fkhannouf/objc-bootstrap/tree/5d2ffc1d67204a598037542b86582a7a2631dbdc).\nThe build runs one job with a 1 GiB address-space limit and 16 MiB stack.\nIt uses GNU C89 and unoptimized, unfortified headers because the historical\nparser does not accept modern fortified glibc declarations.
