This eliminates merge conflicts that occur when multiple PRs bump the version in `package.json`.\n\n### Adding a Changeset\n\nWhen you make changes that affect users, add a changeset:\n\n```bash\nbun run changeset\n# or\nnpm run changeset\n```\n\nThis will prompt you to:\n\n1. Select the type of change (patch/minor/major)\n2. Provide a summary of the changes\n\nThe changeset will be saved as a markdown file in `.changeset/` and should be committed with your PR.\n\n### Changeset Guidelines\n\n| Type      | When to Use                          | Examples                                            |\n| --------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |\n| **Patch** | Bug fixes, internal changes          | Fix typo, update dependency, refactor internal code |\n| **Minor** | New features, non-breaking additions | Add new function, new optional parameter            |\n| **Major** | Breaking changes                     | Remove function, change API signature               |\n\nExample changeset summary:\n\n```markdown\nAdd support for custom configuration via config file\n```\n\n### What Changes Need Changesets?\n\n**Required** for:\n\n- Bug fixes\n- New features\n- Breaking changes\n- Public API changes\n\n**Not required** for:\n\n- Documentation-only changes (in `./docs` folder)\n- Changes to markdown files\n- CI/CD workflow updates (unless they affect users)\n\n### PR guard comparison and local validation\n\nVersion and changeset guards compare the PR head with its merge base. CI passes\n`GITHUB_BASE_SHA` and `GITHUB_HEAD_SHA`; local runs default to `origin/main` and\n`HEAD`. Fetch the base before running the guards. Missing refs, Git failures,\nand invalid package metadata fail validation.\n\nThe changeset guard counts added fragments only. Exact file moves do not count\nas new fragments; replacing a deleted fragment with different content does.\nBoth paths of a move are checked when deciding whether code requires a fragment.\nMarkdown, `docs/`, `examples/`,\n`experiments/`, `dev/log/`, and changeset metadata are exempt. In multi-language\nrepositories, unrelated language roots are exempt; shared workflows still\nrequire a fragment. For local directory validation without Git comparison, use\n`ALLOW_LOCAL_CHANGESET_SCAN=true node scripts/validate-changeset.mjs`. This\nexplicit mode is forbidden in CI. Set `DEBUG=1` to print comparison details.\n\nAutomated release PRs are exempt only when their author matches the release\nactor, both repositories match `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, and their branch uses a\nrelease prefix. The default author is `github-actions[bot]`. When a dedicated\nrelease token creates PRs as another account, configure repository variable\n`RELEASE_PR_ACTOR` to that account's exact login. A branch name alone never\ngrants an exemption.\n\n## Release Process\n\nThe release process is fully automated:\n\n1. **PR with changeset merged** - The changeset is added to `.changeset/`\n2. **CI detects changesets** - On push to main, CI checks for pending changesets\n3. **Version bump** - Package version is updated based on changeset type\n4. **Changelog update** - `CHANGELOG.md` is updated automatically\n5. **npm publish** - Package is published via OIDC trusted publishing\n6. **GitHub Release** - A release is created with formatted notes\n\nChangesets explicitly uses Prettier in `.changeset/config.json`, matching\n`format:check`. Keep that setting when adding runtime configs: auto-detection\nselects Deno for any `deno.json`, independently of the npm package-manager\ndeclaration. PR lint checks dry-run `npm run changeset:version` after the fresh\nmerge simulation and restore the generated metadata and consumed fragments.\nThis requires no publishing credentials and runs independently of release\ncredential preflight.\n\n### Multiple Changesets\n\nIf multiple PRs are merged before a release:\n\n- All changesets are merged into one\n- The highest version bump type wins (major > minor > patch)\n- All descriptions are preserved in chronological order\n\n## Pull Request Guidelines\n\n### PR Title\n\nUse a clear, descriptive title that summarizes the change:\n\n```\nfeat: Add support for custom configuration\nfix: Resolve race condition in async handler\ndocs: Update API documentation for v2\n```\n\n### PR Description\n\nInclude:\n\n- **What** - Describe the change\n- **Why** - Explain the motivation\n- **Testing** - How the change was tested\n\n### CI Checks\n\nAll PRs must pass:\n\n- [ ] Test compilation (syntax check)\n- [ ] Lint, format, and secrets scan\n- [ ] File line limits check\n- [ ] Changeset validation (for code changes)\n- [ ] Documentation validation (when docs change)\n- [ ] Rust tests and JavaScript/Rust translation parity on Ubuntu\n- [ ] Tests on all runtimes (Node.js, Bun, Deno)\n\n### Fresh Merge Simulation\n\nThe CI workflow automatically:\n\n1. Merges the latest `main` into your PR branch\n2. Runs checks against the merged state\n\nIf this fails with merge conflicts, you need to:\n\n```bash\ngit fetch origin main\ngit merge origin/main\n# Resolve conflicts\ngit push\n```\n\n## Dependency advisories\n\nThe Security workflow audits every committed npm lock with\n`scripts/npm-audit-report.mjs`. Every advisory, at any severity, becomes an\nannotation and a row in the step summary, so a green run states what it\naccepted. Only\n// nodes reachable from the accepted parse become productions in the CST.\nexport function concreteParser(parser, source) {\n  const locate = sourceLocator(source);\n  for (const token of parser.tokens) {\n    if (token.rawSpan) {\n      withOrigin(token, locate(...token.rawSpan));\n    }\n  }\n  const locations = new WeakMap();\n  const methods = new Map();\n  const proxy = new Proxy(parser, {\n    get(target, key, receiver) {\n      const value = Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);\n      if (typeof value !== 'function' || key === 'constructor') {\n        return value;\n      }\n      if (!methods.has(key)) {\n        methods.set(key, (...args) => {\n          const start = target.position;\n          const result = value.apply(receiver, args);\n          if (result?.kind && !locations.has(result)) {\n            const consumed = target.tokens.slice(start, target.position);\n            const first = consumed.find((token) => token.rawSpan);\n            const last = consumed.findLast((token) => token.rawSpan);\n            if (first && last) {\n              locations.set(result, {\n                rule: String(key),\n                start: first.rawSpan[0],\n                end: last.rawSpan[1],\n              });\n              withOrigin(result, locate(first.rawSpan[0], last.rawSpan[1]));\n            }\n          }\n          return result;\n        });\n      }\n      return methods.get(key);\n    },\n  });\n  return { parser: proxy, locations };\n}\n\nfunction productions(tree, locations, offsets) {\n  const result = [];\n  const visit = (value) => {\n    if (!value || typeof value !== 'object') {\n      return;\n    }\n    const location = locations.get(value);\n    if (location) {\n      result.push({\n        kind: 'Production',\n        rule: location.rule,\n        concept: value.kind,\n        start: offsets[location.start],\n        end: offsets[location.end],\n      });\n    }\n    Object.values(value).forEach(visit);\n  };\n  visit(tree);\n  return result;\n}\n\n// Token boundaries use the lexer's string offsets; the public CST uses UTF-8\n// byte ranges, matching Meta Language and tree-sitter across both runtimes.\nexport function concreteSyntax(\n  source,\n  language,\n  tokens,\n  tree,\n  locations = new WeakMap()\n) {\n  const offsets = byteOffsets(source);\n  const children = [];\n  let position = 0;\n  const append = (kind, type, start, end) => {\n    if (end > start) {\n      children.push({\n        kind,\n        type,\n        start: offsets[start],\n token.rawSpan;\n    append('Trivia', 'layout', position, start);\n    append('Token', token.type, start, end);\n    position = end;\n  }\n  append('Trivia', 'layout', position, source.length);\n errors: [],\n  };\n}\n\nexport const reconstructConcrete = (syntax) =>\n  syntax.children.map((child) => child.text).join('');\n## Summary\n\nFixes #16\nFixes #1\nFixes #2\nFixes #10\nFixes #6\nFixes Changesets\n\nThis project uses [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets) to manage versions and changelogs. This eliminates merge conflicts that occur when multiple PRs bump the version in `package.json`.\n\n### Adding a Changeset\n\nWhen you make changes that affect users, add a changeset:\n\n```bash\nbun run changeset\n# or\nnpm run changeset\n```\n\nThis will prompt you to:\n\n1. Select the type of change (patch/minor/major)\n2. CI passes\n`GITHUB_BASE_SHA` and `GITHUB_HEAD_SHA`; local runs default to `origin/main` and\n`HEAD`. Fetch the base before running the guards. Missing refs, Git failures,\nand invalid package metadata fail validation.\n\nThe changeset guard counts added fragments only. Exact file moves do not count\nas new fragments; replacing a deleted fragment with different content does.\nBoth paths of a move are checked when deciding whether code requires a fragment.\nMarkdown, `docs/`, `examples/`,\n`experiments/`, `dev/log/`, and changeset metadata are exempt. In multi-language\nrepositories, unrelated language roots are exempt; shared workflows still\nrequire a fragment. Set `DEBUG=1` to print comparison details.\n\nAutomated release PRs are exempt only when their author matches the release\nactor, both repositories match `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, and their branch uses a\nrelease prefix. The default author is `github-actions[bot]`. When a dedicated\nrelease token creates PRs as another account, configure repository variable\n`RELEASE_PR_ACTOR` to that account's exact login. Pull requests and pushes fail at `high`, the same level as\n`dependency-review`: a moderate advisory with no patched release would\notherwise block every contributor. The weekly scheduled run also fails on a\nmoderate advisory that `npm audit fix` resolves without `--force`. Fix it with\n`npm update <package>` or an `overrides` entry. When only a breaking upgrade\nwould remove an advisory, the run stays green and keeps reporting it.\n\nThe same audit matrix looks up each locked package version in the npm registry,\nincluding optional and development dependencies. Its scanner ignores\ncomment markers inside quoted strings, including doubled quotes, and rejects an\nunclosed comment string. .skip_while(|c| c.is_whitespace())\n            .take(7)\n            .collect();\n        if !after.starts_with(\"include\") && !after.starts_with(\"import\") {\n            return false;\n }\n\n    fn text(&mut self) -> Result<bool, GrammarError> {\n        let Some(character) = self.at(0) else {\n            return Ok(false);\n        };\n      </form>\n    </div>\n  </div><div id=\"language.basic-syntax.phpmode\" class=\"sect1\">\n   <h2 class=\"title\">Escaping from HTML</h2>\n   <p class=\"para\">\n    Everything outside of a pair of opening and closing tags is ignored by the\n    PHP parser which allows PHP files to have mixed content. and Parse-Affecting Attributes\nSQLite understands these operators, listed in precedence\n1\norder\n(top to bottom / highest to lowest):\ntd.optab { color: #2c2cf0; border: 2px solid black; padding: }\nOperators\n2\n~\n[expr]\n+\n[expr]\n-\n[expr]\n[expr]\nCOLLATE (collation-name)\n3\n||   ->   ->>\n*   /   %\n+   -\n&  |   <<  >>\n[expr]\nESCAPE [escape-character-expr]\n4\n<  >  <=  >=\n=  ==  <>  !=  IS   IS NOT\nIS DISTINCT FROM   IS NOT DISTINCT FROM\n[expr]\nBETWEEN\n5\n[expr]\nAND\n[expr]\nIN\n5\nMATCH\n5\nLIKE\n5\nREGEXP\n5\nGLOB\n5\n[expr]\nISNULL\n[expr]\nNOTNULL\n[expr]\nNOT NULL\nNOT\n[expr]\nAND\nOR\nOperators shown within the same table cell share precedence.\n\"\n[expr]\n\" denotes operand locations for non-binary operators.\nOperators with no \"[expr]\" adjunct are binary and left-associative.\nThe COLLATE clause (with its collation-name) acts as a single postfix operator.\nThe ESCAPE clause (with its escape character) acts as a single postfix operator.\nIt can only bind to a preceding [expr] LIKE [expr] expression.\nEach keyword in (BETWEEN IN GLOB LIKE MATCH REGEXP) may be prefixed\nby NOT, retaining the bare operator's precedence and associativity.\nThe COLLATE operator is a unary postfix\noperator that assigns a\ncollating sequence\nto an expression.\nThe collating sequence set by the COLLATE operator overrides the\ncollating sequence determined by the COLLATE clause in a table\ncolumn definition\n.\nSee the\ndetailed discussion on collating sequences\nin the\nDatatype In SQLite3\ndocument for additional information.\nThe unary operator\n+\nis a no-op.  It can be applied\nto strings, numbers, blobs or NULL and it always returns a result\nwith the same value as the operand.\nNote that there are two variations of the equals and not equals\noperators.  Equals can be either\n=\nor\n==\n.\nThe not-equal operator can be either\n!=\nor\n<>\n.\nThe\n||\noperator is \"concatenate\" - it joins together\nthe two strings of its operands.\nThe\n->\nand\n->>\noperators are \"extract\";\nthey extract the RHS component from the LHS.\nFor an example, see\nJSON subcomponent extraction\n.\nThe\n%\noperator\ncasts\nboth of its operands to type\nINTEGER and then computes the remainder after dividing the left integer\nby the right integer. The other arithmetic operators perform integer\narithmetic if both operands are integers and no overflow would result,\nor floating point arithmetic, per IEEE Standard 754, if either operand\nis a real value or integer arithmetic would produce an overflow.\nInteger divide yields an integer result, truncated toward zero.\nThe result of any binary operator is either a numeric value or\nNULL, except for the\n||\nconcatenation operator,\nand the\n->\nand\n->>\nextract operators\nwhich can return values of any type.\nAll operators generally evaluate to NULL when any operand is NULL,\nwith specific exceptions as stated below. This is in accordance with\nthe SQL92 standard.\nWhen paired with NULL:\nAND\nevaluates to 0 (false) when\nthe other operand is false; and\nOR\nevaluates to 1 (true)\nwhen the other operand is true.\nThe\nIS\nand\nIS NOT\noperators work\nlike\n=\nand\n!=\nexcept when one or both of the\noperands are NULL. In this case, if both operands are NULL, then the\nIS operator evaluates to 1 (true) and the IS NOT operator evaluates\nto 0 (false). If one operand is NULL and the other is not, then the\nIS operator evaluates to 0 (false) and the IS NOT operator is 1 (true).\nIt is not possible for an IS or IS NOT expression to evaluate to NULL.\nThe\nIS NOT DISTINCT FROM\noperator is an alternative spelling\nfor the\nIS\noperator.\nLikewise, the\nIS DISTINCT FROM\noperator means the same thing\nas\nIS NOT\n.  Standard SQL does not support the compact IS and IS NOT\nnotation.  Those compact forms are an SQLite extension.  You must use\nthe less readable IS NOT DISTINCT FROM and\nIS DISTINCT FROM operators in most other SQL database engines.\n3.\nLiteral Values (Constants)\nA literal value represents a constant.\nLiteral values may be integers, floating point numbers, strings,\nBLOBs, or NULLs.\nThe syntax for integer and floating point literals (collectively\n\"numeric literals\") is shown by the following diagram:\nnumeric-literal:\ndigit\n_\n.\nE\ne\ndigit\n_\n.\ndigit\n_\n-\ndigit\n_\n+\n0x\n0X\nhexdigit\n_\nIf a numeric literal has a decimal point or an exponentiation\nclause or if it is less than -9223372036854775808 or\ngreater than 9223372036854775807, then it is a floating point literal.\nOtherwise it is an  integer literal.\nThe \"E\" character that begins the exponentiation\nclause of a floating point literal can be either upper or lower case.\nThe \".\" character is always used\nas the decimal point even if the locale setting specifies \",\" for\nthis role - the use of \",\" for the decimal point would result in\nsyntactic ambiguity.\nBeginning in SQLite version 3.46.0 (2024-05-23), a single extra underscore (\"_\")\ncharacter can be added between any two digits.  The underscores are purely\nfor human readability and are ignored by SQLite.\nHexadecimal integer literals follow the C-language notation of\n\"0x\" or \"0X\" followed by hexadecimal digits.\nFor example, 0x1234 means the same as 4660\nand 0x8000000000000000 means the same as -9223372036854775808.\n Hexadecimal integer literals are interpreted as 64-bit\ntwo's-complement integers and are thus limited\nto sixteen significant digits of precision.\nSupport for hexadecimal integers was added to SQLite\nversion 3.8.6 (2014-08-15).\nFor backwards compatibility, the \"0x\" hexadecimal integer\nnotation is only understood by the SQL language parser, not by the\ntype conversions routines.\nString variables that\ncontain text formatted like hexadecimal integers are not\ninterpreted as hexadecimal integers when coercing the string value\ninto an integer due to a\nCAST expression\nor for a\ncolumn affinity\ntransformation or prior to performing a numeric operation or for\nany other run-time conversions.  When coercing a\nstring value in the format of a hexadecimal integer into an integer\nvalue, the conversion process stops when the 'x' character is seen\nso the resulting integer value is always zero.\nSQLite only understands the hexadecimal integer notation when it\nappears in the SQL statement text, not when it appears as\npart of the content of the database.\nA string constant is formed by enclosing the\nstring in single quotes (').  A single quote within the string can\nbe encoded by putting two single quotes in a row - as in Pascal.\nC-style escapes using the backslash character are not supported because\nthey are not standard SQL.\nBLOB literals are string literals containing hexadecimal data and\npreceded by a single \"x\" or \"X\" character.  Example: X'53514C697465'\nA literal value can also be the token \"NULL\".\n4.\nParameters\nA \"variable\" or \"parameter\" token\nspecifies a placeholder in the expression for a\nvalue that is filled in at runtime using the\nsqlite3_bind()\nfamily of C/C++ interfaces.\nParameters can take several forms:\n?\nNNN\nA question mark followed by a number\nNNN\nholds a spot for the\nNNN-th parameter.  NNN must be between 1 and\nSQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER\n.\n?\nA question mark that is not followed by a number creates a parameter\nwith a number one greater than the largest parameter number already assigned.\nIf this means the parameter number is greater than\nSQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER\n, it is an error.\nThis parameter format is provided for compatibility with other database\nengines.  But because it is easy to miscount the question marks, the\nuse of this parameter format is discouraged.  Programmers are encouraged\nto use one of the symbolic formats below or the ?NNN format above instead.\n:\nAAAA\nA colon followed by an identifier name holds a spot for a\nnamed parameter\nwith the name :AAAA.\nNamed parameters are also numbered. The number assigned is one greater than\nthe largest parameter number already assigned. If this means the parameter\nwould be assigned a number greater than\nSQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER\n, it is\nan error. To avoid confusion, it is best to avoid mixing named and numbered\nparameters.\n@\nAAAA\nAn \"at\" sign works exactly like a colon, except that the name of\nthe parameter created is @AAAA.\n$\nAAAA\nA dollar-sign followed by an identifier name also holds a spot for a named\nparameter with the name $AAAA.  The identifier name in this case can include\none or more occurrences of \"::\" and a suffix enclosed in \"(...)\" containing\nany text without whitespace.  This syntax is the form of a variable name in the\nTcl programming language\n.  The presence\nof this syntax results from the fact that SQLite is really a\nTcl extension\nthat has escaped into the wild.\nParameters that are not assigned values using\nsqlite3_bind()\nare treated\nas NULL.  The\nsqlite3_bind_parameter_index()\ninterface can be used\nto translate a symbolic parameter name into its equivalent numeric index.\nThe maximum parameter number is set at compile-time by\nthe\nSQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER\nmacro.  An individual\ndatabase connection\nD can reduce its maximum parameter number below the compile-time maximum\nusing the\nsqlite3_limit\n(D,\nSQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER\n,...) interface.\n5.\nThe LIKE, GLOB, REGEXP, MATCH, and extract operators\nThe LIKE operator does a pattern matching comparison. The operand\nto the right of the LIKE operator contains the pattern and the left hand\noperand contains the string to match against the pattern.\n\nA percent symbol (\"%\") in the LIKE pattern matches any\nsequence of zero or more characters in the string.  An underscore\n(\"_\") in the LIKE pattern matches any single character in the\nstring.  Any other character matches itself or its lower/upper case\nequivalent (i.e. case-insensitive matching).\nImportant Note:\nSQLite only\nunderstands upper/lower case for ASCII characters by default.  The\nLIKE operator is case sensitive by default for unicode characters that are\nbeyond the ASCII range.  For example,\nthe expression\n'a' LIKE 'A'\nis TRUE but\n'æ' LIKE 'Æ'\nis FALSE.\nThe ICU extension to SQLite includes an enhanced version of the\nLIKE operator that does case folding across all unicode characters.\nIf the optional ESCAPE clause is present, then the expression\nfollowing the ESCAPE keyword must evaluate to a string consisting of\na single character. This character may be used in the LIKE pattern\nto include literal percent or underscore characters. The escape\ncharacter followed by a percent symbol (%), underscore (_), or a second\ninstance of the escape character itself matches a\nliteral percent symbol, underscore, or a single escape character,\nrespectively.\nThe infix LIKE operator is implemented by calling the\napplication-defined SQL functions\nlike(\nY\n,\nX\n)\nor\nlike(\nY\n,\nX\n,\nZ\n)\n.\nThe LIKE operator can be made case sensitive using the\ncase_sensitive_like pragma\n.\nThe GLOB operator is similar to LIKE but uses the Unix\nfile globbing syntax for its wildcards.  Also, GLOB is case\nsensitive, unlike LIKE.  Both GLOB and LIKE may be preceded by\nthe NOT keyword to invert the sense of the test.  The infix GLOB\noperator is implemented by calling the function\nglob(\nY\n,\nX\n)\nand can be modified by overriding\nthat function.\nThe REGEXP operator is a special syntax for the regexp()\nuser function.  No regexp() user function is defined by default\nand so use of the REGEXP operator will normally result in an\nerror message.  If an\napplication-defined SQL function\nnamed \"regexp\"\nis added at run-time, then the \"\nX\nREGEXP\nY\n\" operator will\nbe implemented as a call to \"regexp(\nY\n,\nX\n)\".\nThe MATCH operator is a special syntax for the match()\napplication-defined function.  The default match() function implementation\nraises an exception and is not really useful for anything.\nBut extensions can override the match() function with more\nhelpful logic.\nThe extract operators act as a special syntax for functions\n\"->\"() and \"->>\"(). Default implementations for these functions\nperform\nJSON subcomponent extraction\n,\nbut extensions can override them for other purposes.\n6.\nThe BETWEEN operator\nThe BETWEEN operator is logically equivalent to a pair of comparisons.\n\"\nx\nBETWEEN\ny\nAND\nz\n\" is\nequivalent to\n\"\nx\n>=\ny\nAND\nx\n<=\nz\n\" except\nthat with BETWEEN, the\nx\nexpression is only evaluated once.\n7.\nThe CASE expression\nA CASE expression serves a role similar to IF-THEN-ELSE in other\nprogramming languages.\nThe optional expression that occurs in between the CASE keyword and the\nfirst WHEN keyword is called the \"base\" expression. There are two\nfundamental forms\nof the CASE expression: those with a base expression and those without.\nIn a CASE without a base expression, each WHEN expression is evaluated\nand the result treated as a boolean, starting with the leftmost and continuing\nto the right. The result of the CASE expression is the evaluation of the THEN\nexpression that corresponds to the first WHEN expression that evaluates to\ntrue. Or, if none of the WHEN expressions evaluate to true, the result of\nevaluating the ELSE expression, if any. If there is no ELSE expression and\nnone of the WHEN expressions are true, then the overall result is NULL.\nA NULL result is considered untrue when evaluating WHEN terms.\nIn a CASE with a base expression, the base expression is evaluated just\nonce and the result is compared against the evaluation of each WHEN\nexpression from left to right. The result of the CASE expression is the\nevaluation of the THEN expression that corresponds to the first WHEN\nexpression for which the comparison is true. Or, if none of the WHEN\nexpressions evaluate to a value equal to the base expression, the result\nof evaluating the ELSE expression, if any. If there is no ELSE expression and\nnone of the WHEN expressions produce a result equal to the base expression,\nthe overall result is NULL.\nWhen comparing a base expression against a WHEN expression, the same\ncollating sequence, affinity, and NULL-handling rules apply as if the\nbase expression and WHEN expression are respectively the left- and\nright-hand operands of an\n=\noperator.\nIf the base\nexpression is NULL then the result of the CASE is always the result\nof evaluating the ELSE expression if it exists, or NULL if it does not.\nBoth forms of the CASE expression use lazy, or short-circuit,\nevaluation.\nThe only difference between the following two CASE expressions is that\nthe\nx\nexpression is evaluated exactly once in the first example but\nmight be evaluated multiple times in the second:\nCASE x WHEN w1 THEN r1 WHEN w2 THEN r2 ELSE r3 END\nCASE WHEN x=w1 THEN r1 WHEN x=w2 THEN r2 ELSE r3 END\nThe built-in\niif(x,y,z) SQL function\nis logically\nequivalent to \"CASE WHEN x THEN y ELSE z END\".  The iif() function\nis found in SQL Server and is included in SQLite for compatibility.\nSome developers prefer the iif() function because it is more\nconcise.\n8.\nThe IN and NOT IN operators\nThe IN and NOT IN operators take an expression on the\nleft and a list of values or a subquery on the right.\nWhen the right operand of an IN or NOT IN operator is a subquery, the\nsubquery must have the same number of columns as there are columns in\nthe\nrow value\nof the left operand.  The subquery on the\nright of an IN or NOT IN operator must be a scalar subquery if the left\nexpression is not a\nrow value\nexpression.\nIf the right operand of an IN or NOT IN operator is a list of values,\neach of those values must be scalars and the left expression must also\nbe a scalar.\nThe right-hand side of an IN or NOT IN operator can be a\ntable\nname\nor\ntable-valued function\nname\nin which\ncase the right-hand side is understood to be a subquery of\nthe form \"(SELECT * FROM\nname\n)\".\nWhen the right operand is an empty set, the result of IN is false and the\nresult of NOT IN is true, regardless of the left operand and even if the\nleft operand is NULL.\nThe result of an IN or NOT IN operator is determined by the following\nmatrix:\nLeft operand\nis NULL\nRight operand\ncontains NULL\nRight operand\nis an empty set\nLeft operand found\nwithin right operand\nResult of\nIN operator\nResult of\nNOT IN operator\nno\nno\nno\nno\nfalse\ntrue\ndoes not matter\nno\nyes\nno\nfalse\ntrue\nno\ndoes not matter\nno\nyes\ntrue\nfalse\nno\nyes\nno\nno\nNULL\nNULL\nyes\ndoes not matter\nno\ndoes not matter\nNULL\nNULL\nNote that SQLite allows the parenthesized list of scalar values on\nthe right-hand side of an IN or NOT IN operator to be an empty list but\nmost other SQL database engines and the SQL92 standard require\nthe list to contain at least one element.\n9.\nTable Column Names\nA column name can be any of the names defined in the\nCREATE TABLE\nstatement or one of the following special identifiers: \"\nROWID\n\",\n\"\nOID\n\", or \"\n_ROWID_\n\".\nThe three special identifiers describe the\nunique integer key (the\nrowid\n) associated with every\nrow of every table and so are not available on\nWITHOUT ROWID\ntables.\nThe special identifiers only refer to the row key if the\nCREATE TABLE\nstatement does not define a real column with the same name.\nThe rowid can be used anywhere a regular\ncolumn can be used.\n10.\nThe EXISTS operator\nThe EXISTS operator always evaluates to one of the integer values 0\nand 1. If executing the SELECT statement specified as the right-hand\noperand of the EXISTS operator would return one or more rows, then the\nEXISTS operator evaluates to 1. If executing the SELECT would return\nno rows at all, then the EXISTS operator evaluates to 0.\nThe number of columns in each row returned by the SELECT statement\n(if any) and the specific values returned have no effect on the results\nof the EXISTS operator. In particular, rows containing NULL values are\nnot handled any differently from rows without NULL values.\n11.\nSubquery Expressions\nA\nSELECT\nstatement enclosed in parentheses is a subquery.\nAll types of SELECT statement, including\naggregate and compound SELECT queries (queries with keywords like\nUNION or EXCEPT) are allowed as scalar subqueries.\nThe value of a subquery expression is the first row of the result\nfrom the enclosed\nSELECT\nstatement.\nThe value of a subquery expression is NULL if the enclosed\nSELECT\nstatement returns no rows.\nA subquery that returns a single column is a scalar subquery and can\nbe used most anywhere.\nA subquery that returns two or more columns is a\nrow value\nsubquery and can only be used as an operand of a comparison operator or as\nthe value in an UPDATE SET clause whose column name list has the same size.\n12.\nCorrelated Subqueries\nA\nSELECT\nstatement used as either a scalar subquery or as the\nright-hand operand of an IN, NOT IN or EXISTS expression may contain\nreferences to columns in the outer query. Such a subquery is known as\na correlated subquery. A correlated subquery is reevaluated each time\nits result is required. An uncorrelated subquery is evaluated only once\nand the result reused as necessary.\n13.\nCAST expressions\nA CAST expression of the form \"CAST(\nexpr\nAS\ntype-name\n)\"\nis used to convert the value of\nexpr\nto\na different\nstorage class\nspecified by\ntype-name\n.\nA CAST conversion is similar to the conversion that takes\nplace when a\ncolumn affinity\nis applied to a value except that with\nthe CAST operator the conversion always takes place even if the conversion is\nlossy and irreversible, whereas column affinity only changes the data type\nof a value if the change is lossless and reversible.\nIf the value of\nexpr\nis NULL, then the result of the CAST\nexpression is also NULL. Otherwise, the storage class of the result\nis determined by applying the\nrules for determining column affinity\nto\nthe\ntype-name\n.\nAffinity of\ntype-name\nConversion Processing\nNONE\nCasting a value to a\ntype-name\nwith no affinity\n  causes the value to\n  be converted into a BLOB.  Casting to a BLOB consists of first casting\n  the value to TEXT in the\nencoding\nof the database connection, then\n  interpreting the resulting byte sequence as a BLOB instead of as TEXT.\nTEXT\nTo cast a BLOB value to TEXT, the sequence of bytes that make up the\n  BLOB is interpreted as text encoded using the database encoding.\nCasting an INTEGER or REAL value into TEXT renders the value as if via\nsqlite3_snprintf()\nexcept that the resulting TEXT uses the\nencoding\nof\n    the database connection.\nREAL\nWhen casting a BLOB value to a REAL, the value is first converted to\n        TEXT.\nWhen casting a TEXT value to REAL, the longest possible prefix of\n        the value that can be interpreted as a real number is extracted from\n        the TEXT value and the remainder ignored. Any leading spaces in the\n        TEXT value are ignored when converting from TEXT to REAL. If there is\n        no prefix that can be interpreted as a real number, the result of the\n        conversion is 0.0.\nINTEGER\nWhen casting a BLOB value to INTEGER, the value is first converted to\n        TEXT.\nWhen casting a TEXT value to INTEGER, the longest possible prefix of\n        the value that can be interpreted as an integer number is extracted from\n        the TEXT value and the remainder ignored. Any leading spaces in the\n        TEXT value when converting from TEXT to INTEGER are ignored. If there\n        is no prefix that can be interpreted as an integer number, the result\n        of the conversion is 0.  If the prefix integer is greater than\n        +9223372036854775807 then the result of the cast is exactly\n        +9223372036854775807.  Similarly, if the prefix integer is\n        less than -9223372036854775808 then the result of the cast is\n        exactly -9223372036854775808.\nWhen casting to INTEGER, if the text looks like a floating point\n        value with an exponent, the exponent will be ignored because it is\n        not part of the integer prefix.  For example,\n        \"CAST('123e+5' AS INTEGER)\" results in 123, not in 12300000.\nThe CAST operator understands decimal\n        integers only — conversion of\nhexadecimal integers\nstops\n        at the \"x\" in the \"0x\" prefix of the hexadecimal integer string\n        and thus result of the CAST is always zero.\nA cast of a REAL value into an INTEGER results in the integer\n      between the REAL value and zero that is closest to the REAL value.\n      If a REAL is greater than the greatest possible signed\n      integer (+9223372036854775807) then the result is the greatest possible\n      signed integer and if the REAL is less than the least possible signed\n      integer (-9223372036854775808) then the result is the least possible\n      signed integer.\nPrior to SQLite version 3.8.2 (2013-12-06),\n      casting a REAL value greater than\n      +9223372036854775807.0 into an integer resulted in the most negative\n      integer, -9223372036854775808.  This behavior was meant to emulate the\n      behavior of x86/x64 hardware when doing the equivalent cast.\nNUMERIC\nCasting a TEXT or BLOB value into NUMERIC yields either an INTEGER or\n   a REAL result.\n   If the input text looks like an integer (there is no decimal point nor\n   exponent) and the value is small enough to fit in a 64-bit signed integer,\n   then the result will be INTEGER.\n   Input text that looks like floating point (there is a decimal point and/or\n   an exponent) and the text describes a value that\n   can be losslessly converted back and forth between IEEE 754 64-bit float and a\n   51-bit signed integer, then the result is INTEGER.\n   (In the previous sentence, a 51-bit integer is specified since that is one\n   bit less than the length of the mantissa of an IEEE 754 64-bit float and\n   thus provides a 1-bit of margin for the text-to-float conversion operation.)\n   Any text input that describes a value outside the range of a 64-bit\n   signed integer yields a REAL result.\nCasting a REAL or INTEGER value to NUMERIC is a no-op, even if a real\n   value could be losslessly converted to an integer.\nNote that the result from casting any non-BLOB value into a\nBLOB and the result from casting any BLOB value into a non-BLOB value\nmay be different depending on whether the database\nencoding\nis UTF-8,\nUTF-16be, or UTF-16le.\n14.\nBoolean Expressions\nThe SQL language features several contexts where an expression is\nevaluated and the result converted to a boolean (true or false) value. These\ncontexts are:\nthe WHERE clause of a SELECT, UPDATE or DELETE statement,\nthe ON or USING clause of a join in a SELECT statement,\nthe HAVING clause of a SELECT statement,\nthe WHEN clause of an SQL trigger, and\nthe WHEN clause or clauses of some CASE expressions.\nTo convert the results of an SQL expression to a boolean value, SQLite\nfirst casts the result to a NUMERIC value in the same way as a\nCAST expression\n. A numeric zero value (integer value 0 or real\nvalue 0.0) is considered to be false.  A NULL value is still NULL.\nAll other values are considered true.\nFor example, the values NULL, 0.0, 0, 'english' and '0' are all considered\nto be false. Values 1, 1.0, 0.1, -0.1 and '1english' are considered to\nbe true.\nBeginning with SQLite 3.23.0 (2018-04-02), SQLite recognizes the\nidentifiers \"TRUE\" and \"FALSE\" as boolean literals, if and only if those\nidentifiers are not already used for some other meaning.  If there already\nexists columns or tables or other objects named TRUE or FALSE, then for\nthe sake of backwards compatibility, the TRUE and FALSE identifiers refer\nto those other objects, not to the boolean values.\nThe boolean identifiers TRUE and FALSE are usually just aliases for\nthe integer values 1 and 0, respectively.  However, if TRUE or FALSE\noccur on the right-hand side of an IS operator, then the IS operator\nevaluates the left-hand operand as a boolean value and returns an appropriate\nanswer.\n15.\nFunctions\nSQLite supports many\nsimple\n,\naggregate\n,\nand\nwindow\nSQL functions.  For presentation purposes, simple functions are further\nsubdivided into\ncore functions\n,\ndate-time functions\n,\nmath functions\n, and\nJSON functions\n.\nApplications can add new functions, written in C/C++, using the\nsqlite3_create_function()\ninterface.\nThe main expression bubble diagram above shows a single syntax for\nall function invocations.  But this is merely to simplify the expression\nbubble diagram.  In reality, each type of function has a slightly different\nsyntax, shown below.  The function invocation syntax shown in the main\nexpression bubble diagram is the union of the three syntaxes shown here:\nsimple-function-invocation:\nsimple-func\n(\nexpr\n)\n,\n*\naggregate-function-invocation:\naggregate-func\n(\nDISTINCT\nexpr\n)\nfilter-clause\n,\n*\nORDER\nBY\nordering-term\n,\nwindow-function-invocation:\nwindow-func\n(\nexpr\n)\nfilter-clause\nOVER\nwindow-name\nwindow-defn\n,\n*\nThe OVER clause is required for\nwindow functions\nand is prohibited\notherwise.  The DISTINCT keyword and the ORDER BY clause is only allowed\nin\naggregate functions\n.\nThe FILTER clause may not appear on a\nsimple function\n.\nIt is possible to have an aggregate function with the same name as a\nsimple function, as long as the number of arguments for the two forms of the\nfunction are different.  For example, the\nmax()\nfunction with a\nsingle argument is an aggregate and the\nmax()\nfunction with two or more\narguments is a simple function.  Aggregate functions can usually also\nbe used as window functions.\nThis page was last updated on 2026-08-14 19:21:30Z\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Selection queries and natural questions\n\nThis work in [PR 17](https://github.com/link-foundation/universal-translator/pull/17)\nimplements a compositional selection subset of requirement 16.12. The full query\nand inherited language-coverage requirements remain open.\n\n## Shared meaning\n\n`Query` holds ordinary expressions for `source`, `condition` and `projection`,\na scoped range `variable`, and an `eager` evaluation flag. It can appear as an\nexpression in a binding, return or another query. `Evaluate(Query)` asks for the\nresult. This separates selection questions from the earlier introspection\n`Question` expression; SQL does not implement Python reflection.\n\nReaders recognize SQL `SELECT … FROM … [AS …] [WHERE …]`, C# LINQ\n`from … in … [where …] select …`, Python list/generator comprehensions, and\nsingle-parameter JavaScript/TypeScript `filter`/`map` chains. All 71 controlled\nnatural grammars compose their own expression slots into question and answer\nforms. The 30 base languages have native phrases; restricted profiles derive\nclauses from their own allowed loop/condition/result vocabulary. Minimal profiles\nuse quoted technical operation tags. No vocabulary limits are expanded.\n\nSQL is listed as a query target separately from the 33 imperative grammars and\nseven machine dialects. Its reader preserves quoted identifier case and SQL\nstring escaping; its writer rejects imperative programs and common-library\nmode. The public capability flag prevents old algorithm-coverage tests from\nclaiming that a query language implements imperative entry points.\n\n## Evaluation, types and scope\n\nC# query expressions enumerate lazily. `ToArray()` materializes their results;\nthis is described by Microsoft's [query execution documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/get-started/introduction-to-linq-queries).\nPython list comprehensions are eager while generator expressions defer their\nbodies, as documented in the [Python expression reference](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#generator-expressions).\nThe native example changes a source row between construction and enumeration\nto make this distinction observable. SQL output rejects a deferred iterator,\nand JavaScript output rejects deferred queries until it has a lazy writer.\n\nEager filter/map chains with function calls remain nested query expressions:\nall filtering effects finish before projection effects start. Combining\nside-effect-free predicates and projections is supported for ordinary data\nrecords. Arbitrary getters, custom iterators and overloaded operations still\nneed additional semantic modeling.\n\nCollection types retain the projected element and evaluation strategy as\n`array<element>` or `sequence<element>`. C# emits inferred query bindings with\n`var`, typed array/enumerable function returns, and expression-position array\nconstructors. A local range variable receives the source element type, rather\nthan inheriting an unrelated outer binding's type. Free-variable rewrites stop\nat nested binders while still traversing their source expressions. C# receives\nfresh range names where its local-name rules require them.\n\n## Reproduction and evidence\n\n- `experiments/issue-16-queries.mjs` exercises four source grammars against four\n  targets and records explicit unsupported evaluation strategies.\n- `experiments/issue-16-query-typing.mjs` records binding, function-return and\n  nested-scope translations.\n- `js/tests/queries.test.js` checks registration/detection, formal round trips,\n  all natural grammars, vocabulary constraints, eager/deferred strategies,\n  quoted SQL names, collection types, scope, filter/map side effects and native\n  SQLite/Python/Node agreement.\n- `rust/tests/queries.rs` covers the matching shared representation, formal and\n  natural round trips, strategy rejection, collection types and scopes.\n- `examples/queries/verify-native.mjs` compiles the generated C# methods and\n  bindings and compares finite results across four native runtimes. The existing\n  native CI job includes it with a finite step budget.\n- Focused logs: `logs/queries-js-regressions.txt`, `logs/queries-rust-regressions.txt`,\n  `logs/queries-final-js.txt`, `logs/queries-final-rust.txt`,\n  `logs/queries-native.txt`, `logs/queries-clippy.txt`, `logs/queries-lint.txt`,\n  `logs/queries-natural-goldens.txt` and `logs/queries-requirements.txt`.\n\nPrimary sources are compressed and checksummed in\n`data/prior-art/questions/manifest.json`. The historical requirements gate's\nold completion labels are not acceptance evidence for the broader inventory.\n\n## SQL negation and Python comparison grouping\n\nThe shared imperative precedence table treated `NOT age = 18` as\n`(NOT age) = 18`. SQL's prefix NOT has lower precedence than comparisons and\nhigher precedence than AND, as specified by the\n[SQLite expression reference](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_expr.html#operators_and_parse_affecting_attributes).\nThe SQL readers now use a dialect-specific precedence parser. Unary minus,\ncomparison/equality levels, mixed-case keywords and explicit groups compose\nwith the existing selection reader; both SQL writers group negation explicitly.\n\nNative execution also exposed two Python emission faults. A nested boolean\ncomparison must be parenthesized so Python does not interpret it as a chained\ncomparison, and a negated comparison used as another comparison's operand\nneeds grouping. Both shared Python writers now retain those boundaries. The\n[Python expression reference](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#comparisons)\ndefines the chaining behavior. These changes preserve operation trees; they do\nnot infer SQL NULL behavior from host-language booleans.\n\n`examples/queries/negation.json` contains 23 finite predicates over nine integer\nrows. `node experiments/issue-16-sql-negation.mjs --before` substitutes the old\nSQL reader at `175f50f`: 16 cases disagree with native SQLite. The independent\n`--before-writer` mode substitutes only the old shared writer: four cases\nproduce a different Python result or invalid Python syntax. The current path\nhas zero failures. `examples/queries/verify-native.mjs` executes all 23 predicates\nin SQLite, Python, Node and generated C#; all results agree. The verifier's\nadditional queries use an independent range name to avoid collisions with its\nseparately generated shadowing example.\n\nMatching JavaScript/Rust tests check the NOT operation tree and all predicates\nthrough SQL, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C#, English and Russian. The arguments must either both be numbers, or one argument must be an integer and the other must be a sequence. In the former case, the numbers are converted to a common real type and then multiplied together. In the latter case, sequence repetition is performed; a negative repetition factor yields an empty sequence.\\n\\nThis operation can be customized using the special __mul__() and __rmul__() methods.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.14: If only one operand is a complex number, the other operand is converted to a floating-point number.\\n\\nThe @ (at) operator is intended to be used for matrix multiplication. The numeric arguments are first converted to a common type. Division of integers yields a float, while floor division of integers results in an integer; the result is that of mathematical division with the ‘floor’ function applied to the result. The floor division operation can be customized using the special __floordiv__() and __rfloordiv__() methods.\\n\\nThe % (modulo) operator yields the remainder from the division of the first argument by the second. The numeric arguments are first converted to a common type. A zero right argument raises the ZeroDivisionError exception. The arguments may be floating-point numbers, e.g., 3.14%0.7 equals 0.34 (since 3.14 equals 4*0.7 + 0.34.) The modulo operator always yields a result with the same sign as its second operand (or zero); the absolute value of the result is strictly smaller than the absolute value of the second operand [1].\\n\\nThe floor division and modulo operators are connected by the following identity: x == (x//y)*y + (x%y). Floor division and modulo are also connected with the built-in function divmod(): divmod(x, y) == (x//y, x%y). [2].\\n\\nIn addition to performing the modulo operation on numbers, the % operator is also overloaded by string objects to perform old-style string formatting (also known as interpolation). Perl `int(...)`, PHP 5's\ninteger cast and other wrapper writers shared the same fault. The shared\nJavaScript and Rust emitters calculated correctly grouped operand strings, then\nrecomputed both operands at the lowest precedence when adding the wrapper.\n\nBoth engines now reuse the division's grouped operands inside its wrapper.\nAdditive numerators/denominators, multiplicative denominators, nested quotients\nand negation keep their operation trees. Function-call and method division\nspellings retain their existing argument boundaries.\n\nThe [ECMAScript multiplicative grammar](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/ecmascript-language-expressions.html#sec-multiplicative-operators)\nplaces multiplication/division above additive expressions;\n[Math.trunc](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/numbers-and-dates.html#sec-math.trunc)\nthen truncates the resulting quotient toward zero. Perl's\n[int reference](https://perldoc.perl.org/functions/int) specifies truncation toward\nzero and documents floating-point limitations.
